Bayesian Inference and Learning in Gaussian Process State-Space Models with Particle MCMC

This paper presents a novel framework for Bayesian inference and learning in Gaussian Process State-Space Models (GP-SSMs) using Particle Markov Chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC) methods. GP-SSMs provide a flexible class of nonparametric models for dynamical systems, where Gaussian processes are used to describe the transition dynamics and/or observation functions. Despite their theoretical appeal, inference in GP-SSMs remains challenging due to the analytically intractable posterior distributions that arise from the nonlinear dynamics and the potentially high-dimensional latent state space. We address these challenges by developing efficient PMCMC algorithms that combine the strengths of sequential Monte Carlo methods for state inference with MCMC techniques for hyperparameter learning. Our approach enables fully Bayesian treatment of both the latent states and model hyperparameters, providing uncertainty quantification across all aspects of the model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods on synthetic and real-world time series datasets, showing improved performance compared to existing variational and sampling-based approaches. The proposed framework offers a principled solution to learning complex dynamical systems with limited prior knowledge about the underlying dynamics, with applications ranging from robotics and control to econometrics and computational neuroscience.

Addressing Visual Search in Open and Closed Set Settings

Visual search systems face fundamentally different challenges when operating in closed set environments, where all query objects exist within a predefined database, versus open set scenarios, where novel objects may be encountered. This paper presents a unified framework that effectively addresses both settings while maintaining robust performance. Our approach leveres a dual-branch architecture that combines discriminative embedding learning for closed set retrieval with a generative component that handles open set scenarios through semantic feature modeling. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in closed set retrieval while significantly outperforming existing approaches when confronted with previously unseen objects. We further analyze the trade-offs between retrieval accuracy and computational efficiency, providing practical guidelines for deploying visual search systems across diverse real-world applications. Our work bridges an important gap in visual search technology by offering a single solution adaptable to varying degrees of domain openness without requiring prior knowledge about the operational setting.

Understanding Higher-order Structures in Evolving Graphs: A Simplicial Complex based Kernel Estimation Approach

This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing higher-order structures in dynamic networks through the lens of simplicial complexes and kernel methods. While traditional graph analysis focuses primarily on pairwise interactions (edges), many complex systems exhibit meaningful multi-way relationships that cannot be captured by conventional approaches. We propose a simplicial complex representation that encodes these higher-order interactions and develop kernel estimators to track their evolution over time. Our method leverages persistent homology to identify topological features across different scales and employs specialized kernel functions that respect the geometric constraints of simplicial data. Through theoretical analysis, we establish consistency and convergence properties of our estimators under mild assumptions on the underlying graph processes. Empirical evaluation on both synthetic and real-world temporal networks—including collaboration networks, protein interactions, and social media data—demonstrates that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in detecting structural changes, predicting emerging patterns, and identifying functionally important higher-order structures. The framework provides new insights into the organization and dynamics of complex systems while maintaining computational tractability for large-scale evolving networks.

Grid R-CNN Plus: Faster and Better

We present Grid R-CNN Plus, an enhanced framework for object detection that builds upon the Grid R-CNN architecture with significant improvements in both speed and accuracy. Our approach refines the grid guided localization mechanism by introducing an adaptive grid point selection strategy that focuses computational resources on the most informative regions. We propose a lightweight feature alignment module that efficiently extracts and integrates spatial information, reducing computational overhead while improving boundary localization. Additionally, we incorporate a novel loss function that better handles objects of varying scales and aspect ratios. Extensive experiments on the COCO dataset demonstrate that Grid R-CNN Plus achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing its predecessor by 2.2% in AP while reducing inference time by 30%. The improvements are particularly notable for small objects and objects with occlusion. Our method maintains compatibility with various backbone networks and can be integrated into existing detection pipelines with minimal modifications, offering a practical solution for real-world applications requiring both accuracy and efficiency.

PBP-Net: Point Projection and Back-Projection Network for 3D Point Cloud Segmentation

This paper introduces PBP-Net, a novel deep learning architecture for 3D point cloud segmentation that leverages an efficient point projection and back-projection mechanism. 3D point cloud segmentation remains challenging due to the irregular structure of point clouds, varying point densities, and complex spatial relationships. Our proposed PBP-Net addresses these challenges by first projecting 3D points into optimized 2D representations that preserve geometric relationships, then applying powerful 2D convolutional operations in the projected space, and finally back-projecting the learned features to the original 3D space for fine-grained segmentation. This projection-based approach enables the network to exploit the efficiency of 2D convolutions while maintaining the critical spatial information of the original point cloud. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including S3DIS, ScanNet, and ShapeNet-Part demonstrate that PBP-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance with lower computational complexity compared to existing methods. Our approach shows particular strength in handling large-scale point clouds with varying densities, achieving a 3.2% improvement in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) over previous methods. The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate further research in 3D point cloud analysis.

Pure Exploration and Regret Minimization in Matching Bandits

This paper investigates the challenging problem of matching bandits, where a decision-maker must iteratively select a maximum-weight matching in a bipartite graph with initially unknown edge weights. We study this problem from two complementary perspectives: pure exploration, where the goal is to identify the optimal matching with high confidence using minimal samples, and regret minimization, where the objective is to maximize cumulative rewards over time. For the pure exploration setting, we develop a novel algorithm that adaptively samples edges based on confidence bounds and eliminates suboptimal matchings, achieving sample complexity that depends logarithmically on the confidence parameter and scales with the gap between optimal and suboptimal matchings. In the regret minimization framework, we propose an upper confidence bound (UCB) based approach that balances exploration and exploitation, establishing an O(√T log T) regret bound where T is the time horizon. Our theoretical analysis reveals interesting structural properties of the matching bandit problem, highlighting the interplay between combinatorial optimization and sequential decision-making. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our algorithms significantly outperform existing approaches across various problem instances. These results advance our understanding of complex combinatorial bandit problems and offer practical tools for applications in online marketplaces, resource allocation, and recommendation systems.

InterpretML: A Unified Framework for Machine Learning Interpretability

As machine learning models increasingly influence critical decision-making processes across domains, the need for interpretability has become paramount. This paper introduces InterpretML, a comprehensive open-source framework designed to address the interpretability challenges in modern machine learning systems. The framework unifies diverse approaches to model explanation, offering both intrinsically interpretable models and post-hoc explanation methods for black-box systems. InterpretML implements state-of-the-art techniques including SHAP values, LIME, GAMs with shape functions, decision trees, and counterfactual explanations within a consistent API, enabling practitioners to seamlessly compare multiple interpretation strategies. Our framework supports local explanations for individual predictions and global explanations for overall model behavior, with visualization tools that make complex model dynamics accessible to both technical and non-technical stakeholders. Through extensive empirical evaluation across diverse datasets and model types, we demonstrate InterpretML's effectiveness in providing accurate, consistent, and actionable insights while maintaining competitive predictive performance. The framework addresses critical interpretability needs in regulated industries, scientific research, and high-stakes decision contexts, ultimately advancing the field toward more transparent and accountable machine learning.

DAM: Deliberation, Abandon and Memory Networks for Generating Detailed and Non-repetitive Responses in Visual Dialogue

Visual dialogue systems that can engage in meaningful conversations about images face significant challenges in generating detailed, coherent, and non-repetitive responses. This paper introduces DAM (Deliberation, Abandon and Memory Networks), a novel framework that enhances response generation in visual dialogue through three key mechanisms. The Deliberation module enables the model to carefully consider multiple potential response paths before committing to an answer, improving response accuracy and relevance. The Abandon mechanism identifies and discards low-quality response candidates during generation, reducing the likelihood of producing generic or irrelevant content. Finally, our Memory Networks component maintains a comprehensive dialogue history, allowing the model to avoid repetition while maintaining conversational coherence across multiple turns. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that DAM significantly outperforms existing approaches across multiple metrics, including response diversity, detail richness, and human preference ratings. Our qualitative analysis further reveals that DAM generates responses that are not only more informative about visual content but also more engaging from a human perspective. This work represents an important step toward more natural and effective visual dialogue systems.

Image Captioning with Compositional Neural Module Networks

This paper introduces a novel approach to image captioning using Compositional Neural Module Networks (CNMNs). We address the limitations of traditional end-to-end captioning models by decomposing the captioning task into specialized sub-tasks handled by distinct neural modules. Our CNMN architecture dynamically assembles these modules based on the visual content, enabling more interpretable and accurate caption generation. The modules are designed to perform specific functions such as object detection, attribute recognition, relationship modeling, and language generation, working together in a compositional framework. Experiments on benchmark datasets including MSCOCO and Flickr30k demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics (BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr) and human evaluations. Furthermore, the modular nature of our system provides enhanced explainability, allowing for better understanding of the caption generation process. We also show that our model exhibits improved generalization to novel object combinations and rare visual concepts, addressing a key challenge in image captioning systems.

Guiding Global Placement With Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a novel approach to electronic design automation (EDA) by applying reinforcement learning (RL) techniques to the global placement problem in integrated circuit design. Global placement, a critical step in physical design that determines the initial positions of circuit components, traditionally relies on analytical methods that often struggle with complex modern designs. Our framework formulates placement as a sequential decision-making process where an RL agent learns to make incremental placement decisions that optimize for wirelength, congestion, and timing objectives simultaneously. Through extensive experimentation on industry-standard benchmarks including ISPD and ICCAD contest circuits, our approach demonstrates significant improvements over state-of-the-art analytical placers, achieving 18% reduction in wirelength, 24% reduction in congestion, and 15% improvement in timing closure. The RL agent effectively captures the intricate interdependencies between placement decisions and their long-term impact on design quality metrics. Furthermore, our method shows remarkable adaptability to different technology nodes and design constraints without requiring manual parameter tuning. This work establishes a promising direction for incorporating machine learning techniques into EDA workflows to address the growing complexity of modern chip design challenges.

Deep Reinforcement Learning Methods for Structure-Guided Processing Path Optimization

This paper presents a novel approach to processing path optimization that leverages deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques informed by structural characteristics of the target domain. Traditional path optimization methods often rely on heuristics or geometric approaches that fail to account for complex material properties and structural constraints. Our framework integrates domain-specific structural information directly into the learning process, enabling the DRL agent to discover processing paths that optimize for both efficiency and quality outcomes. We develop a custom state representation that encodes local and global structural features, coupled with a reward function that balances processing time, energy consumption, and structural integrity. Experiments across multiple manufacturing scenarios—including CNC machining, 3D printing, and composite layup processes—demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms conventional methods by 18-27% in processing time while maintaining or improving quality metrics. The framework exhibits strong generalization capabilities to unseen geometries and adaptability to changing process conditions. This research establishes a promising direction for structure-aware manufacturing optimization that can significantly impact production efficiency in advanced manufacturing environments.

A Robust 3D-2D Interactive Tool for Scene Segmentation and Annotation

This paper presents a novel interactive tool that seamlessly integrates 3D and 2D approaches for efficient scene segmentation and annotation. Despite recent advances in computer vision, creating high-quality labeled datasets for complex 3D scenes remains labor-intensive and time-consuming. Our system addresses this challenge through a robust framework that allows users to leverage the complementary strengths of both 3D geometric data and 2D image features. The tool employs an intuitive interface where annotations made in either domain are automatically propagated to the other, significantly reducing manual effort. We introduce a new algorithm that maintains consistency between the 3D point cloud and corresponding 2D image projections while handling occlusions and varying levels of detail. Experiments demonstrate that our approach reduces annotation time by 47% compared to purely 2D or 3D methods while achieving 93.5% agreement with ground truth labels. User studies with both expert and novice annotators confirm the tool's effectiveness across various indoor and outdoor scenes. Our contribution enables more efficient creation of high-quality training data for machine learning applications in robotics, autonomous navigation, and augmented reality.

Partially Shared Semi-supervised Deep Matrix Factorization with Multi-view Data

This paper introduces a novel approach to matrix factorization that effectively handles multi-view data in semi-supervised learning scenarios. Our Partially Shared Semi-supervised Deep Matrix Factorization (PS-SDMF) model leverages the complementary information from multiple data views while addressing the challenges of incomplete labeling and heterogeneous data structures. The proposed framework employs a deep architecture that factorizes data matrices into shared and view-specific latent components, allowing for both common patterns across views and unique characteristics within individual views to be captured. By incorporating a semi-supervised learning mechanism, our method efficiently utilizes both labeled and unlabeled samples to enhance representation learning. Extensive experiments on benchmark multi-view datasets demonstrate that PS-SDMF significantly outperforms state-of-the-art matrix factorization and multi-view learning approaches, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. Our model shows improved performance in clustering, classification, and retrieval tasks while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis on the convergence properties and representation capacity of the proposed framework, establishing its solid foundation for multi-view data analysis.

Learning to Imagine Manipulation Goals for Robot Task Planning

Effective task planning for robotic manipulation requires the ability to imagine feasible goal states that satisfy task objectives. In this paper, we present a novel learning-based approach that enables robots to generate realistic and achievable manipulation goals for complex tasks. Our framework, which we call Imagination-Augmented Planning (IAP), combines deep generative models with task-oriented constraints to synthesize goal states that guide subsequent motion planning. The system learns from demonstrations to capture the distribution of valid goal configurations across various manipulation scenarios. We train our model on a diverse dataset of successful manipulation episodes, enabling it to generalize to novel objects and task variations. Experimental results demonstrate that IAP significantly improves planning success rates and efficiency compared to traditional approaches that rely on predefined goal templates or random sampling. In ablation studies, we show that incorporating physical feasibility constraints and task-specific priors into the generative process is crucial for producing actionable goals. Our approach bridges the gap between high-level task specifications and low-level motion planning, enabling robots to autonomously determine how to configure objects to accomplish specified tasks without exhaustive search or human guidance.

Training Spiking Neural Networks Using Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a novel approach to training spiking neural networks (SNNs) using reinforcement learning (RL) techniques. SNNs, which more closely mimic biological neural networks through discrete spike events rather than continuous activations, have shown promise for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing but remain challenging to train with traditional gradient-based methods. We propose a framework that leverages policy gradient methods to optimize SNN parameters by treating spike patterns as actions and network performance as rewards. Our approach circumvents the non-differentiability problem inherent in spike-based computation while enabling the networks to learn complex temporal patterns. Experimental results across several benchmark tasks demonstrate that RL-trained SNNs achieve comparable accuracy to backpropagation-trained artificial neural networks while maintaining the energy efficiency advantages of spike-based computation. Additionally, we show that this training methodology enables SNNs to solve tasks requiring precise timing-based information processing, which are difficult to address with conventional neural networks. This work bridges reinforcement learning and neuromorphic computing, offering new possibilities for training brain-inspired computing systems.

On Generation of Adversarial Examples using Convex Programming

This paper introduces a novel framework for generating adversarial examples in deep neural networks through convex programming techniques. We formulate the adversarial example generation problem as a constrained optimization task and develop efficient convex relaxations that provide theoretical guarantees on the minimal perturbations required to cause misclassification. Unlike existing methods that rely on gradient-based heuristics, our approach leverages convex optimization theory to systematically explore the decision boundaries of neural networks. We demonstrate that the proposed method can generate adversarial examples with significantly smaller perturbations compared to state-of-the-art techniques across multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we establish formal bounds on the robustness of neural networks against our adversarial attacks and analyze the transferability of these examples across different model architectures. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of our approach and provide insights into the fundamental vulnerability of deep learning models. Our convex programming framework not only advances the understanding of adversarial examples but also offers a principled approach for evaluating and enhancing the robustness of neural networks in security-critical applications.

Neural Motifs: Scene Graph Parsing with Global Context

Scene graph parsing, the task of extracting objects and their relationships from images, remains a significant challenge in computer vision due to the complex interplay between visual elements and their semantic connections. In this paper, we present Neural Motifs, a novel framework that leverages global contextual reasoning to improve scene graph generation. Our approach is motivated by the observation that objects and their relationships in visual scenes follow statistical patterns—or motifs—that can be exploited to enhance prediction accuracy. Unlike previous methods that process objects and relationships in isolation, Neural Motifs employs a bidirectional LSTM architecture to capture higher-order dependencies across the entire scene. Through this global context modeling, our system effectively learns common visual patterns and semantic regularities that constrain the space of likely interpretations. We evaluate our approach on the challenging Visual Genome dataset, demonstrating substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods across multiple scene graph prediction tasks, including predicate classification, scene graph classification, and scene graph generation. Further analysis reveals that Neural Motifs successfully captures meaningful statistical biases present in visual relationships, providing both improved performance and better interpretability of the scene parsing process. Our work highlights the importance of global contextual reasoning in understanding complex visual scenes.

6D Object Pose Estimation with Depth Images: A Seamless Approach for Robotic Interaction and Augmented Reality

This paper presents a novel approach for accurate 6D object pose estimation using depth image data, with applications spanning both robotic manipulation and augmented reality environments. Our method integrates deep learning techniques with geometric reasoning to achieve robust pose estimation across varying lighting conditions, occlusions, and complex scene arrangements. The proposed architecture employs a two-stage pipeline: first detecting object instances via a modified point cloud segmentation network, then refining pose estimates through an iterative registration process that leverages both local and global geometric features. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (YCB-Video, LineMOD) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, achieving mean average precision of 93.7% and average translation error of 0.92cm. We further validate our approach in real-world scenarios, implementing the system on robotic manipulation tasks and AR applications, where it maintains real-time performance (24fps) on consumer hardware. The seamless integration between virtual and physical environments enables new possibilities for human-robot collaboration and immersive mixed-reality experiences. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available to facilitate further research in this domain.

Lasso Guarantees for Time Series Estimation Under Subgaussian Tails and $\beta$-Mixing

This paper establishes novel theoretical guarantees for Lasso estimation in time series models under minimal assumptions. We consider high-dimensional settings where the number of parameters may exceed the sample size, but the true model exhibits sparsity. Our analysis focuses on dependent data satisfying two key conditions: subgaussian tail behavior and $\beta$-mixing temporal dependence structure. We derive non-asymptotic bounds on the estimation error that explicitly account for the mixing coefficients, demonstrating how the rate of decay in temporal dependence affects estimation accuracy. Our results show that under geometric $\beta$-mixing, the Lasso estimator achieves nearly the same convergence rates as in the independent case, up to logarithmic factors, while polynomial mixing rates incur additional penalties. We establish both $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ error bounds and provide sufficient conditions for model selection consistency. Numerical simulations and an empirical application to financial time series data validate our theoretical findings, showing the practical relevance of our guarantees in realistic settings where both non-Gaussian tails and temporal dependence are present. Our work extends the applicability of Lasso methods to a broader class of time series models than previously established in the literature.

Learning Generalizable Physiological Representations from Large-scale Wearable Data

The proliferation of consumer wearable devices has created unprecedented opportunities to monitor human physiological signals continuously in real-world settings. However, extracting meaningful and generalizable representations from these heterogeneous, noisy, and often incomplete datasets remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we present a novel deep learning framework for learning robust physiological representations from large-scale wearable sensor data. Our approach leverages self-supervised learning techniques to extract latent representations from multimodal physiological signals (heart rate, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and accelerometry) collected from over 10,000 participants during daily activities. We demonstrate that these learned representations capture fundamental physiological patterns that generalize across different demographic groups, behavioral contexts, and downstream health prediction tasks. Through extensive experiments, we show that our pre-trained representations significantly outperform traditional feature engineering approaches and task-specific models, particularly in low-data regimes and when transferring to previously unseen populations. Additionally, we identify interpretable physiological patterns within the learned embedding space that correspond to known biometric responses. Our work establishes a foundation for developing more personalized, robust, and generalizable health monitoring systems using ubiquitous wearable technology.

Zoom, Enhance! Measuring Surveillance GAN Up-sampling

This study investigates the capabilities and limitations of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for enhancing low-resolution surveillance footage. While popular media often portrays unrealistic "enhance" capabilities, recent advances in deep learning have made significant progress in image super-resolution. We evaluate several state-of-the-art GAN architectures specifically optimized for surveillance footage up-sampling across diverse real-world datasets. Our quantitative analysis measures both objective metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) and human perception studies to determine the reliability of enhanced details for identification purposes. Results indicate that while GANs produce visually convincing up-sampled images with up to 4× resolution enhancement, they frequently hallucinate plausible but potentially inaccurate details in critical identification features. We further analyze the legal and ethical implications of using such technology in forensic contexts, highlighting the need for confidence metrics and appropriate guidelines for admissibility in investigations. This work provides a comprehensive benchmark for surveillance image enhancement capabilities and establishes practical boundaries for their application in security and law enforcement scenarios.

Probabilistic Color Constancy

This paper presents a novel probabilistic framework for addressing the color constancy problem in computer vision. Rather than producing a single point estimate of the illuminant color, our approach generates a complete probability distribution over possible illuminants, thereby capturing the inherent uncertainty in this ill-posed problem. We formulate color constancy as Bayesian inference, incorporating both statistical priors derived from natural image statistics and contextual scene information. Our framework unifies existing computational color constancy algorithms within a single probabilistic model while providing principled mechanisms for integrating multiple estimation techniques. Experiments conducted on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our probabilistic approach not only achieves state-of-the-art performance in illuminant estimation accuracy but also provides meaningful confidence measures that correlate strongly with actual error rates. Furthermore, we show how these uncertainty estimates can be propagated to downstream computer vision tasks, improving robustness in applications such as object recognition and scene categorization under varying illumination conditions. The proposed framework offers new insights into the fundamental limitations of color constancy algorithms and suggests promising directions for adaptive illuminant estimation strategies.

Learning Shape Features and Abstractions in 3D Convolutional Neural Networks for Detecting Alzheimer's Disease

This study investigates the capability of 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn and utilize morphological features from structural brain MRI for early detection of Alzheimer's disease (AD). While traditional approaches rely on predefined volumetric biomarkers, our work explores how deep learning architectures can autonomously identify subtle shape deformations and structural patterns associated with AD pathology. We developed a specialized 3D CNN architecture incorporating shape-aware attention mechanisms and geometric feature extraction pathways to better capture hippocampal atrophy, ventricular enlargement, and cortical thinning. Using a dataset of 1,200 T1-weighted MRI scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), our model achieved 92.7% accuracy in distinguishing AD patients from healthy controls and 86.3% accuracy in identifying mild cognitive impairment likely to progress to AD within 24 months. Visualization techniques revealed that the network learned hierarchical shape abstractions, focusing on clinically relevant regions without explicit annotation. Importantly, our approach demonstrated superior performance compared to volumetric biomarker-based methods, particularly in early-stage detection. These findings suggest that 3D CNNs can effectively learn shape-based representations that capture the complex structural changes in AD progression, potentially enabling earlier and more accurate diagnosis.

Developing a Recommendation Benchmark for MLPerf Training and Inference

This paper presents the development and implementation of a comprehensive recommendation system benchmark for MLPerf, addressing the critical need for standardized performance evaluation in this widely deployed machine learning domain. We introduce a novel benchmark design that captures the complex computational patterns of modern recommendation models while maintaining practicality for industry-wide adoption. Our benchmark encompasses both training and inference scenarios, with carefully calibrated metrics that reflect real-world deployment constraints including latency requirements, memory limitations, and accuracy targets. Through extensive collaboration with industry stakeholders, we developed reference implementations across multiple frameworks and hardware platforms, enabling fair comparisons between diverse systems. Experimental results demonstrate the benchmark's ability to effectively differentiate system performance characteristics across various architectures, from cloud-scale deployments to edge devices. The benchmark also incorporates representative datasets and workloads derived from production environments while preserving user privacy. This work represents a significant contribution to the MLPerf suite, providing the ML systems community with a robust tool for evaluating and optimizing recommendation system performance, which accounts for a substantial portion of machine learning inference cycles in industry today.

Fast classification using sparse decision DAGs

This paper introduces a novel approach to classification problems using sparse decision directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). While traditional decision trees offer interpretability but often suffer from limited accuracy, and ensemble methods provide improved performance at the cost of increased computational complexity, our proposed sparse decision DAG framework achieves an optimal balance between accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency. By allowing nodes to have multiple parents while maintaining a directed acyclic structure, decision DAGs can represent more complex decision boundaries than trees while requiring fewer nodes. We present an efficient algorithm for learning these sparse structures that employs regularization techniques to prevent overfitting and encourage feature reuse across decision paths. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable accuracy to ensemble methods while requiring significantly less computation time during inference—a critical advantage for resource-constrained or real-time applications. Furthermore, the sparse nature of the resulting models facilitates visualization and interpretation of the decision process. Our work provides both theoretical guarantees on the expressiveness of sparse decision DAGs and practical guidelines for their implementation in various classification tasks.

Learning Dynamic and Personalized Comorbidity Networks from Event Data using Deep Diffusion Processes

Understanding the complex relationships between medical conditions as they evolve over time and vary across individuals remains a significant challenge in healthcare analytics. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages deep diffusion processes to learn dynamic and personalized comorbidity networks from longitudinal electronic health records. Our approach models the temporal progression of diseases as a continuous-time stochastic process, where the diffusion of medical conditions through a patient-specific network captures the underlying comorbidity relationships. By combining recurrent neural networks with graph neural networks, we develop a deep learning architecture that can simultaneously infer the latent comorbidity structure and predict future disease trajectories. The model incorporates patient-specific attributes to personalize the comorbidity networks, allowing for heterogeneity across different demographic groups and clinical profiles. Experiments on large-scale healthcare datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in disease prediction tasks while providing interpretable insights into how comorbidities develop and interact over time. The learned dynamic networks reveal temporal patterns in disease progression that static models fail to capture, offering potential for improved risk stratification and personalized care planning. Our work contributes a powerful computational framework for analyzing complex temporal event data in healthcare, with implications for clinical decision support and population health management.

Abstract

This paper presents a novel approach to fish recognition by integrating robust feature selection, image segmentation, and geometrical parameter techniques with Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Decision Tree classifiers. The proposed method addresses the challenges of fish species identification in varying underwater environments through a multi-stage process. Initially, fish images undergo preprocessing to reduce noise and enhance quality, followed by segmentation using an adaptive threshold-based algorithm to isolate fish from complex backgrounds. A comprehensive set of features is extracted, including shape descriptors, texture patterns, and color distributions, from which the most discriminative features are selected using correlation-based feature selection and information gain ranking. The geometrical parameters, such as aspect ratio, eccentricity, and morphological measurements, provide species-specific characteristics that improve classification accuracy. Experimental evaluation on a diverse dataset of 1,000 images comprising 20 fish species demonstrates that our hybrid approach achieves 94.7% recognition accuracy, outperforming single-classifier methods. The ANN excels in handling complex feature relationships, while the Decision Tree provides interpretable classification rules. The proposed system shows robustness to variations in illumination, orientation, and partial occlusion, making it suitable for real-world applications in marine biology research, fisheries management, and ecological monitoring.

Auto-GNN: Neural Architecture Search of Graph Neural Networks

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful architectures for learning on graph-structured data, but their design typically relies on manual architecture engineering. This paper introduces Auto-GNN, a comprehensive framework for automated architecture search of graph neural networks. Our approach leverages reinforcement learning to efficiently explore the vast design space of GNN architectures, including various aggregation functions, neighborhood sampling strategies, and layer connectivity patterns. We formulate a flexible search space that encompasses both spatial and spectral GNN variants, allowing for the discovery of novel architectural components beyond standard message-passing paradigms. Extensive experiments across diverse graph benchmarks demonstrate that Auto-GNN consistently discovers architectures that outperform hand-crafted GNN models, achieving state-of-the-art results on node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks. The automatically discovered architectures reveal interesting structural patterns and design principles that challenge conventional wisdom in GNN design. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Auto-GNN requires significantly fewer computational resources compared to prior GNN architecture search methods while producing more efficient models. Our work provides new insights into optimal GNN design and establishes a foundation for the automated discovery of task-specific graph neural architectures.

Representation Sharing for Fast Object Detector Search and Beyond

Neural architecture search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automatically designing efficient object detection models, but its computational demands remain prohibitively expensive for widespread adoption. In this paper, we introduce Representation Sharing NAS (RS-NAS), a novel approach that significantly accelerates detector architecture search by exploiting the redundancy in feature representation computations across candidate architectures. Our key insight is that many candidate detector architectures share common components and intermediate representations during evaluation, which can be cached and reused rather than recomputed. We formalize this insight through a representation sharing graph that identifies and eliminates redundant computations across the search space. Experimental results demonstrate that RS-NAS reduces the computational cost of architecture search by up to 7× while maintaining detection performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. On the COCO dataset, our approach achieves 42.3 mAP with search costs of only 0.8 GPU days. Furthermore, we show that our representation sharing methodology generalizes beyond object detection to other computer vision tasks including instance segmentation and keypoint detection. This work represents a significant step toward making neural architecture search more accessible and practical for real-world applications in computer vision.

Graph Learning Network: A Structure Learning Algorithm

This paper introduces the Graph Learning Network (GLN), a novel approach to structure learning in graph-based representations. The GLN algorithm simultaneously learns both the underlying graph structure and the node representations from complex, relational data. Unlike traditional methods that require predefined graph topologies, our approach dynamically infers edge connections through a differentiable attention mechanism that optimizes for downstream task performance. We formulate structure learning as a joint optimization problem, balancing graph sparsity with representational capacity. Experiments on benchmark datasets from diverse domains including social networks, molecular structures, and citation networks demonstrate that GLN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art graph neural networks with fixed topologies. Our approach shows particular strength in scenarios with noisy or partially observed graph structures, achieving up to 15% improvement in classification accuracy and 23% reduction in reconstruction error. Additionally, the learned graph structures provide interpretable insights into the relational patterns within the data. These results establish GLN as a powerful framework for automatically discovering meaningful graph representations from complex data.

Surveillance Video Parsing with Single Frame Supervision

This paper addresses the challenging problem of surveillance video parsing, which aims to segment video frames into different semantic regions (e.g., person, car, road) for comprehensive scene understanding. While fully supervised approaches require pixel-wise annotations for all frames—an extremely labor-intensive process—we propose a novel weakly supervised learning framework that requires annotations for only a single frame per video. Our approach leverages temporal consistency and spatial context to propagate the semantic information from the labeled frame to the entire video sequence. We introduce a dual-branch network architecture that simultaneously learns from the sparse labeled data and exploits motion cues and appearance similarities across frames. The model incorporates a temporal consistency regularization term that enforces coherent predictions between adjacent frames while allowing for natural scene changes. Extensive experiments on several surveillance video datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves parsing accuracy comparable to fully supervised methods while reducing the annotation cost by orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we show that our method is robust to camera motion and lighting variations, making it particularly suitable for real-world surveillance applications. The proposed single-frame supervision paradigm opens up new possibilities for efficiently parsing large-scale surveillance video data with minimal human annotation effort.

Hybrid modeling of the human cardiovascular system using NeuralFMUs

This paper presents a novel hybrid modeling approach for simulating the human cardiovascular system using Neural Functional Mock-up Units (NeuralFMUs). We combine physics-based modeling with data-driven neural networks to overcome the limitations of traditional cardiovascular models. The physics-based components capture well-understood hemodynamic principles through differential equations, while neural networks learn complex, patient-specific patterns from clinical data. Our approach implements this hybrid framework within the Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI) standard, allowing for modular, interoperable cardiovascular simulations. We validate the NeuralFMU model using both synthetic data and clinical measurements from 50 patients with various cardiovascular conditions. Results demonstrate that our hybrid approach achieves 37% lower prediction error compared to purely physics-based models and requires 65% less training data than fully data-driven approaches. Furthermore, the model maintains physiological consistency even when extrapolating beyond training data ranges—a critical feature for clinical applications. This work establishes a foundation for personalized cardiovascular modeling that balances mechanistic understanding with the flexibility of machine learning, potentially enabling more accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and real-time monitoring in clinical settings.

Time-Series Event Prediction with Evolutionary State Graph

This paper introduces a novel approach to time-series event prediction through the development of Evolutionary State Graphs (ESG). Traditional time-series prediction methods often struggle with capturing complex temporal dependencies and evolving patterns in dynamic systems. Our proposed ESG framework addresses these limitations by constructing a graph-based representation that explicitly models the evolutionary states of temporal data and the transitions between them. The ESG dynamically updates its structure as new data arrives, allowing it to adapt to concept drift and evolving patterns. We formulate event prediction as a path traversal problem on this graph, where future events are predicted by analyzing potential trajectories based on historical state transitions. Our approach incorporates both local temporal dependencies and global structural patterns by leveraging graph neural networks with attention mechanisms to weight the importance of different historical states. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets, including financial transactions, healthcare events, and social media activities, demonstrate that ESG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with an average improvement of 17.3% in prediction accuracy and 22.1% in F1-score. The model shows particular strength in scenarios with irregular sampling intervals and multivariate dependencies, making it applicable to a wide range of real-world time-series event prediction tasks.

High-dimensional Nonlinear Profile Monitoring based on Deep Probabilistic Autoencoders

This paper introduces a novel approach to nonlinear profile monitoring in high-dimensional manufacturing processes using deep probabilistic autoencoders. Traditional profile monitoring methods often struggle with the curse of dimensionality and complex nonlinear relationships in modern manufacturing data. Our proposed framework leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) with a probabilistic latent space to effectively capture the underlying structure of high-dimensional profiles while accounting for uncertainty. The method transforms complex profile data into a lower-dimensional latent representation, enabling efficient anomaly detection through probabilistic distance metrics. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional techniques such as functional principal component analysis and shallow autoencoder networks across several performance metrics. Experiments conducted on both simulated and real manufacturing datasets show that the deep probabilistic framework achieves superior detection rates for subtle process shifts while maintaining low false alarm rates. The proposed method is particularly effective for monitoring complex spatial and temporal profiles in semiconductor manufacturing, automotive assembly, and other advanced manufacturing contexts where traditional approaches fail to capture intricate nonlinear patterns. This research contributes a computationally efficient, interpretable, and robust solution to the challenging problem of monitoring high-dimensional nonlinear profiles in modern manufacturing environments.

DISK: Learning Local Features with Policy Gradient

This paper presents DISK (Deep Interest-based Spatial Keypoints), a novel approach for learning local feature detectors and descriptors using policy gradient reinforcement learning. Unlike traditional handcrafted features or supervised learning methods, DISK frames the feature detection problem as a sequential decision-making process where the model learns to identify keypoints that maximize downstream matching performance. Our reinforcement learning framework enables end-to-end optimization without requiring ground truth keypoint annotations, instead using matching quality as a reward signal. The policy network learns to select discriminative keypoints while the descriptor network extracts robust feature representations that are invariant to viewpoint changes, illumination differences, and other image transformations. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including HPatches, KITTI, and ETH demonstrate that DISK outperforms state-of-the-art methods in image matching, homography estimation, and visual localization tasks. Our approach shows particular strength in challenging scenarios with significant viewpoint changes and low-texture regions. The code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this direction.

Bi-GANs-ST for Perceptual Image Super-resolution

This paper presents Bi-GANs-ST, a novel bidirectional generative adversarial network framework with spatial-temporal constraints for perceptual image super-resolution. Unlike conventional approaches that focus solely on minimizing pixel-wise errors, our method emphasizes the generation of visually pleasing high-resolution images that preserve perceptual quality. The bidirectional architecture employs two complementary GANs—one operating in the low-to-high resolution direction and the other in the high-to-low resolution direction—creating a cycle-consistency that significantly improves fidelity and stability during training. We incorporate spatial-temporal constraints that exploit both local spatial relationships and temporal coherence across feature spaces, enabling the model to generate fine-grained textures while maintaining structural integrity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that Bi-GANs-ST outperforms state-of-the-art methods in perceptual metrics, achieving superior visual quality with realistic details while maintaining competitive PSNR and SSIM scores. Our approach bridges the gap between perceptually realistic super-resolution and mathematical fidelity, offering a promising direction for real-world applications in computer vision and graphics.

Communication-efficient distributed SGD with Sketching

Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a fundamental optimization method for training large-scale machine learning models across multiple computing nodes. However, the communication overhead of gradient exchanges between workers remains a significant bottleneck in distributed training systems. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that integrates gradient sketching techniques into distributed SGD to substantially reduce communication costs while maintaining convergence guarantees. Our method employs randomized dimensionality reduction to compress gradient information before transmission, allowing for efficient communication without significant loss in statistical accuracy. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that our approach achieves a favorable trade-off between communication efficiency and convergence rate. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets show that our sketching-based method reduces communication volume by up to 95% compared to standard distributed SGD, with minimal impact on model quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach scales effectively with increasing numbers of workers and is robust across various network conditions. These results suggest that gradient sketching offers a promising direction for enabling more efficient distributed training of machine learning models in communication-constrained environments.

Stepwise Regression for Unsupervised Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to unsupervised learning through the adaptation of stepwise regression techniques. While stepwise regression has traditionally been confined to supervised learning contexts, we demonstrate how its iterative feature selection principles can be effectively repurposed for unsupervised dimensionality reduction and pattern discovery. Our method, Stepwise Regression for Unsupervised Learning (SRUL), iteratively identifies latent structures in unlabeled data by treating each feature as a potential dependent variable and remaining features as predictors. Through a bidirectional elimination process, SRUL constructs an optimal feature subset that captures the inherent relationships within the data. Experimental results on diverse datasets show that SRUL outperforms traditional unsupervised methods like PCA and t-SNE in preserving cluster structures and identifying meaningful feature relationships. Additionally, SRUL offers enhanced interpretability compared to black-box approaches, making it particularly valuable in exploratory data analysis contexts. The computational efficiency and statistical foundations of our approach make it a promising addition to the unsupervised learning toolkit, especially for high-dimensional datasets where understanding feature interactions is crucial.

Classification with Abstention but Without Disparities

In high-stakes decision-making environments, classification systems that can abstain from making predictions under uncertainty are increasingly valuable. However, the interaction between abstention mechanisms and fairness considerations remains understudied. This paper investigates how to design classification systems with abstention capabilities while ensuring that disparities across demographic groups are minimized or eliminated. We formalize the problem of fair classification with abstention and propose a framework that optimizes the trade-off between accuracy, abstention rates, and fairness metrics. Our approach introduces a novel constrained optimization formulation that allows the classifier to selectively abstain from making predictions when confidence is low, while maintaining similar abstention and error rates across protected groups. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our method achieves Pareto-optimal solutions with respect to accuracy and fairness objectives. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets from healthcare, criminal justice, and financial domains show that our approach significantly reduces demographic disparities compared to existing abstention methods while maintaining competitive overall performance. We also provide practical guidelines for implementing fair abstention policies in various application contexts where both uncertainty awareness and fairness are essential requirements.

Spatial-Temporal Block and LSTM Network for Pedestrian Trajectories Prediction

This paper introduces a novel deep learning architecture that combines spatial-temporal blocks with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for accurate prediction of pedestrian trajectories in crowded environments. Our approach addresses the challenges of modeling both spatial interactions between multiple pedestrians and the temporal dependencies in movement patterns. The proposed framework consists of spatial-temporal blocks that extract relevant features from pedestrian positions and velocities across consecutive frames, followed by LSTM layers that capture long-term dependencies in movement sequences. We evaluate our model on standard pedestrian trajectory datasets including ETH and UCY, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods with average displacement error reduced by 18.2% and final displacement error reduced by 21.5%. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the spatial-temporal block design in capturing social interactions between pedestrians. The proposed architecture maintains computational efficiency while providing more accurate trajectory predictions, making it suitable for real-time applications in autonomous vehicles, surveillance systems, and social robots.

Gated-SCNN: Gated Shape CNNs for Semantic Segmentation

This paper introduces Gated Shape CNNs (Gated-SCNN), a novel architecture for semantic segmentation that explicitly leverages boundary information to improve feature representation and segmentation accuracy. Unlike conventional approaches that process semantic information as a single pathway, our two-stream architecture disentangles shape processing from texture-based recognition, allowing for specialized feature extraction. The shape stream, regulated by a learnable gating mechanism, focuses exclusively on boundary detection and shape information while remaining resistant to appearance variations. Through this gating mechanism, the two streams exchange complementary information, with the shape stream providing structural cues to refine the semantic predictions. We propose a new loss function that encourages consistency between semantic boundaries and the predicted shape information, further enhancing boundary localization. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and COCO-Stuff datasets demonstrate that Gated-SCNN achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly significant improvements in boundary regions and thin structures while maintaining computational efficiency. Our approach shows that explicit shape processing is beneficial for semantic segmentation tasks, especially in complex urban scenes with multiple object categories.

Empirical Upper Bound, Error Diagnosis and Invariance Analysis of Modern Object Detectors

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of modern object detection frameworks to establish performance boundaries, diagnose error sources, and evaluate invariance properties. We systematically investigate state-of-the-art object detectors across diverse datasets to empirically determine upper-bound performance limits under ideal conditions. Through a novel error taxonomy, we decompose detection failures into distinct categories—localization errors, classification confusions, missed detections, and false positives—revealing that localization precision remains the primary bottleneck in current architectures. Our invariance analysis quantifies detector robustness against common image transformations including rotation, scale, illumination, and occlusion, demonstrating significant vulnerability to viewpoint changes across all evaluated models. Additionally, we propose a diagnostic benchmark that isolates specific challenging scenarios to guide future research. Our findings indicate that despite impressive progress, modern detectors still fall substantially short of theoretical performance ceilings, with an estimated 15-20% improvement potential before architectural redesign becomes necessary. This work provides valuable insights for the research community by identifying critical limitations and suggesting targeted approaches for advancing object detection capabilities.

RaWaNet: Enriching Graph Neural Network Input via Random Walks on Graphs

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various graph-based learning tasks, but their effectiveness is often limited by the local neighborhood aggregation paradigm, which struggles to capture long-range dependencies and global structural information. In this paper, we introduce RaWaNet, a novel framework that enhances GNN input representations through random walk-based graph augmentation. Our approach systematically samples random walks of varying lengths to extract multi-scale structural patterns and integrates this information into node feature representations before standard GNN processing. By encoding both local connectivity and global graph topology, RaWaNet creates enriched initial representations that help overcome the limitations of traditional message-passing GNNs. We conduct extensive experiments across diverse benchmark datasets, including citation networks, social networks, and molecular graphs. Results demonstrate that RaWaNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN architectures on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks, with particularly significant improvements on graphs with complex structures and long-range dependencies. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm that the random walk augmentation provides complementary information to existing GNN mechanisms rather than merely increasing model capacity. RaWaNet offers a conceptually simple yet effective approach to enhance GNN performance without requiring architectural modifications to the underlying neural network.

Learn molecular representations from large-scale unlabeled molecules for drug discovery

Developing effective molecular representations is a critical challenge in computational drug discovery. In this work, we present a novel self-supervised learning approach that leverages large-scale unlabeled molecular data to generate robust and transferable molecular representations. Our method, MolRep, employs a contrastive learning framework to capture the intrinsic chemical and structural properties of molecules without requiring costly labeled data. We pre-trained MolRep on over 10 million unlabeled molecules from PubChem and ZINC databases, followed by comprehensive evaluation on multiple downstream tasks including binding affinity prediction, toxicity assessment, and ADMET property prediction. Results demonstrate that MolRep significantly outperforms traditional fingerprint-based methods and other deep learning approaches, with average improvements of 15-20% across benchmark datasets. Further analysis reveals that our learned representations effectively capture meaningful chemical patterns and pharmacophore features relevant to drug-target interactions. The transferability of MolRep to low-data regimes makes it particularly valuable for exploring novel chemical spaces where labeled data is scarce. Our work demonstrates the potential of self-supervised learning from massive unlabeled molecular data to accelerate drug discovery pipelines.

Semantics-aware Multi-modal Domain Translation: From LiDAR Point Clouds to Panoramic Color Images

This paper presents a novel approach for translating 3D LiDAR point clouds into high-fidelity panoramic color images while preserving semantic information across modalities. The proposed semantics-aware translation framework addresses the fundamental challenge of mapping sparse geometric data to dense visual representations with accurate color, texture, and semantic consistency. Our method employs a two-stage architecture: first, a point cloud encoder extracts geometric and contextual features while maintaining semantic segmentation information; second, a generative network synthesizes panoramic images with corresponding semantic maps. We introduce a semantic consistency loss that ensures preservation of object classes and spatial relationships across domains, alongside adversarial and reconstruction objectives. Extensive experiments on diverse urban and natural environments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in visual quality metrics, semantic accuracy, and cross-modal alignment. The framework shows particular robustness in handling complex scenes with varying lighting conditions and occlusions. This work enables new capabilities for autonomous vehicle perception, virtual reality applications, and multi-modal dataset augmentation by bridging the gap between 3D sensing and visual representation while maintaining semantic integrity.

Place Recognition in Gardens by Learning Visual Representations: Data Set and Benchmark Analysis

This paper addresses the challenging problem of visual place recognition in garden environments, which present unique difficulties due to seasonal variations, vegetation changes, and similar repetitive structures. We introduce GardenNet, a comprehensive dataset comprising over 20,000 images captured across 15 distinct gardens throughout multiple seasons and varying weather conditions. The dataset includes GPS-tagged images with temporal spans of up to two years, providing a robust foundation for evaluating place recognition algorithms under natural environmental changes. We benchmark several state-of-the-art visual place recognition methods, including both traditional feature-based approaches and deep learning techniques, to establish performance baselines on this novel dataset. Our analysis reveals that while current methods perform adequately in short-term recognition scenarios, they struggle significantly with seasonal variations and long-term garden changes. The proposed attention-based convolutional network architecture, GardenMatch, demonstrates superior performance by focusing on persistent garden features while minimizing the impact of transient elements. Experimental results show that GardenMatch achieves 78% recall at precision 1 under challenging cross-seasonal conditions, outperforming existing methods by an average of 23%. This work provides valuable insights into the specific challenges of garden environments for visual place recognition and establishes a foundation for future research in this domain.

On Learning Sets of Symmetric Elements

This paper explores the theoretical foundations and practical applications of learning algorithms for sets of symmetric elements. We introduce a novel framework that leverages symmetry properties to enhance both the efficiency and expressiveness of set-based machine learning models. Our approach addresses the fundamental challenge of permutation invariance in set-structured data, where the ordering of elements carries no intrinsic meaning. We demonstrate that by explicitly modeling the symmetric structure of these sets, we can develop more sample-efficient learning algorithms that require significantly fewer parameters than traditional methods. Through theoretical analysis, we establish generalization bounds that depend on the symmetric properties rather than the cardinality of the sets. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including point clouds, molecular structures, and multi-object scenes, show that our symmetric set learning approach consistently outperforms conventional deep learning architectures while providing interpretable representations. Our findings suggest that exploiting symmetry constraints provides a promising direction for developing more powerful and efficient set-based learning algorithms with applications across various domains.

Fast Generation of High Fidelity RGB-D Images by Deep-Learning with Adaptive Convolution

This paper presents a novel deep learning approach for generating high-fidelity RGB-D images using adaptive convolutional neural networks. While traditional RGB-D image synthesis methods often struggle with computational efficiency and depth accuracy, our proposed framework addresses these limitations through a specialized architecture that dynamically adapts convolution parameters based on scene content. We introduce an adaptive convolution module that selectively processes spatial information at varying scales, enabling more precise depth estimation while maintaining color fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method generates RGB-D images up to 3.5× faster than state-of-the-art alternatives while achieving superior quality metrics, with a 17% improvement in depth accuracy and 12% enhancement in structural similarity. Our approach shows particular strength in handling complex scenes with fine details and varying depth discontinuities. The proposed technique has significant implications for applications including augmented reality, robotics, and 3D scene understanding, where both speed and accuracy of RGB-D data are critical factors.

FinGAT: Financial Graph Attention Networks for Recommending Top-K Profitable Stocks

This paper introduces FinGAT, a novel graph attention network architecture designed specifically for financial stock recommendation. Unlike traditional stock prediction models that consider stocks as independent entities, FinGAT leverages the inherent interconnectedness of the financial market by modeling stocks and their relationships as a dynamic graph structure. Our approach integrates multiple sources of information—historical price movements, fundamental indicators, market sentiment from financial news, and inter-stock relationships based on industry sectors, supply chains, and correlation patterns. The proposed model employs a hierarchical attention mechanism that captures both temporal dependencies in individual stock data and the complex relational dependencies across different stocks. Extensive experiments on data from major stock markets over a five-year period demonstrate that FinGAT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods in recommending top-K profitable stocks, achieving 18.7% higher risk-adjusted returns and 23.4% improved prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our ablation studies reveal that the graph attention component contributes substantially to the model's performance, particularly during periods of market volatility. FinGAT offers both theoretical contributions to financial deep learning and practical value for investment decision-making.

Coregionalised Locomotion Envelopes - A Qualitative Approach

This paper introduces a novel qualitative framework for modeling and analyzing locomotion patterns through the concept of coregionalised locomotion envelopes (CLEs). Unlike traditional quantitative approaches that focus primarily on numerical parameters, our method emphasizes the relational and contextual aspects of movement across different domains and environments. By employing coregionalisation techniques, we establish mathematical mappings between disparate locomotion spaces, enabling the identification of shared underlying movement principles despite surface-level differences. The framework incorporates multi-output Gaussian processes to capture the complex interdependencies between movement variables and environmental factors, resulting in a more holistic representation of locomotion envelopes. Through case studies spanning human gait analysis, robotic locomotion, and animal movement patterns, we demonstrate how this qualitative approach reveals previously unrecognized commonalities in movement strategies and facilitates knowledge transfer between domains. Our findings suggest that CLEs provide a powerful theoretical foundation for understanding the fundamental principles governing efficient and adaptive locomotion across biological and artificial systems, with significant implications for fields ranging from biomechanics and rehabilitation to robotics and computer animation.

DuPLO: A DUal view Point deep Learning architecture for time series classificatiOn

Time series classification remains a challenging task across numerous domains due to complex temporal dependencies and varying signal characteristics. In this paper, we introduce DuPLO, a novel dual viewpoint deep learning architecture specifically designed for time series classification. Our approach uniquely combines global and local perspectives of temporal data through a two-stream network architecture. The global stream captures overarching patterns and long-term dependencies using dilated convolutions, while the parallel local stream focuses on fine-grained, localized features through attention mechanisms and specialized temporal filters. This dual perspective enables DuPLO to simultaneously model both macro and micro temporal dynamics. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that DuPLO outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average improvement of 4.3% in classification accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Further ablation studies confirm the complementary nature of the dual viewpoints and their contribution to the model's robustness across various time series classification tasks, including those with limited training data. DuPLO offers a promising framework for enhancing time series analysis in applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to industrial anomaly detection.

Variational Empowerment as Representation Learning for Goal-Based Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to representation learning for goal-based reinforcement learning by leveraging the principle of empowerment through a variational framework. We propose Variational Empowerment Representation Learning (VERL), which constructs a latent space where states with high mutual information regarding an agent's future influence are clustered meaningfully. By maximizing empowerment—the information-theoretic measure of an agent's control over its environment—we derive state and goal representations that capture the underlying action-relevant structure of the environment. Our variational formulation enables efficient computation of the typically intractable empowerment objective while simultaneously learning representations that support effective goal-directed policies. Experimental results across diverse environments, including complex visual domains and sparse-reward settings, demonstrate that VERL significantly outperforms existing representation learning methods in goal-reaching tasks. The learned representations exhibit improved sample efficiency, better generalization to unseen goals, and more effective exploration. Our analysis reveals that empowerment-based representations naturally capture the controllable aspects of an environment while ignoring task-irrelevant features, making them particularly suitable for hierarchical and transfer learning scenarios in reinforcement learning.

A Metric for Evaluating 3D Reconstruction and Mapping Performance with No Ground Truthing

This paper introduces a novel metric for assessing the quality of 3D reconstruction and mapping algorithms without relying on ground truth data. Traditional evaluation approaches typically require carefully constructed reference datasets, which are expensive to produce and often unavailable in many real-world applications. Our proposed metric leverages internal consistency measurements derived from the reconstructed model itself, including geometric coherence, topological continuity, and texture consistency across multiple viewpoints. By analyzing the self-consistency of reconstructions through cross-validation techniques, we demonstrate that our approach can reliably identify artifacts, distortions, and inaccuracies in 3D models. We validate our metric on diverse datasets spanning indoor environments, outdoor scenes, and object-level reconstructions, showing strong correlation with human quality assessments. Experimental results indicate that our ground truth-free evaluation framework can effectively rank different reconstruction algorithms and parameter settings, providing a practical alternative when reference data is unavailable. This approach enables more accessible benchmarking of 3D reconstruction systems in unconstrained environments where ground truth acquisition is impractical.

Transform the Set: Memory Attentive Generation of Guided and Unguided Image Collages

This paper introduces a novel framework for generating visually coherent image collages through a memory-attentive approach. We present a dual-pathway architecture capable of producing both guided collages, which follow specific user instructions, and unguided collages that autonomously arrange visual elements in aesthetically pleasing compositions. Our method, Transform-the-Set (TTS), employs a transformer-based memory attention mechanism that effectively captures relationships between disparate visual elements while maintaining their individual semantic integrity. We introduce a hierarchical encoding scheme that represents both local features of individual images and global compositional patterns across potential arrangements. Experiments demonstrate that TTS outperforms existing collage generation methods on standard metrics including Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and user preference studies. For guided generation, our approach achieves 87% alignment with user instructions while maintaining visual coherence. The memory-attentive mechanism proves particularly effective at handling diverse input sets, successfully generating compelling collages from up to 25 distinct visual elements. This work advances computational creativity in visual design and offers new possibilities for both professional designers seeking inspiration and casual users creating personalized visual content.

Generative Model for Heterogeneous Inference

This paper introduces a novel framework for heterogeneous inference using generative models that can seamlessly integrate diverse data types and inference methodologies. Traditional inference approaches often struggle with heterogeneous data sources, varying uncertainty representations, and domain-specific knowledge integration. Our proposed generative model addresses these challenges by learning a unified latent representation that captures the shared structure across heterogeneous inputs while preserving their unique characteristics. The framework employs a hierarchical Bayesian architecture with modality-specific encoders and a joint latent space that facilitates cross-modal inference. We demonstrate that our approach enables robust inference across tabular, textual, visual, and temporal data, outperforming specialized single-domain methods on benchmark datasets. Empirical evaluations show significant improvements in prediction accuracy (12-18%), uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. Additionally, the model exhibits strong performance in low-data regimes through effective knowledge transfer between heterogeneous sources.
