This study presents a novel approach to wildlife image segmentation in camera-trap data using a multi-layer robust principal component analysis (ML-RPCA) framework. Camera traps generate vast quantities of images essential for ecological monitoring, but automated processing remains challenging due to environmental variability, poor lighting conditions, and partial occlusions. Our proposed ML-RPCA method addresses these challenges by decomposing camera-trap images into multiple layers representing foreground objects (wildlife), background elements, and noise components. Unlike traditional segmentation techniques that rely heavily on supervised learning with extensive labeled datasets, our approach leverages the mathematical properties of RPCA to separate moving objects from static backgrounds while requiring minimal training data. Experimental results on diverse camera-trap datasets demonstrate that ML-RPCA achieves superior segmentation accuracy (average IoU of 0.87) compared to conventional methods, particularly in challenging low-light conditions and with partially occluded subjects. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of our algorithm makes it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. This work contributes to advancing automated wildlife monitoring systems by improving the accuracy and reliability of animal detection and identification in camera-trap imagery.

Unsupervised Speech Representation Learning Using WaveNet Autoencoders

This paper introduces a novel approach to learning speech representations without supervision using WaveNet-based autoencoder architectures. Our method leverages the powerful generative capabilities of WaveNet to create an encoder-decoder framework that extracts meaningful latent representations directly from raw waveform inputs. Unlike traditional supervised approaches that require labeled data, our system learns to encode the underlying structure of speech signals through reconstruction objectives alone. We explore various architectural configurations and training strategies to optimize the learned representations, demonstrating that our approach captures phonetic, speaker, and prosodic information without explicit annotations. Experimental evaluations on downstream tasks including phoneme classification, speaker identification, and speech recognition show that our unsupervised representations achieve performance competitive with supervised alternatives while requiring no labeled training data. Additionally, we analyze the latent space properties, revealing interpretable organization of speech attributes and demonstrating effective disentanglement of content and style factors. Our WaveNet autoencoder framework provides a promising direction for speech processing in low-resource scenarios where labeled data is scarce or unavailable.

Align Deep Features for Oriented Object Detection

Oriented object detection in aerial images presents unique challenges due to the arbitrary rotation of objects and the complexity of their spatial arrangements. This paper introduces a novel framework, AlignDet, which addresses the fundamental issue of feature misalignment in oriented object detection. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on axis-aligned feature extraction, our method explicitly aligns deep features with the orientation of objects, enabling more accurate representation learning. We propose an Oriented Feature Alignment (OFA) module that adaptively rotates convolutional features according to predicted object orientations, ensuring that the extracted features are consistently aligned regardless of object rotation. Additionally, we design a Direction-aware Attention Mechanism (DAM) that enhances the network's sensitivity to orientation-specific cues. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including DOTA, HRSC2016, and UCAS-AOD demonstrate that AlignDet achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in detecting objects with large aspect ratios and dense arrangements. Our approach not only improves detection accuracy but also enhances orientation estimation, reducing angle prediction errors by an average of 23% compared to existing methods. The proposed feature alignment strategy proves to be a simple yet effective solution for the challenging task of oriented object detection.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equation Control of Dynamics on Graphs

This paper presents a novel framework for controlling dynamical systems on graphs using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs). We address the fundamental challenge of modeling and controlling complex network dynamics by integrating graph theory with the continuous-depth representation capabilities of Neural ODEs. Our approach enables effective control of both node-level and edge-level dynamics across various graph structures, including directed, undirected, and time-varying networks. We formulate the control problem as a learnable continuous-time optimization task where Neural ODEs capture the underlying dynamics while respecting graph-theoretic constraints. Through extensive experimentation on synthetic and real-world networks, including traffic flow, epidemic spreading, and social influence processes, we demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional discrete control strategies and classical ODE-based approaches. Our framework exhibits superior performance in terms of control accuracy, computational efficiency, and generalization to unseen graph topologies. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the stability and convergence properties of our controlled systems. This work opens new avenues for understanding and controlling complex networked systems through the lens of differentiable continuous-time models.

Explainable Ordinal Factorization Model: Deciphering the Effects of Attributes by Piece-wise Linear Approximation

This paper introduces a novel Explainable Ordinal Factorization Model (EOFM) designed to enhance interpretability in ordinal prediction tasks while maintaining high predictive performance. Traditional factorization models often operate as black-box systems, offering limited insights into how specific attributes influence predictions across different value ranges. Our proposed EOFM addresses this limitation by incorporating piece-wise linear approximation techniques to model the non-linear relationships between attributes and ordinal outcomes. The approach decomposes complex feature interactions into interpretable segments, allowing practitioners to understand how attribute effects vary across different thresholds of the ordinal scale. We formulate the model within a regularized optimization framework that balances prediction accuracy with model simplicity and explainability. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that EOFM achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art ordinal regression methods while providing transparent, actionable insights into attribute contributions. Case studies in healthcare risk assessment and consumer preference modeling illustrate how the piece-wise linear components enable domain experts to identify critical thresholds where attribute effects change significantly. The proposed model represents an important step toward reconciling the often competing goals of predictive power and model interpretability in ordinal prediction tasks.

TransGAN: Two Pure Transformers Can Make One Strong GAN, and That Can Scale Up

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable success in image generation tasks, yet their architectural design has predominantly relied on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). In this paper, we introduce TransGAN, the first purely transformer-based GAN architecture that entirely dispenses with convolutions. Our approach leverages the long-range dependency modeling capabilities of transformers by implementing a transformer-based generator and discriminator that operate directly on sequences of image patches. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that TransGAN achieves competitive performance compared to CNN-based counterparts across multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet. Notably, TransGAN exhibits superior scaling properties as the model size and training data increase, consistently improving FID scores and image quality. We also introduce novel techniques to stabilize transformer-based adversarial training, including data-efficient attention mechanisms and progressive growing strategies specifically adapted for transformer architectures. Our work not only establishes transformers as viable alternatives to CNNs in generative modeling but also opens new research directions for scalable, high-resolution image synthesis using pure transformer architectures.

Learning Metric Graphs for Neuron Segmentation In Electron Microscopy Images

Accurate segmentation of neuronal structures in electron microscopy (EM) images is crucial for understanding brain connectivity and function, yet remains challenging due to the complex morphology of neurons and imaging artifacts. In this paper, we present a novel approach for neuron segmentation based on metric graph learning. Our method leverages the inherent graph-like structure of neuronal processes to improve segmentation accuracy in EM volumes. We first train a deep convolutional neural network to predict local affinity maps that capture the likelihood of voxel connectivity. These affinity maps are then transformed into a metric space where distances reflect neuronal boundaries. Using this metric representation, we construct a weighted graph and apply specialized graph partitioning algorithms that respect the topological constraints of neuronal structures. Our approach effectively handles thin neuronal processes and complex branch points that traditional methods often miss. Experiments on multiple public EM datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, reducing merge and split errors by 18% and improving Rand and variation of information scores. Additionally, our graph-based representation enables efficient correction of segmentation errors through minimal user interaction. This work represents a significant advancement in automated neuron reconstruction from EM data, facilitating large-scale connectomics research.

How is Gaze Influenced by Image Transformations? Dataset and Model

Understanding how visual attention and gaze patterns are affected by image transformations is crucial for applications in computer vision, human-computer interaction, and visual neuroscience. In this paper, we present a novel dataset and computational model that systematically investigate the relationship between various image transformations and human gaze behavior. Our dataset comprises eye-tracking data collected from 45 participants viewing 1,200 images under multiple transformation conditions, including rotation, scaling, color manipulation, and various distortions. We observed that while certain gaze patterns remain invariant across specific transformations, others exhibit significant shifts in attention allocation. Building on these insights, we developed a deep learning model that predicts gaze distribution on transformed images with higher accuracy than existing state-of-the-art approaches. The model incorporates a dual-stream architecture that processes both transformation parameters and image features to generate transformation-aware saliency maps. Our findings provide new theoretical understanding of human visual attention mechanisms and practical tools for applications requiring gaze prediction on manipulated images. The dataset and model code are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this domain.

Hidden Tree Markov Networks: Deep and Wide Learning for Structured Data

This paper introduces Hidden Tree Markov Networks (HTMNs), a novel probabilistic framework that extends traditional sequence models to effectively learn from tree-structured data. HTMNs combine the hierarchical representation capabilities of tree-based models with the expressive power of deep neural networks to capture complex dependencies in structured data. We formulate a principled approach that simultaneously learns both deep representations along tree paths and wide representations across tree siblings, enabling the model to capture both vertical and horizontal relationships within hierarchical structures. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that HTMNs generalize several existing probabilistic models while maintaining computational tractability through specialized message-passing algorithms. Empirical evaluations on diverse domains including natural language parsing, XML document classification, and phylogenetic analysis show that HTMNs consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods, with particularly significant improvements on datasets with complex hierarchical dependencies. Additionally, we demonstrate that the interpretable nature of HTMNs provides valuable insights into the learned hierarchical patterns. The proposed framework opens new avenues for applying deep learning techniques to structured data while preserving the inherent tree-based relationships.

Adversarial Attacks to Machine Learning-Based Smart Healthcare Systems

The integration of machine learning (ML) technologies into healthcare systems has revolutionized patient care, diagnostics, and treatment planning. However, these smart healthcare systems face emerging security challenges in the form of adversarial attacks that threaten their reliability and patient safety. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of adversarial attack vectors targeting ML-based healthcare applications, including manipulation of medical imaging data, corruption of electronic health records, and interference with real-time monitoring systems. We categorize attack methodologies across different healthcare domains and evaluate their potential impacts on clinical decision-making processes. Our experimental results demonstrate that even state-of-the-art healthcare ML models remain vulnerable to carefully crafted perturbations, with success rates of up to 89% for targeted attacks while maintaining clinical plausibility. We further propose a multi-layered defense framework combining adversarial training, input sanitization, and anomaly detection techniques that reduces attack success rates by 76% without compromising diagnostic accuracy. This work highlights the urgent need for security-aware design in healthcare AI systems and provides guidelines for developing robust ML models that can withstand adversarial manipulation in critical healthcare environments.

Assessing Capsule Networks With Biased Data

Capsule Networks (CapsNets) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional convolutional neural networks, offering potential advantages in preserving spatial hierarchies and viewpoint invariance. However, their performance and robustness when trained on biased datasets remain underexplored. This study systematically evaluates CapsNets under various data bias conditions, including class imbalance, demographic skew, and viewpoint limitations. We compare standard CapsNet architectures against conventional CNNs across multiple datasets with controlled bias introduction. Our findings reveal that while CapsNets demonstrate inherent resilience to certain viewpoint biases, they exhibit unexpected vulnerability to demographic and class representation skews. We propose modifications to the dynamic routing algorithm that significantly improve CapsNet performance under biased training conditions without compromising their performance on balanced data. These results provide important insights into the practical deployment of CapsNets in real-world scenarios where training data biases are inevitable, and offer concrete strategies for mitigating these effects in capsule-based architectures.

Self-supervised Learning from a Multi-view Perspective

This paper presents a theoretical framework for understanding self-supervised learning (SSL) through the lens of multi-view information processing. We demonstrate that many successful SSL methods—including contrastive learning, masked autoencoding, and invariant prediction approaches—can be unified under a common multi-view perspective where different transformations or corruptions of the same data create complementary views. Our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of SSL methods depends critically on how they balance view redundancy and view sufficiency, with optimal performance achieved when views share task-relevant information while discarding view-specific nuisance factors. We formalize these relationships using information-theoretic principles and introduce a novel multi-view InfoMax objective that explicitly maximizes shared information across views while minimizing view-specific noise. Empirical evaluations across vision, language, and multi-modal domains demonstrate that our framework not only provides theoretical insights into existing SSL methods but also guides the development of more effective algorithms that achieve state-of-the-art performance on benchmark tasks. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of why SSL works and offers principled directions for designing robust representation learning approaches that require minimal human supervision.

Reconstruction of Simulation-Based Physical Field by Reconstruction Neural Network Method

This paper presents a novel approach for reconstructing physical fields from simulation data using a specialized reconstruction neural network (RNN) method. We address the challenge of accurately recovering continuous physical field distributions from discrete simulation outputs, which is essential in various scientific and engineering applications. The proposed RNN architecture leverages the underlying physics governing the simulated phenomena while maintaining computational efficiency. By incorporating domain-specific constraints and employing a multi-scale feature extraction strategy, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional interpolation techniques and standard deep learning approaches. Extensive validation using datasets from computational fluid dynamics, electromagnetic field simulations, and heat transfer problems shows that the RNN method achieves up to 30% improvement in reconstruction accuracy while requiring significantly fewer training samples. Furthermore, the method exhibits robust performance when dealing with noisy or sparse simulation data. This work contributes to bridging the gap between discrete numerical simulations and continuous field representations, offering a promising tool for real-time physical field reconstruction in simulation-based engineering applications.

State Entropy Maximization with Random Encoders for Efficient Exploration

Efficient exploration remains a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning, particularly in environments with high-dimensional observations and sparse rewards. This paper introduces State Entropy Maximization with Random Encoders (SEMRE), a novel exploration approach that encourages agents to visit diverse states without requiring complex representation learning. SEMRE leverages fixed random encoders to project high-dimensional observations into a lower-dimensional latent space, where entropy maximization is computationally tractable. By avoiding the need to train representation networks, our method significantly reduces computational overhead while maintaining exploration efficacy. We theoretically analyze the relationship between entropy in the encoded space and coverage in the original state space, establishing formal guarantees under mild assumptions. Empirical evaluations across various environments, including challenging visual domains and sparse-reward tasks, demonstrate that SEMRE outperforms state-of-the-art exploration methods while requiring substantially less computation. Our approach proves particularly effective in procedurally generated environments where transfer learning is essential. These results suggest that sophisticated representation learning may be unnecessary for effective exploration, opening new directions for designing computationally efficient exploration algorithms.

Deep Sets for Generalization in RL

This paper explores the application of Deep Sets, a permutation-invariant neural network architecture, to enhance generalization capabilities in reinforcement learning (RL). Despite recent advances in RL, agents often struggle to generalize beyond their training environments, limiting their practical applicability. We propose a novel framework that leverages the permutation-invariant properties of Deep Sets to create state representations that capture underlying structural patterns across varying environment configurations. Our approach treats environment elements as sets, enabling the agent to reason about the relationships between entities rather than their specific arrangements. Through extensive experiments across procedurally generated environments with varying numbers of objects, obstacles, and goals, we demonstrate that our Deep Sets-based architecture significantly outperforms conventional RL architectures in zero-shot transfer to unseen scenarios. Results show a 37% improvement in sample efficiency during training and a 42% increase in performance on out-of-distribution tasks. This work provides important insights into how inductive biases inspired by set theory can be incorporated into RL systems to achieve more robust generalization, paving the way for more adaptable autonomous agents.

Domain-invariant Stereo Matching Networks

Stereo matching, a fundamental task in computer vision, often suffers from significant performance degradation when deployed in domains different from the training data. This paper introduces Domain-invariant Stereo Matching Networks (DSMN), a novel approach that addresses the challenge of domain shift in stereo correspondence estimation. Our framework incorporates an adversarial domain adaptation strategy that aligns feature representations across domains while preserving the geometric consistency essential for accurate disparity estimation. We propose a two-stage training methodology: first learning robust domain-agnostic features through a domain discriminator, then fine-tuning the matching process with a consistency regularization term that enforces invariance to domain-specific artifacts. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets (KITTI, Middlebury, ETH3D, and DrivingStereo) demonstrate that DSMN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods under cross-domain scenarios, reducing the disparity error by up to 25% compared to domain-specific approaches. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component in our framework, particularly highlighting the importance of our proposed feature disentanglement mechanism. DSMN represents an important step toward developing stereo matching systems that can generalize reliably across diverse real-world environments without requiring domain-specific fine-tuning.

Scalable Dictionary Classifiers for Time Series Classification

Time series classification (TSC) presents significant challenges due to high dimensionality, temporal dependencies, and the increasing volume of data in modern applications. This paper introduces a novel approach to TSC through scalable dictionary classifiers that effectively balance computational efficiency with classification accuracy. Our method constructs discriminative dictionaries by extracting representative subsequences from training data and employs efficient matching techniques to classify new time series instances. Unlike traditional dictionary-based approaches that suffer from computational bottlenecks with large datasets, we propose a hierarchical dictionary structure and parallelized matching algorithms that achieve logarithmic rather than linear scaling with dictionary size. Experiments on diverse benchmark datasets from the UCR Time Series Archive demonstrate that our approach maintains competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing computational complexity. For large-scale datasets containing millions of time points, our method achieves up to 50× speedup over existing dictionary-based classifiers with minimal accuracy trade-offs. The proposed framework also incorporates an adaptive dictionary pruning mechanism that optimizes memory usage while preserving discriminative power. These contributions make dictionary-based classification feasible for real-time and resource-constrained applications across domains including healthcare monitoring, industrial diagnostics, and financial forecasting.

Extending Adversarial Attacks and Defenses to Deep 3D Point Cloud Classifiers

Recent advances in deep learning have enabled significant progress in 3D point cloud processing, with applications spanning autonomous vehicles, robotics, and augmented reality. However, the vulnerability of these models to adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored compared to their 2D counterparts. In this paper, we investigate the robustness of state-of-the-art deep 3D point cloud classifiers against adversarial perturbations. We propose novel attack methodologies specifically designed for the unique characteristics of point cloud data, including point perturbation, addition, and removal strategies that preserve the physical integrity of the represented objects while causing misclassification. Our experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that current architectures like PointNet, PointNet++, and DGCNN are highly susceptible to these attacks, with success rates exceeding 90% under certain scenarios. Furthermore, we develop defensive techniques including adversarial training and point cloud purification methods that significantly enhance model robustness. We also introduce a new evaluation metric that accounts for both classification accuracy and geometric distortion. Our findings highlight critical security implications for real-world 3D sensing systems and provide a foundation for designing more robust point cloud processing algorithms.

Logarithmic Landscape and Power-law Escape Rate of SGD

This paper investigates the interplay between loss landscape geometry and the dynamics of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in deep learning. We establish that many modern neural networks converge toward regions characterized by a logarithmic landscape structure, where the loss increases logarithmically with distance from local minima. Through theoretical analysis and empirical validation across various architectures, we demonstrate that this logarithmic landscape induces a power-law escape rate for SGD trajectories. Specifically, the probability of SGD escaping a local minimum decreases according to a power-law with respect to time, rather than the exponential decay observed in quadratic landscapes. This finding explains several previously puzzling phenomena, including the remarkable stability of SGD solutions despite the apparent flatness of loss basins. Our work provides a novel framework for understanding generalization properties of deep networks and offers practical insights for optimization strategies in non-convex high-dimensional spaces. The power-law behavior we identify suggests that the effective barriers in neural network loss landscapes are fundamentally different from traditional energy barriers in physical systems, with significant implications for model selection and training dynamics.

Safe Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Systems with Continuous Action Spaces

This paper addresses the critical challenge of ensuring safety in multi-agent systems operating with continuous action spaces while leveraging deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques. We propose a novel framework that integrates safety constraints into the learning process without compromising performance or scalability. Our approach combines control barrier functions with actor-critic architectures to guarantee safety during both training and deployment phases. We formulate safety as a constrained optimization problem and develop a differentiable safety layer that projects potentially unsafe actions onto the safe action manifold. Extensive evaluations across various multi-agent scenarios, including autonomous driving, drone swarm navigation, and robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrate that our method achieves up to 97% reduction in safety violations compared to baseline approaches while maintaining competitive performance on task objectives. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of our algorithm and safety assurance under bounded disturbances. This work represents a significant step toward deploying DRL-based multi-agent systems in safety-critical real-world applications where continuous control is essential.

Robust and Subject-Independent Driving Manoeuvre Anticipation through Domain-Adversarial Recurrent Neural Networks

Anticipating driving manoeuvres before they occur is a critical component for developing advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles that can operate safely in complex traffic environments. However, existing approaches often suffer from poor generalization across different drivers due to individual driving styles and behaviors. This paper introduces a novel framework leveraging domain-adversarial training with recurrent neural networks to achieve robust, subject-independent driving manoeuvre anticipation. Our approach explicitly addresses the domain shift problem between drivers by learning features that are both predictive of upcoming manoeuvres and invariant to driver-specific characteristics. We implement a domain-adversarial recurrent neural network architecture that simultaneously optimizes for manoeuvre prediction while minimizing the model's ability to identify the driver, thereby extracting universal driving patterns. Extensive evaluation on multiple naturalistic driving datasets demonstrates that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving 87.4% prediction accuracy with an average time-to-manoeuvre of 3.8 seconds, while maintaining consistent performance across unseen drivers. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our domain adaptation strategy, showing a 23.6% improvement in cross-driver generalization compared to non-adversarial baselines. These results highlight the potential of domain-adversarial techniques for creating robust driving assistance systems that can reliably anticipate manoeuvres regardless of individual driving styles.

Causal Mediation Analysis with Hidden Confounders

This paper addresses a critical challenge in causal mediation analysis: the presence of hidden confounders that bias estimates of direct and indirect effects. While traditional mediation methods assume no unmeasured confounding, this assumption is often violated in observational studies. We develop a novel framework that identifies and adjusts for hidden confounders affecting both mediator and outcome variables. Our approach combines structural causal modeling with sensitivity analysis to quantify the robustness of mediation estimates to unobserved confounding. We introduce a semi-parametric estimation strategy that leverages instrumental variables and negative controls to partially identify causal mediation effects under weaker assumptions than conventional methods. Through simulation studies and application to healthcare data examining how treatment affects outcomes through specific biological pathways, we demonstrate that our method provides more accurate estimates of direct and indirect effects compared to standard approaches when hidden confounding is present. This work contributes methodological tools that help researchers conduct more reliable causal mediation analyses in the presence of unmeasured confounding variables.

Bilinear Factor Matrix Norm Minimization for Robust PCA: Algorithms and Applications

This paper introduces a novel approach to Robust Principal Component Analysis (RPCA) through bilinear factor matrix norm minimization. We formulate RPCA as a non-convex optimization problem that directly factorizes the low-rank component while simultaneously identifying sparse corruptions in the data. Unlike traditional methods that rely on nuclear norm minimization, our bilinear factorization approach significantly reduces computational complexity and memory requirements for large-scale problems. We develop efficient algorithms based on alternating minimization and provide theoretical guarantees for convergence to statistically meaningful solutions under mild conditions. Our formulation demonstrates superior robustness to outliers and missing data compared to existing methods. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets validate our theoretical results, while applications to real-world problems—including background subtraction in video surveillance, facial recognition under occlusion, and collaborative filtering with corrupted entries—demonstrate the practical utility of our approach. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, making it particularly suitable for high-dimensional data analysis tasks where robustness to corruption is essential.

Variance-Based Rewards for Approximate Bayesian Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to Bayesian reinforcement learning by incorporating variance-based reward functions into the decision-making process. While traditional reinforcement learning methods focus on maximizing expected returns, they often struggle with the exploration-exploitation dilemma, particularly in environments with sparse or delayed rewards. Our approach augments the standard reward signal with a variance-based component that explicitly encourages exploration in regions of high posterior uncertainty. We develop an approximate Bayesian framework that maintains a distribution over possible environment dynamics, enabling efficient computation of posterior variance estimates without requiring full Bayesian updates. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our method achieves sublinear Bayesian regret bounds under reasonable assumptions about the environment. Empirical evaluations across benchmark domains, including grid worlds, continuous control tasks, and partially observable environments, show that variance-based rewards significantly improve sample efficiency and final performance compared to state-of-the-art exploration methods. This work provides a practical bridge between Bayesian optimality and computational tractability in reinforcement learning, offering insights into uncertainty-guided exploration for complex decision-making problems.

Building Reliable Explanations of Unreliable Neural Networks: Locally Smoothing Perspective of Model Interpretation

As neural networks increasingly influence critical decision-making processes, the need for reliable interpretation methods has become paramount. However, existing explanation techniques often produce unstable and inconsistent attributions when faced with minor input perturbations, undermining trust in both the explanations and the underlying models. This paper introduces a novel framework for generating reliable explanations of neural networks by adopting a locally smoothing perspective of model interpretation. We formalize the notion of explanation reliability and demonstrate theoretically that local smoothness is a key property for robust interpretability. Our approach, Local Smoothing Interpretation (LSI), applies controlled neighborhood sampling and aggregation to stabilize attribution maps without compromising explanation fidelity. Through extensive experiments across image classification, natural language processing, and healthcare applications, we demonstrate that LSI significantly improves explanation consistency against input perturbations, adversarial attacks, and distribution shifts compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we establish formal guarantees on the stability-fidelity trade-off and provide practical guidelines for selecting optimal smoothing parameters. This work bridges the gap between the inherent unreliability of complex neural networks and the need for trustworthy explanations, offering a principled approach to model interpretation that remains reliable even when the underlying model exhibits vulnerability to perturbations.

Unsupervised Remote Sensing Super-Resolution via Migration Image Prior

This paper presents a novel unsupervised approach to remote sensing image super-resolution that leverages migration image prior knowledge. Unlike conventional super-resolution methods that rely on paired low-resolution and high-resolution images for training, our framework operates in an unsupervised manner, eliminating the need for ground truth high-resolution data. We introduce a migration image prior (MIP) that transfers structural and textural information from source domains to guide the super-resolution process for remote sensing imagery. Our method employs a dual-branch architecture: one branch extracts transferable priors from high-quality natural images, while the second branch adapts these priors to the specific characteristics of remote sensing data. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple satellite and aerial image datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing unsupervised super-resolution methods by significant margins (3.2dB PSNR improvement on average). The proposed method effectively preserves fine details and structural integrity while suppressing artifacts common in remote sensing imagery, such as spectral distortion and blur. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the migration prior mechanism and its robustness across different resolution scales and imaging conditions. The proposed technique offers a promising solution for enhancing the spatial resolution of remote sensing data without requiring paired training samples, making it particularly valuable for practical earth observation applications.

Estimating Node Importance in Knowledge Graphs Using Graph Neural Networks

Knowledge graphs (KGs) have become essential data structures for organizing information in numerous domains, from search engines to recommendation systems. However, not all nodes in a KG carry equal importance, and identifying the most significant entities remains a challenging task. This paper presents a novel approach for estimating node importance in knowledge graphs using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Unlike traditional centrality measures that rely solely on graph topology, our method learns representations that capture both structural information and semantic content encoded in the KG. We propose a specialized GNN architecture that aggregates multi-relational neighborhood information while incorporating entity type and attribute features. Through extensive experiments on several real-world knowledge graphs, including DBpedia, Wikidata, and domain-specific KGs, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in identifying influential nodes as measured by multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we show that our node importance estimations can enhance downstream tasks such as knowledge graph completion, question answering, and summarization. Our work provides valuable insights into the hierarchical nature of information in knowledge graphs and offers a powerful tool for knowledge graph refinement and analysis.

Human Activity Recognition using Continuous Wavelet Transform and Convolutional Neural Networks

This study presents a novel approach to Human Activity Recognition (HAR) by combining Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). While traditional HAR systems often rely on handcrafted features from time-domain or frequency-domain representations, our method leverages CWT's ability to capture both time and frequency information simultaneously, preserving temporal dynamics crucial for activity distinction. We transform raw sensor data from wearable devices into scalogram images via CWT, which serve as rich, two-dimensional inputs for a custom CNN architecture. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our CWT-CNN framework achieves superior classification accuracy (94.7%) compared to conventional methods, with particular improvements in distinguishing between activities with similar temporal patterns but different frequency characteristics. The model shows robust performance across various sensor placements and user variations, with minimal preprocessing requirements. Our approach offers promising applications in healthcare monitoring, sports analytics, and human-computer interaction systems where accurate activity recognition is essential.

Instance Explainable Temporal Network For Multivariate Timeseries

This paper introduces the Instance Explainable Temporal Network (IETN), a novel deep learning framework designed specifically for multivariate time series analysis with built-in explainability. Unlike traditional black-box models, IETN provides instance-level explanations that identify the most influential features and temporal segments contributing to each prediction. Our architecture combines attention mechanisms with temporal convolutional networks to capture complex dependencies across both time and features, while simultaneously generating importance weights that quantify feature contributions. Through extensive experiments on healthcare, financial, and industrial datasets, we demonstrate that IETN achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance while offering interpretable insights without sacrificing accuracy. The model's explainability component reveals meaningful patterns that align with domain knowledge and can assist practitioners in understanding model decisions. Additionally, we show that IETN's explanations remain consistent across similar instances, enhancing trust in the model's decision-making process. Our approach addresses the critical need for transparent yet powerful models in time series analysis, particularly for high-stakes applications requiring both accuracy and interpretability.

Cross-modal registration using point clouds and graph-matching in the context of correlative microscopies

This study presents a novel approach for cross-modal registration in correlative microscopy using point cloud data and graph-matching algorithms. Correlative microscopy, which combines multiple imaging modalities to analyze the same specimen, faces significant challenges in accurately aligning images with different resolutions, contrasts, and fields of view. Our method addresses these challenges by extracting distinctive feature points from different microscopy modalities and representing them as point clouds. We then employ a graph-matching framework that leverages both the spatial distribution of these points and their local geometric relationships to establish correspondences between modalities. The algorithm demonstrates robustness to the inherent differences in scale, orientation, and information content across imaging techniques such as electron microscopy, fluorescence microscopy, and X-ray tomography. Experimental results on diverse biological samples show that our approach achieves sub-pixel registration accuracy with a mean error of 0.85 μm, outperforming traditional intensity-based and feature-based registration methods by 37%. Furthermore, the method exhibits computational efficiency, enabling practical implementation in high-throughput correlative microscopy workflows. This work provides a significant advancement in multimodal image integration, facilitating more comprehensive structural and functional analysis of biological specimens across different spatial scales and imaging contrasts.

Learning without Forgetting for 3D Point Cloud Objects

This paper addresses the critical challenge of catastrophic forgetting in deep learning models trained on 3D point cloud data. As 3D vision systems increasingly need to learn new object categories incrementally, traditional approaches suffer from severe performance degradation on previously learned tasks when trained on new data. We propose a novel framework for Learning without Forgetting (LwF) specifically designed for 3D point cloud object recognition and segmentation. Our approach combines knowledge distillation techniques with a dynamic regularization strategy that preserves critical geometric features from previously learned object categories while accommodating new ones. Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including ModelNet40, ShapeNet, and ScanObjectNN, we demonstrate that our method achieves up to 27% higher average accuracy on previously learned categories compared to conventional fine-tuning approaches, while maintaining competitive performance on newly introduced classes. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation protocol specifically designed to assess incremental learning capabilities in 3D point cloud networks. Our framework provides a promising solution for real-world applications such as robotics and autonomous systems that require continuous adaptation to new object categories without catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge.

Skeletor: Skeletal Transformers for Robust Body-Pose Estimation

Human pose estimation remains a challenging problem in computer vision, particularly in scenarios with occlusions, complex backgrounds, or unusual body configurations. In this paper, we present Skeletor, a novel transformer-based architecture specifically designed for robust human skeletal pose estimation from RGB images. Our approach leverages the inherent hierarchical structure of the human skeleton by introducing a specialized attention mechanism that models both local joint relationships and global body configurations. Unlike previous methods that rely heavily on CNN backbones, Skeletor processes skeletal data as structured sequences, allowing the model to better capture long-range dependencies between body joints. We introduce a novel positional encoding scheme that incorporates anatomical constraints and biomechanical priors, significantly improving estimation accuracy for challenging poses. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets (COCO, MPII, and Human3.6M) demonstrate that Skeletor achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in occluded and complex pose scenarios, showing an average 8.7% reduction in pose estimation error compared to previous approaches. Additionally, our model demonstrates enhanced robustness to varying lighting conditions and camera viewpoints, making it suitable for real-world applications. Code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research.

Reinforcement Learning and its Connections with Neuroscience and Psychology

This paper explores the interdisciplinary relationships between reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, neuroscientific findings, and psychological theories of learning and decision-making. We review how computational RL frameworks have both informed and been informed by our understanding of neural reward processing, particularly involving dopaminergic systems and the basal ganglia. The temporal difference learning algorithm's prediction error signals show remarkable parallels with dopamine neuron activity during reward-based learning tasks. We examine how these connections have led to testable hypotheses about human and animal learning, memory consolidation, and adaptive behavior. Additionally, we analyze how psychological concepts such as operant conditioning, intrinsic motivation, and cognitive biases have influenced modern RL algorithm development, including curiosity-driven exploration and hierarchical reinforcement learning approaches. The bidirectional knowledge transfer between these fields has accelerated progress in artificial intelligence while deepening our understanding of biological learning systems. We conclude by discussing future research directions that could further strengthen these connections, potentially leading to more human-like artificial agents and novel therapeutic approaches for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

Image Transformer: A Novel Approach to Visual Data Processing

The Image Transformer introduces a self-attention-based architecture specifically designed for image processing tasks, extending the success of transformer models from natural language processing to computer vision. Unlike convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that process images through local filtering operations, our proposed model captures global dependencies across image regions through multi-head self-attention mechanisms. By treating image patches as sequential tokens, the Image Transformer effectively models long-range interactions between distant image elements while maintaining computational efficiency through attention masking and positional encodings adapted for 2D data. Our extensive evaluations across image classification, segmentation, and generation tasks demonstrate that the Image Transformer achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN architectures, particularly for tasks requiring global context understanding. The model's ability to process variable-sized inputs without architectural changes and its interpretability through attention visualization offer significant advantages for practical computer vision applications. This work establishes transformers as a powerful alternative paradigm for visual data processing, opening new research directions at the intersection of attention-based models and computer vision.

GuidedStyle: Attribute Knowledge Guided Style Manipulation for Semantic Face Editing

This paper introduces GuidedStyle, a novel framework for semantic face editing that leverages attribute knowledge to guide style manipulation in generative models. While existing approaches to face editing have demonstrated impressive results, they often struggle with disentangling specific facial attributes without affecting unrelated features or maintaining identity preservation. Our method addresses these limitations by incorporating attribute-specific knowledge into the style manipulation process of StyleGAN-based architectures. GuidedStyle employs a two-stage approach: first, it learns disentangled attribute representations through a knowledge distillation process from pre-trained facial attribute classifiers; second, it utilizes these representations to guide precise manipulations in the style space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance in attribute-specific editing compared to state-of-the-art methods, with significantly improved disentanglement scores and identity preservation. Additionally, GuidedStyle enables intuitive control over edit magnitude and direction, allowing for fine-grained adjustments of facial attributes. Our user study further confirms that edited images generated by GuidedStyle are perceived as more realistic and faithful to the intended manipulations. The proposed framework advances the field of semantic face editing by providing a more controlled and interpretable approach to facial attribute manipulation.

HandFoldingNet: A 3D Hand Pose Estimation Network Using Multiscale-Feature Guided Folding of a 2D Hand Skeleton

This paper presents HandFoldingNet, a novel approach for accurate 3D hand pose estimation from single RGB images. Unlike previous methods that directly regress 3D joint coordinates or estimate depth values separately, our approach introduces a skeleton folding mechanism that transforms 2D hand skeletons into 3D space using multiscale feature guidance. The network architecture consists of two main components: (1) a 2D skeleton estimation module that leverages a multiscale feature extractor to capture hand structures at different resolutions, and (2) a feature-guided folding module that progressively lifts the 2D skeleton into 3D space by incorporating contextual information across multiple scales. Our folding operation maintains the anatomical constraints of hand structure while allowing for flexible adaptation to various hand poses and viewpoints. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks including FreiHAND, RHD, and STB datasets demonstrate that HandFoldingNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in challenging cases involving occlusion and complex articulations. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our multiscale feature guidance and the anatomically-aware folding process. The proposed method offers a computationally efficient solution for real-time 3D hand pose estimation applicable to human-computer interaction, augmented reality, and gesture recognition systems.

A Transformer-based Framework for Multivariate Time Series Representation Learning

This paper introduces a novel Transformer-based framework for learning robust representations from multivariate time series data. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on recurrent neural networks or convolutional architectures, our framework leverages the self-attention mechanism of Transformers to capture complex temporal dependencies and variable interactions simultaneously. We propose a specialized positional encoding scheme that preserves both absolute and relative temporal information, along with a hierarchical attention structure that effectively models relationships across multiple time scales. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets spanning healthcare monitoring, financial forecasting, and industrial sensor readings demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in downstream tasks including classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection. The learned representations exhibit strong generalization capabilities even with limited labeled data, making our framework particularly valuable for real-world applications where annotation is costly. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into the framework's capacity to model nonlinear dynamics and its computational efficiency compared to existing approaches. Our code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in multivariate time series analysis.

Unsupervised Features Learning for Sampled Vector Fields

This paper presents a novel approach to unsupervised feature learning for sampled vector fields, addressing the challenges of extracting meaningful patterns from complex vector field data without labeled examples. We introduce a framework that leverages deep learning architectures to discover intrinsic features in vector fields sampled across various domains including fluid dynamics, electromagnetic simulations, and geophysical flows. Our method combines convolutional neural networks with custom-designed loss functions that preserve topological and geometric properties of the vector fields while enabling dimensionality reduction and feature extraction. Through extensive experimentation on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our approach successfully identifies critical points, vortices, and other significant flow structures without prior annotation. The learned representations enable improved visualization, efficient compression, and enhanced analysis of vector field data. Comparative evaluations show that our unsupervised approach achieves comparable performance to supervised methods while eliminating the need for labor-intensive labeling. These results suggest promising applications in scientific visualization, computational physics, and data-driven simulation, particularly for large-scale vector field datasets where manual annotation is impractical.

Graph-based State Representation for Deep Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to state representation in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) using graph-based structures. Traditional DRL methods often struggle with complex environments that contain relational information and structural dependencies between entities. We propose a graph-based state representation framework that explicitly models these relationships, enabling more efficient learning and better generalization. Our approach leverages graph neural networks to process states represented as graphs where nodes correspond to entities in the environment and edges capture their relationships. Through extensive experimentation across diverse domains including robotic manipulation, multi-agent systems, and combinatorial optimization problems, we demonstrate that our graph-based representation consistently outperforms conventional tensor-based approaches. Results show significant improvements in sample efficiency (reducing required interactions by up to 45%), learning speed, and final performance on complex tasks. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis establishing the representational advantages of graph-based approaches for certain environment classes. This work bridges the gap between graph representation learning and reinforcement learning, opening new avenues for tackling complex decision-making problems with inherent relational structure.

Rethinking ImageNet Pre-training

In this paper, we critically examine the widely-adopted paradigm of ImageNet pre-training for visual recognition tasks. While transfer learning from ImageNet has become a standard practice in computer vision, we present empirical evidence challenging the necessity of this approach. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets and architectures, we demonstrate that models trained from random initialization can match or even surpass the performance of their pre-trained counterparts, provided they are trained with sufficient data and appropriate optimization strategies. Our analysis reveals that the primary benefits of pre-training are faster convergence and improved performance in data-constrained regimes, rather than superior asymptotic performance. Furthermore, we show that for several detection and segmentation tasks, the advantages of ImageNet pre-training diminish as training recipes improve and training time increases. These findings suggest that the field may benefit from exploring alternative training paradigms that do not rely on large-scale supervised pre-training. Our work provides valuable insights for practitioners regarding when pre-training is beneficial and when training from scratch is a viable or even preferable option.

Graphs for Deep Learning Representations

This paper explores the use of graph structures as a powerful framework for representing and analyzing deep learning models. We demonstrate how graph-based representations can capture the complex relationships between components of neural networks, enabling more interpretable and efficient deep learning systems. By modeling neural architectures as graphs, we establish formal methods to analyze information flow, identify critical pathways, and optimize network topologies. Our approach leverages graph theory to address key challenges in deep learning, including model interpretability, knowledge transfer, and architecture search. Experimental results across multiple domains show that graph-based representations facilitate improved visualization of model behavior, more effective transfer learning, and discovery of optimal architectural patterns. Furthermore, we introduce novel graph algorithms specifically designed for analyzing deep neural networks, providing theoretical guarantees on their computational properties. This work bridges the gap between graph theory and deep learning, offering a unified mathematical framework that enhances our understanding of neural network representations and opens new directions for model development and analysis.

Significant Wave Height Prediction based on Wavelet Graph Neural Network

This study presents a novel approach for significant wave height (SWH) prediction by integrating wavelet transform techniques with graph neural networks (GNNs). Ocean wave forecasting is crucial for maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal management, yet remains challenging due to the complex, non-stationary, and spatially correlated nature of ocean dynamics. Our proposed Wavelet Graph Neural Network (WGNN) framework addresses these challenges by decomposing wave time series data into multiple frequency components using wavelet transforms, while simultaneously capturing spatial dependencies through graph-based representations of oceanic monitoring stations. The multi-resolution analysis provided by wavelets effectively handles the multi-scale temporal patterns in wave data, while the GNN architecture models the intricate spatial correlations between different monitoring locations. Experiments conducted using buoy data from the National Data Buoy Center demonstrate that our WGNN model outperforms traditional statistical methods, conventional deep learning approaches, and existing hybrid models, achieving a 17% reduction in prediction error for 24-hour forecasts. The model shows particular strength in predicting extreme wave events, which are of critical importance for maritime safety applications. This research contributes a powerful new methodology for ocean wave forecasting that effectively leverages both temporal frequency information and spatial correlation structures.

SegCodeNet: Color-Coded Segmentation Masks for Activity Detection from Wearable Cameras

This paper introduces SegCodeNet, a novel approach for human activity detection using egocentric video from wearable cameras. Our method leverages semantic segmentation to generate color-coded masks that represent key scene elements relevant to activity recognition. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on RGB frames or optical flow, SegCodeNet transforms raw video frames into compact semantic representations where each pixel's color encodes specific object categories and their spatial relationships. These color-coded segmentation masks serve as efficient input representations that emphasize activity-relevant elements while suppressing background noise. We demonstrate that this approach significantly reduces computational requirements while maintaining high accuracy for activity detection. Our experiments across multiple egocentric datasets show that SegCodeNet outperforms conventional RGB-based methods by 4.7% in accuracy while reducing model size by 38% and inference time by 42%. The approach is particularly effective for activities involving object interactions, where scene understanding is crucial. Furthermore, the color-coded masks provide inherent interpretability, allowing for visual explanation of model decisions. SegCodeNet represents a promising direction for efficient and accurate activity recognition in resource-constrained wearable computing environments.

Progressive Transformers for End-to-End Sign Language Production

This paper introduces Progressive Transformers, a novel architecture for end-to-end sign language production. Unlike prior approaches that rely on intermediate representations or sequential modeling, our method directly translates from spoken language to continuous 3D sign language motion. The Progressive Transformer extends the standard Transformer architecture with a progressive decoding mechanism that generates human skeletal pose sequences with natural temporal coherence. Our model captures the linguistic nuances of sign languages including non-manual features and spatial references. Experiments on multiple sign language datasets demonstrate that Progressive Transformers outperform existing methods across production quality metrics, achieving more fluid and linguistically accurate animations. Human evaluation by native signers confirms that our approach produces significantly more comprehensible and natural signing compared to previous state-of-the-art systems. We also introduce a new benchmark dataset and evaluation protocol to standardize assessment in this emerging field. This work represents an important step toward creating accessible communication technologies for Deaf communities while preserving the rich expressivity of sign languages.

Baking Neural Radiance Fields for Real-Time View Synthesis

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have emerged as a powerful representation for novel view synthesis, but their computational demands make real-time rendering challenging. In this paper, we present a novel approach that "bakes" pre-trained NeRF models into a more efficient representation that enables real-time view synthesis without sacrificing visual quality. Our method transforms the continuous volumetric representation of NeRF into a sparse spatial data structure that can be efficiently queried during rendering. By carefully analyzing the information density in the radiance field, we selectively allocate computational resources to visually significant regions while pruning redundant areas. We introduce an adaptive compression scheme that preserves high-frequency details while substantially reducing memory requirements. Our rendering algorithm leverages modern GPU architectures to achieve interactive frame rates on consumer hardware. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baked representation achieves rendering speeds up to 100× faster than original NeRF implementations while maintaining comparable image quality across diverse scenes. This approach bridges the gap between the high-quality results of neural representations and the real-time performance demands of practical applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and interactive visualization.

Scale-Based Gaussian Coverings: Combining Intra and Inter Mixture Models in Image Segmentation

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation by introducing Scale-Based Gaussian Coverings (SBGC), a framework that seamlessly integrates both intra-region and inter-region statistical models. While traditional segmentation methods often rely solely on either region-based or boundary-based features, our approach leverages multi-scale Gaussian mixture models to simultaneously characterize pixel distributions within regions and across region boundaries. By formulating segmentation as an optimization problem over Gaussian coverings at varying scales, we capture both local texture details and global structural information. Our method adaptively determines the appropriate scale for analysis based on local image complexity, allowing for precise delineation of complex boundaries while maintaining coherent segmentation in homogeneous areas. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including BSDS500, PASCAL VOC, and medical imaging collections demonstrate that SBGC outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 12% improvement in boundary detection accuracy and 9% enhancement in region consistency metrics. The proposed framework is particularly effective for images with textural variations and ambiguous boundaries, making it suitable for applications in medical image analysis, remote sensing, and computer vision tasks requiring precise segmentation.

Aerial Vehicle Tracking by Adaptive Fusion of Hyperspectral Likelihood Maps

This paper presents a novel approach for tracking aerial vehicles using adaptive fusion of hyperspectral likelihood maps. While traditional tracking methods often rely on RGB or infrared imaging, we leverage the rich spectral information available in hyperspectral data to improve tracking robustness in challenging conditions such as varying illumination, occlusions, and complex backgrounds. Our method generates likelihood maps from multiple spectral bands and employs an adaptive fusion strategy that dynamically weights each band's contribution based on its discriminative power and reliability. We introduce a new spectral consistency metric that enhances the tracker's ability to distinguish between the target and spectrally similar distractors. Experiments conducted on a diverse dataset of aerial vehicle tracking scenarios demonstrate that our approach achieves 18% higher tracking precision and 23% better success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed framework is particularly effective in scenarios with atmospheric interference and camouflage attempts, where conventional trackers typically fail. Additionally, we provide an analysis of which spectral bands contribute most significantly to tracking performance across different environmental conditions, offering insights for future sensor development and deployment strategies.

C-MI-GAN: Estimation of Conditional Mutual Information using MinMax Formulation

Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) is a fundamental measure in information theory that quantifies the relationship between random variables while accounting for additional conditioning information. Despite its theoretical importance, accurately estimating CMI from finite samples remains challenging, particularly in high-dimensional settings. This paper introduces C-MI-GAN, a novel approach for CMI estimation based on a minimax formulation implemented within a generative adversarial network framework. Our method leverages the dual representation of CMI as a constrained optimization problem, where a discriminator network attempts to distinguish between samples from joint and product distributions while a generator network produces adversarial examples to tighten the estimation bounds. Unlike previous estimators that suffer from high variance or restrictive assumptions, C-MI-GAN demonstrates robust performance across various data distributions and dimensionalities. We provide theoretical guarantees on the consistency of our estimator and establish convergence rates under standard assumptions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that C-MI-GAN outperforms existing methods, particularly when dealing with complex, nonlinear dependencies and limited sample sizes. Our approach opens new avenues for applications in causal discovery, feature selection, and information-theoretic analyses of complex systems.

Generative Models and Model Criticism via Optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy

This paper introduces a novel framework for both training generative models and evaluating their quality using an optimized version of the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) criterion. While generative models have seen remarkable advances, robust evaluation metrics remain challenging. We propose optimizing the kernel of the MMD test statistic to maximize its power against a specific alternative, creating a more sensitive measure of the discrepancy between generated and real data distributions. Our approach offers two key contributions: (1) a training objective for generative models based on this optimized MMD, which we demonstrate produces high-quality samples across various data types, and (2) a principled model criticism technique that provides fine-grained analysis of where generated samples deviate from real data. Through extensive experiments on synthetic distributions, image datasets, and scientific data, we show that our optimized MMD framework outperforms traditional MMD implementations and provides comparable results to adversarial approaches while offering better stability and interpretability. Our method bridges the gap between theoretical statistical tests and practical generative modeling, providing both a training criterion and evaluation metric within a unified framework.

FedNILM: Applying Federated Learning to NILM Applications at the Edge

Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) techniques have emerged as promising solutions for energy disaggregation in smart homes, enabling appliance-level consumption insights without intrusive metering. However, traditional NILM approaches face significant challenges in real-world deployments, including privacy concerns, data heterogeneity across households, and computational constraints on edge devices. This paper introduces FedNILM, a novel framework that leverages federated learning to address these limitations by enabling collaborative model training across distributed edge devices without sharing raw energy consumption data. Our approach allows smart meters and home energy management systems to collectively improve disaggregation accuracy while preserving user privacy and accommodating household-specific appliance signatures. Experimental results across diverse household datasets demonstrate that FedNILM achieves comparable disaggregation performance to centralized approaches (within 3-5% accuracy) while eliminating privacy risks and reducing communication overhead by up to 87%. Additionally, we present an adaptive compression technique that optimizes model updates for resource-constrained edge devices. FedNILM represents a significant advancement toward practical, privacy-preserving energy disaggregation systems that can scale effectively in heterogeneous smart home environments.

Joint Blind Motion Deblurring and Depth Estimation of Light Field

This paper presents a novel framework for simultaneously estimating scene depth and removing motion blur from light field images. Motion blur in light field photography presents unique challenges due to the multi-view nature of the captured data, but also offers opportunities through the rich spatial and angular information available. Our approach leverages the complementary relationship between depth estimation and deblurring: accurate depth maps can improve motion deblurring performance, while sharp images enable more precise depth estimation. We formulate this interdependence as a joint optimization problem within a unified computational framework. The proposed method alternates between depth estimation using epipolar plane images and motion kernel estimation across sub-aperture views, with each process informing the other iteratively. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world light field datasets demonstrate that our joint approach significantly outperforms sequential methods that address depth estimation and deblurring separately. Quantitative evaluations show improvements of up to 3.2dB in PSNR for deblurred images and 28% reduction in depth estimation error compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Our method is particularly effective for scenes with varying depth complexities and different motion blur severities, making it a promising solution for computational photography applications involving dynamic scenes.

Positional Contrastive Learning for Volumetric Medical Image Segmentation

This paper introduces a novel positional contrastive learning framework for volumetric medical image segmentation. While traditional contrastive learning approaches have shown promise in representation learning for medical imaging, they often fail to leverage the crucial spatial context inherent in volumetric data. Our proposed method, Positional Contrastive Learning (PCL), explicitly incorporates spatial position information into the contrastive learning objective, enabling the model to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and spatially aware. By contrasting features from different spatial positions within and across volumetric samples, PCL encourages the network to capture both local and global anatomical structures. We evaluate our approach on multiple challenging 3D medical image segmentation benchmarks, including brain MRI, abdominal CT, and cardiac MRI datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that PCL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods, with particular improvements in boundary delineation and handling of small anatomical structures. Furthermore, our method exhibits strong generalization capabilities with limited labeled data, making it particularly valuable for medical applications where annotation is expensive and time-consuming. The code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this direction.

ImVoteNet: Boosting 3D Object Detection in Point Clouds with Image Votes

We present ImVoteNet, a novel approach that leverages complementary image and point cloud data to enhance 3D object detection in indoor scenes. While point clouds provide accurate geometric information, they often lack the rich semantic features present in RGB images. Our method addresses this limitation by introducing "image votes"—a mechanism that lifts 2D image features into the 3D space to augment traditional point cloud-based detection frameworks. ImVoteNet first extracts 2D object proposals from RGB images, then projects the corresponding features into 3D space where they generate votes pointing to object centers. These image votes are aggregated with geometric votes from the point cloud in a unified voting framework. Extensive experiments on the SUN RGB-D and ScanNet datasets demonstrate that ImVoteNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods that use either modality alone, improving detection accuracy by 5-7% mAP across various object categories. Our approach is particularly effective for objects with distinctive visual appearances but limited geometric features, highlighting the complementary nature of the two modalities. ImVoteNet provides an efficient and effective solution for multimodal 3D object detection without requiring complex fusion architectures.

Learning Sharing Behaviors with Arbitrary Numbers of Agents

This paper presents a novel framework for learning cooperative sharing behaviors in multi-agent systems with variable agent populations. Unlike traditional approaches that require retraining when the number of agents changes, our method generalizes sharing policies across arbitrary agent counts. We formulate the problem as a population-invariant reinforcement learning task where agents must learn when and how to share resources, information, or tasks to maximize collective utility. Our approach combines graph neural networks with permutation-invariant policy architectures to enable scalability across different population sizes. Experimental results across diverse domains—including resource allocation, distributed sensing, and collaborative transportation—demonstrate that agents trained with our method effectively transfer sharing behaviors to scenarios with previously unseen numbers of participants. The learned policies outperform specialized fixed-population baselines by an average of 18% in efficiency metrics while maintaining robustness to agent additions and removals during execution. These findings suggest that our approach can significantly enhance coordination in dynamic multi-agent systems where population sizes cannot be predetermined.

Constrained Image Generation Using Binarized Neural Networks with Decision Procedures

This paper presents a novel approach to constrained image generation by leveraging binarized neural networks (BNNs) and formal decision procedures. While deep generative models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image synthesis, incorporating explicit constraints into the generation process remains challenging. We address this limitation by reformulating image generation as a constraint satisfaction problem within the discrete representation space of BNNs. Our framework translates high-level image constraints into logical formulas that can be efficiently solved using modern SAT and SMT solvers. By exploiting the binary nature of BNNs, we enable exact reasoning about the generative process while maintaining visual quality.
