Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach successfully generates images satisfying complex constraints including structural, semantic, and relational requirements, while outperforming conventional gradient-based constrained generation methods. Additionally, we show that our decision procedure integration provides formal guarantees about constraint satisfaction, opening new possibilities for reliable image generation in safety-critical applications. Our work bridges the gap between neural generative models and formal methods, offering both theoretical insights and practical benefits for controllable image synthesis.

PPDM: Parallel Point Detection and Matching for Real-time Human-Object Interaction Detection

Human-Object Interaction (HOI) detection is a critical task for understanding human behavior in visual scenes, with applications ranging from surveillance to human-computer interaction. This paper introduces Parallel Point Detection and Matching (PPDM), a novel real-time framework for HOI detection that addresses the efficiency limitations of previous methods. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on costly instance detection followed by interaction classification, PPDM reformulates HOI detection as a keypoint detection and matching problem. Our framework simultaneously detects human and object points along with their interaction points, and then associates these detections through a simple matching process. This parallel architecture eliminates the computational bottleneck of sequential processing and significantly reduces inference time. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including HICO-DET and V-COCO, demonstrate that PPDM achieves competitive accuracy while operating at 20 FPS on a single GPU, substantially outperforming existing methods in terms of speed-accuracy trade-off. Additionally, we provide ablation studies validating our design choices and showing the robustness of our approach across various interaction types and scene complexities. PPDM represents an important step toward deploying HOI detection in real-world applications that require both accuracy and real-time performance.

Dynamical Pose Estimation

This paper presents a novel framework for dynamical pose estimation that addresses the challenges of tracking human posture in complex, real-world scenarios. Unlike traditional static approaches, our method explicitly models the temporal evolution of human poses, incorporating motion dynamics to improve robustness against occlusions, motion blur, and rapid movements. We introduce a hybrid architecture that combines convolutional neural networks for spatial feature extraction with recurrent neural networks to capture temporal dependencies across video frames. Our approach leverages physics-based motion priors to constrain the solution space, resulting in more physically plausible pose trajectories. Extensive evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our dynamical pose estimation framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing the mean per-joint position error by 18% compared to static frame-by-frame methods. Furthermore, we show that our approach generalizes well to unseen activities and can operate in real-time on standard hardware, making it suitable for applications in human-computer interaction, augmented reality, and biomechanical analysis.

XGBoost Energy Consumption Prediction Based on Multi-System Data HVAC

This study presents a novel approach to predict energy consumption in HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning) systems using the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm applied to multi-system data. The increasing complexity of modern building management systems necessitates accurate energy forecasting to optimize operational efficiency and reduce environmental impact. Our research integrates heterogeneous data streams from multiple HVAC subsystems, including temperature sensors, occupancy patterns, equipment operational states, and external weather conditions. The XGBoost model was trained on a comprehensive dataset collected from 15 commercial buildings over a 24-month period, encompassing over 10 million data points. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves 94.3% prediction accuracy, outperforming traditional forecasting methods by 17.2%. Feature importance analysis revealed that thermal inertia patterns and occupancy-driven demand fluctuations were the most significant predictors of energy consumption. The model's robustness was validated through cross-validation across different building types and seasonal variations. This research contributes to the advancement of intelligent building management systems by providing a scalable and adaptive framework for energy consumption prediction that can be implemented in real-time control systems to optimize HVAC operations and reduce energy waste.

Learning to Segment Medical Images with Scribble-Supervision Alone

Medical image segmentation is a critical yet challenging task in computer-aided diagnosis and intervention planning. Traditional deep learning approaches rely on pixel-level annotations, which are time-consuming and expensive to obtain, particularly in the medical domain where expert knowledge is required. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for training deep neural networks for medical image segmentation using only scribble annotations—sparse, user-provided strokes indicating regions of interest. Our approach leverages a combination of partial cross-entropy loss on annotated pixels and a regularization strategy that propagates label information to unlabeled regions through feature similarity and spatial continuity constraints. We evaluate our method across multiple medical imaging modalities, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound datasets for various anatomical structures. Experimental results demonstrate that our scribble-supervised approach achieves segmentation performance comparable to fully-supervised methods (within 3-5% Dice coefficient) while reducing annotation time by up to 95%. Additionally, we show that our method outperforms other weakly-supervised approaches by a significant margin (7-10% improvement in Dice score). These findings suggest that scribble supervision alone is sufficient for accurate medical image segmentation, potentially enabling more rapid development of segmentation tools for clinical applications where annotation resources are limited.

Fault Diagnosis of Helical Gear Box using Large Margin K-Nearest Neighbors Classifier using Sound Signals

This paper presents a novel approach for fault diagnosis of helical gear boxes through acoustic signal analysis using a Large Margin K-Nearest Neighbors (LMKNN) classifier. Early detection of gear faults is crucial for preventing catastrophic failures and reducing maintenance costs in industrial applications. While vibration-based methods have been widely explored, acoustic monitoring offers advantages of non-contact measurement and sensitivity to incipient faults. In this study, sound signals were acquired from helical gear boxes operating under various fault conditions including tooth breakage, pitting, and surface wear at different load conditions. The raw acoustic signals were processed using time-domain, frequency-domain, and time-frequency domain feature extraction techniques to obtain a comprehensive feature set. Dimensionality reduction was performed using Principal Component Analysis to enhance computational efficiency. The proposed LMKNN classifier, which incorporates adaptive margin optimization, demonstrated superior classification accuracy (96.8%) compared to conventional KNN (91.2%) and Support Vector Machine (93.5%) methods. Experimental results validate that the proposed methodology can effectively identify and classify different fault types with high reliability even in the presence of background noise. This approach offers a promising solution for real-time condition monitoring of helical gear boxes in industrial environments.

LEAP: Learning Articulated Occupancy of People

We present LEAP, a novel framework for learning articulated 3D occupancy representations of human bodies from partial observations. Unlike existing approaches that rely on mesh or implicit surface representations, LEAP directly models the volumetric occupancy of the human body conditioned on pose parameters. Our method leverages a part-based canonical occupancy representation that can be efficiently transformed according to skeletal articulation, enabling realistic deformation of the body volume while maintaining anatomical consistency. By employing a neural occupancy field architecture with positional encoding and articulated transformations, LEAP achieves high-fidelity reconstruction of human bodies from sparse inputs such as RGB images, depth maps, or partial point clouds. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy, pose generalization, and computational efficiency. LEAP enables downstream applications including animation, virtual try-on, and human-scene interaction modeling. Our code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate further research in articulated human representation learning.

Learning 3D Semantic Scene Graphs from 3D Indoor Reconstructions

This paper presents a novel approach for automatically generating 3D semantic scene graphs from indoor scene reconstructions. While 3D scene reconstruction methods have advanced significantly, extracting structured, semantically meaningful representations from these reconstructions remains challenging. We introduce a framework that bridges this gap by learning to identify objects, their attributes, and their spatial and functional relationships within 3D indoor environments. Our method employs a hierarchical graph neural network architecture that processes point cloud data to identify objects, followed by relationship reasoning modules that establish connections between entities. We evaluate our approach on several large-scale indoor datasets, including ScanNet, Matterport3D, and 3RScan, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in scene graph construction with 87.3% accuracy in object detection and 83.5% accuracy in relationship prediction. The resulting 3D semantic scene graphs enable numerous downstream applications, including natural language querying of 3D spaces, scene manipulation, and improved human-robot interaction in indoor environments. Our work contributes a critical step toward enabling machines to develop human-like understanding of 3D spaces by capturing both the geometric and semantic structure of indoor scenes.

Learning Generalizable Physiological Representations from Large-scale Wearable Data

The proliferation of wearable devices has created unprecedented opportunities to monitor human physiological signals continuously in real-world settings. However, developing computational models that can extract meaningful, generalizable representations from these complex, noisy, and heterogeneous data streams remains challenging. In this work, we present a novel framework for learning robust physiological representations from large-scale wearable data collected across diverse populations and contexts. Our approach combines self-supervised learning techniques with physiologically-informed inductive biases to capture underlying patterns while maintaining biological plausibility. Using a dataset comprising over 10 million hours of multimodal physiological recordings from 100,000+ individuals, we demonstrate that our learned representations significantly outperform traditional feature engineering approaches and existing deep learning methods across multiple downstream tasks, including stress detection, sleep stage classification, and cardiovascular risk prediction. Importantly, our representations generalize effectively across different demographic groups, device types, and recording conditions, addressing critical limitations of previous approaches. We further show that these representations can be fine-tuned with minimal labeled data for personalized health applications. This work establishes a foundation for scalable, generalizable physiological modeling that can advance digital biomarker development and enable more equitable health monitoring technologies.

Fast and Accurate Image Super-Resolution with Deep Laplacian Pyramid Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to single image super-resolution (SISR) using Deep Laplacian Pyramid Networks (DLPN). While convolutional neural networks have shown remarkable performance in SISR tasks, they often struggle with the inherent ill-posed nature of reconstructing high-frequency details. Our proposed DLPN addresses this challenge by decomposing the super-resolution problem across multiple pyramid levels, progressively reconstructing high-resolution images in a coarse-to-fine manner. The architecture leverages the multi-scale properties of Laplacian pyramids to efficiently model different frequency bands of the target image. Our experiments demonstrate that DLPN achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets while maintaining lower computational complexity compared to existing methods. The model shows particular strength in recovering fine texture details and sharp edges, achieving improvements of up to 0.45dB PSNR over previous approaches. Additionally, DLPN demonstrates faster inference times, making it suitable for real-time applications. Both quantitative evaluations and visual comparisons confirm the effectiveness of our approach for high-quality image super-resolution.

Attention Neural Network for Trash Detection on Water Channels

This study presents a novel approach for automated trash detection in water channels using an attention-based neural network architecture. Water pollution from floating debris poses significant environmental challenges, affecting aquatic ecosystems and water management infrastructure. We propose a deep learning framework that incorporates attention mechanisms to enhance the detection accuracy of diverse trash objects in complex aquatic environments. Our model leverages spatial attention to focus on relevant regions within images while filtering out background noise from water reflections, vegetation, and varying lighting conditions. The network was trained and evaluated on a custom dataset of over 5,000 annotated images collected from urban canals, rivers, and drainage systems across different weather and lighting conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our attention-based approach achieves 92.7% detection accuracy, outperforming conventional CNN architectures by an average of 15.3%. The model successfully identifies various categories of floating debris, including plastic bottles, bags, styrofoam, and organic waste, even in challenging scenarios with partial occlusion or poor visibility. This research contributes to environmental monitoring technologies and provides a foundation for automated cleanup systems that can help mitigate water pollution in urban waterways.

T-CNN: Tubelets with Convolutional Neural Networks for Object Detection from Videos

This paper presents T-CNN, a novel framework for video-based object detection that leverages temporal information across frames to improve detection accuracy and consistency. Unlike traditional frame-by-frame approaches, T-CNN generates tubelets—sequences of bounding boxes linked across consecutive frames—to effectively capture the spatiotemporal nature of objects in videos. Our approach integrates convolutional neural networks with tubelet proposal generation and processing to address key challenges in video object detection, including motion blur, occlusion, and rare object poses. The framework consists of a three-stage pipeline: (1) CNN-based still-image detection, (2) tubelet generation through track-by-detection, and (3) tubelet-based classification and temporal refinement to suppress false positives and improve localization. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet VID dataset demonstrate that T-CNN significantly outperforms single-frame baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a mean average precision of 67.8%. Our approach shows particular strength in detecting objects under challenging conditions while maintaining computational efficiency. The results confirm that effectively incorporating temporal consistency through tubelets provides substantial benefits for object detection in video sequences.

Convolutional Kernel Networks for Graph-Structured Data

This paper introduces a novel approach to graph representation learning through the lens of convolutional kernel networks. While convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable success in grid-structured data domains, extending these architectures to irregular graph structures remains challenging. We present Graph Convolutional Kernel Networks (GCKN), a principled framework that bridges kernel methods with deep learning techniques for graph-structured data. Our approach maps graph inputs into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space through a sequence of kernel feature maps, each corresponding to a layer of graph convolution operations. Unlike traditional graph neural networks, GCKN provides theoretical guarantees while maintaining the flexibility of learned representations. We demonstrate that our kernel-based formulation naturally handles variable-sized graphs and preserves structural information through local graph motifs. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets for molecular property prediction, protein function classification, and social network analysis show that GCKN achieves state-of-the-art performance while offering better interpretability and robustness to structural perturbations. Furthermore, our method exhibits favorable computational complexity compared to existing graph kernel methods while retaining the expressive power of deep architectures. These results suggest that GCKN effectively bridges the gap between classical kernel methods and modern graph neural networks.

Automatic Viseme Vocabulary Construction to Enhance Continuous Lip-reading

Lip-reading, the task of recognizing speech from visual cues alone, remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech patterns and the complexity of mapping these patterns to phonetic units. This paper introduces a novel approach for automatic viseme vocabulary construction that significantly enhances the performance of continuous lip-reading systems. Unlike traditional methods that rely on manually defined viseme-to-phoneme mappings, our approach dynamically constructs an optimal viseme vocabulary by analyzing visual speech patterns in large-scale datasets. We employ a data-driven clustering algorithm that identifies visually similar phonemes and groups them into visemes based on their appearance and motion characteristics. The proposed method adapts to speaker-specific articulation patterns and contextual variations, resulting in a more robust representation of visual speech. Experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our automatic viseme vocabulary construction improves word recognition accuracy by 17.3% and sentence-level recognition by 12.8% compared to conventional phoneme-based approaches. Furthermore, our system shows enhanced resilience to variations in lighting conditions, speaker identity, and speech rate. These results highlight the potential of adaptive viseme modeling for real-world lip-reading applications in areas such as silent speech interfaces, audiovisual speech recognition, and assistive technologies for the hearing-impaired.

Non-binary deep transfer learning for image classification

This study presents a novel approach to transfer learning for image classification that transcends traditional binary classification frameworks. While most transfer learning techniques focus on binary adaptations of pre-trained models, our non-binary approach allows for more nuanced knowledge transfer across multiple domains and classification tasks simultaneously. We propose a hierarchical feature extraction architecture that preserves gradient information across the spectrum of class relationships, rather than reducing transfer to binary decisions. Experiments conducted on diverse image datasets including ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and specialized domain-specific collections demonstrate that our non-binary transfer learning method achieves 8-12% improvement in accuracy over conventional transfer learning approaches when handling complex multi-class problems. Furthermore, our approach reduces the required fine-tuning data by approximately 40% while maintaining comparable performance to fully-supervised methods. The framework also demonstrates enhanced robustness to domain shift and class imbalance scenarios. These results suggest that embracing the inherent non-binary nature of visual knowledge transfer more effectively leverages pre-trained representations for downstream image classification tasks.

Rethinking and Reweighting the Univariate Losses for Multi-Label Ranking: Consistency and Generalization

Multi-label ranking poses unique challenges in machine learning due to its complex label dependencies and diverse evaluation metrics. This paper critically examines the theoretical foundations of univariate loss functions in multi-label ranking frameworks and proposes a novel reweighting approach to address their limitations. We first establish statistical consistency properties for commonly used univariate losses when applied to multi-label ranking problems, identifying conditions under which these losses fail to converge to optimal rankers. Building on this analysis, we introduce an adaptive reweighting mechanism that dynamically adjusts the contribution of each label-specific loss component based on label correlations and ranking importance. Our theoretical results demonstrate that the proposed reweighted framework achieves consistency with respect to ranking-based evaluation metrics while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets across diverse domains show that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on datasets with complex label interactions. Furthermore, we provide generalization bounds that explain the improved sample complexity of our reweighted approach. This work bridges important gaps between the theoretical understanding of multi-label learning and practical ranking performance, offering both algorithmic innovations and theoretical insights for this challenging problem.

Learning Efficient Representation for Intrinsic Motivation

Intrinsic motivation mechanisms have shown promising results in reinforcement learning by enabling agents to explore environments in the absence of external rewards. However, current approaches often suffer from inefficient representation learning, leading to suboptimal exploration strategies. This paper introduces a novel framework for learning compact and efficient state representations specifically tailored for intrinsic motivation systems. Our approach combines variational inference with contrastive learning to distill high-dimensional observations into low-dimensional latent spaces that capture task-relevant information while discarding distracting features. We demonstrate that these learned representations significantly enhance the effectiveness of common intrinsic motivation methods, including curiosity-driven exploration and novelty detection. Extensive experiments across diverse environments show that our method achieves up to 45% improvement in sample efficiency and 30% better asymptotic performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the information content of our learned representations and their relationship to optimal exploration strategies. Our findings suggest that representation learning should be considered a crucial component when designing intrinsic motivation systems for complex reinforcement learning tasks.

Safety-guaranteed Reinforcement Learning based on Multi-class Support Vector Machine

This paper presents a novel approach to safety-guaranteed reinforcement learning (RL) by integrating multi-class support vector machine (SVM) techniques into the learning framework. Safety remains a critical challenge for deploying RL systems in real-world applications where constraint violations could lead to catastrophic consequences. Our method addresses this challenge by utilizing multi-class SVM to construct robust safety boundaries in the state-action space. We formulate the safety constraints as classification problems where unsafe regions are separated from safe ones with maximum margins. This approach enables the agent to learn policies that maintain high performance while providing formal safety guarantees during both training and deployment phases. The multi-class formulation allows our method to handle complex scenarios with multiple types of constraints simultaneously. Experimental results across various control tasks demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art RL algorithms while significantly reducing constraint violations. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis establishing probabilistic safety bounds that tighten with increasing training data. This work contributes to the development of trustworthy RL systems that can be confidently deployed in safety-critical domains.

The Clever Hans Effect in Anomaly Detection

This paper investigates the "Clever Hans effect" in machine learning anomaly detection systems, where models appear to successfully identify anomalies but actually rely on unintended data artifacts rather than meaningful patterns. Similar to the historical case of Clever Hans—the horse believed to perform arithmetic but actually responding to subtle human cues—our research reveals that many anomaly detection algorithms exploit spurious correlations in training data instead of learning generalizable concepts of anomalousness. Through extensive experiments across multiple domains including cybersecurity, manufacturing, and medical diagnostics, we demonstrate how these systems can achieve misleadingly high performance on benchmark datasets while failing in real-world deployment. We propose a novel evaluation framework that systematically identifies and quantifies these shortcut learning behaviors, revealing that up to 43% of apparent detection capability in state-of-the-art models stems from artifact exploitation rather than genuine anomaly recognition. Additionally, we introduce mitigation strategies including adversarial training techniques and causal representation learning approaches that significantly reduce reliance on spurious features. Our findings highlight critical limitations in current anomaly detection evaluation practices and offer practical guidance for developing more robust systems that detect genuine anomalies rather than dataset-specific artifacts.

Modulated Policy Hierarchies

This paper introduces Modulated Policy Hierarchies (MPH), a novel framework for organizing and controlling complex agent behaviors in reinforcement learning systems. MPH addresses the challenge of learning effective policies for tasks requiring multiple skills and adaptable decision-making by structuring policies in a hierarchical architecture where higher-level policies modulate the execution of lower-level ones. Unlike traditional hierarchical reinforcement learning approaches that decompose tasks through temporal abstraction or option frameworks, MPH employs a modulation mechanism that allows continuous parameter adjustment of base policies through context-aware higher-level controllers. Our approach enables flexible skill composition while maintaining end-to-end differentiability, facilitating efficient training through gradient-based optimization. Experimental results across diverse domains—including robotic manipulation, locomotion, and multi-agent coordination—demonstrate that MPH achieves superior sample efficiency, transfer learning capabilities, and performance compared to flat policy architectures and alternative hierarchical methods. We further show that the learned hierarchies exhibit interpretable specialization patterns, with different components naturally assuming distinct functional roles. This work contributes to the broader goal of developing modular, reusable, and interpretable learning systems for complex sequential decision-making problems.

Depth from Monocular Images using a Semi-Parallel Deep Neural Network (SPDNN) Hybrid Architecture

This paper presents a novel approach to monocular depth estimation through a Semi-Parallel Deep Neural Network (SPDNN) hybrid architecture. Accurate depth perception from single images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision with applications spanning autonomous navigation, augmented reality, and scene understanding. Our proposed SPDNN architecture leverages both parallel and sequential processing pathways to effectively capture multi-scale contextual information while maintaining computational efficiency. The network consists of two semi-independent branches that extract complementary features: one focused on global context and scene semantics, the other on local geometric structures and edge information. These branches periodically exchange information through custom cross-branch fusion modules before merging for final depth prediction. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets including NYU Depth V2, KITTI, and Make3D demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing relative error by 8.2% and improving structural similarity metrics by 6.5%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our semi-parallel design over fully parallel or sequential alternatives. The SPDNN architecture presents a promising direction for monocular depth estimation by effectively balancing local detail preservation with global scene understanding.

Multi-Plane Program Induction with 3D Box Priors

We present a novel approach to program induction for 3D scene understanding that leverages multi-plane representations and 3D box priors. Our method addresses the fundamental challenge of inferring structured, interpretable programs from raw visual inputs by decomposing 3D scenes into planar components guided by geometric constraints. By incorporating 3D box priors, we introduce strong inductive biases that significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of program synthesis for man-made environments where rectangular structures predominate. The proposed framework employs a hierarchical inference procedure that first identifies candidate planes from input data, then uses these planes to construct 3D box hypotheses, and finally generates programs that capture the underlying scene structure. Through extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of program correctness, scene reconstruction fidelity, and generalization to novel environments. The induced programs enable various downstream applications including scene editing, procedural generation, and physical reasoning. Our work represents a significant step toward bridging the gap between low-level geometric representations and high-level programmatic scene understanding.

Continuous Graph Neural Networks

This paper introduces Continuous Graph Neural Networks (CGNNs), a novel framework that extends traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to operate in continuous time and space domains. While conventional GNNs process discrete graph structures with fixed connectivity patterns, CGNNs model graph-structured data as a continuous dynamical system, allowing for more flexible representation of complex relational patterns. Our approach formulates message passing as a continuous diffusion process governed by differential equations, enabling the model to capture fine-grained temporal dynamics and smooth spatial relationships between nodes. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that CGNNs generalize existing GNN architectures while offering improved expressivity and stability properties. Experimental results across multiple domains—including molecular dynamics, traffic forecasting, and social network evolution—show that CGNNs consistently outperform discrete counterparts, particularly for problems involving temporally evolving graphs and irregularly sampled data. The continuous formulation also provides natural solutions to common challenges in graph learning, such as over-smoothing and scalability. Our work establishes a promising direction for graph representation learning that bridges discrete combinatorial structures with continuous mathematical formalisms.

Learning Fuzzy Clustering for SPECT/CT Segmentation via Convolutional Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to SPECT/CT image segmentation by integrating fuzzy clustering with convolutional neural networks (CNNs). While SPECT/CT imaging provides valuable functional and anatomical information for clinical diagnosis, accurate segmentation remains challenging due to inherent noise, limited resolution, and the complex nature of radiotracer distribution. Our method leverages the strengths of both fuzzy clustering algorithms, which handle uncertainty in image boundaries, and deep learning architectures, which excel at feature extraction. We propose a CNN framework that learns to predict optimal fuzzy clustering parameters and membership functions directly from multimodal SPECT/CT data. The network architecture incorporates dual pathways to process functional and anatomical information separately before fusion, followed by a fuzzy clustering layer that generates probabilistic segmentation maps. Experiments on a diverse dataset of 250 SPECT/CT scans across multiple anatomical regions demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional clustering methods and standard CNN segmentation models, achieving a 17% improvement in Dice coefficient and 23% reduction in boundary error. Additionally, the fuzzy nature of our segmentation provides clinically relevant uncertainty measures that can guide subsequent diagnostic decisions. This work establishes a promising direction for medical image segmentation that combines the interpretability of fuzzy clustering with the representational power of deep learning.

Evolving Attention with Residual Convolutions

Attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of modern deep learning architectures, particularly in sequence modeling tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel attention framework called Evolving Attention with Residual Convolutions (EARC) that dynamically adapts attention patterns through integration with residual convolutional structures. Our approach combines the global context modeling capabilities of attention mechanisms with the local feature extraction strengths of convolutional neural networks in a unified architecture. The key innovation lies in allowing attention weights to evolve across network layers through residual pathways, enabling more efficient gradient flow and feature reuse. Through extensive experimentation on multiple benchmarks including machine translation, document classification, and image recognition tasks, we demonstrate that EARC consistently outperforms traditional attention mechanisms and state-of-the-art models. Our approach achieves a 4.2% improvement in translation quality on WMT datasets and reduces computational complexity by 27% compared to standard Transformer models. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis showing how our residual attention patterns create implicit regularization effects that enhance model generalization. These results suggest that EARC represents a promising direction for developing more efficient and effective attention-based architectures.

A Simple and Scalable Shape Representation for 3D Reconstruction

This paper introduces a novel shape representation approach for 3D reconstruction that balances simplicity with scalability. Unlike existing methods that often require complex neural architectures or extensive computational resources, our representation decomposes 3D shapes into hierarchical local features that can be efficiently learned and composed. We demonstrate that this representation naturally handles varying levels of geometric detail while maintaining global coherence. Through extensive experiments on diverse datasets including ShapeNet, ScanNet, and real-world scans, we show that our method achieves competitive reconstruction quality compared to state-of-the-art approaches while requiring significantly less memory and computation time. The representation scales linearly with scene complexity and can handle large indoor environments that challenge existing methods. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach through applications in shape completion, novel view synthesis, and scene editing. Our code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in scalable 3D reconstruction.

AutoScaler: Scale-Attention Networks for Visual Correspondence

Visual correspondence, the task of matching points or regions between images, remains challenging due to variations in scale, viewpoint, and appearance. In this paper, we introduce AutoScaler, a novel neural architecture that explicitly addresses scale variation in visual correspondence tasks. Our approach incorporates scale-attention mechanisms that dynamically adapt feature extraction based on local content, enabling robust matching across significant scale differences. AutoScaler consists of a multi-scale feature pyramid network augmented with learnable scale-attention modules that weight features according to their relevance at different scales. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including HPatches, KITTI, and MegaDepth, we demonstrate that AutoScaler outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins, particularly in scenarios with extreme scale variations. Our approach achieves a 15% improvement in matching accuracy on challenging wide-baseline cases while maintaining computational efficiency. Additionally, we provide ablation studies that validate the contribution of each component of our scale-attention mechanism. AutoScaler provides a robust foundation for applications including structure-from-motion, visual localization, and image retrieval.

Co-Evolutionary Compression for Unpaired Image Translation

This paper introduces a novel framework for unpaired image translation that simultaneously addresses the challenges of model efficiency and translation quality. Our approach, Co-Evolutionary Compression (CEC), leverages principles from evolutionary computing to progressively compress and optimize generative adversarial networks while maintaining high-fidelity image translation capabilities. Unlike conventional methods that treat compression as a post-processing step, CEC integrates compression directly into the training process, allowing the translation and compression objectives to co-evolve. Through an iterative process of model mutation, selection, and inheritance, our framework automatically discovers efficient network architectures tailored to specific translation tasks. Extensive experiments across multiple unpaired translation benchmarks demonstrate that CEC achieves up to 85% reduction in model size and 3.2× inference speedup while preserving or even enhancing translation quality compared to uncompressed baselines. Our method generalizes across various GAN architectures, including CycleGAN and UNIT, and produces models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Both quantitative metrics and user studies confirm that CEC effectively balances the trade-off between computational efficiency and translation performance, establishing a new direction for efficient generative modeling.

Rank of Experts: Detection Network Ensemble

This paper presents Rank of Experts (RoE), a novel ensemble approach for object detection networks that significantly improves detection performance across diverse scenarios. Unlike traditional ensemble methods that rely on simple averaging of predictions, RoE introduces a dynamic ranking mechanism that evaluates the expertise of individual detection networks for each input instance. By analyzing confidence patterns, spatial consistency, and historical performance across object categories, our framework assigns varying weights to detector outputs based on their estimated reliability for specific detection tasks. Experiments conducted on COCO, Pascal VOC, and OpenImages datasets demonstrate that RoE achieves substantial improvements over both single-model approaches and conventional ensembles, with a 3.7% increase in mean Average Precision (mAP) compared to the strongest baseline ensemble. Notably, RoE shows particular strength in challenging scenarios involving occlusion, unusual object poses, and small objects. The computational overhead remains minimal during inference, making RoE practical for real-world applications. Our approach provides a principled framework for leveraging the complementary strengths of multiple detection architectures while mitigating their individual weaknesses.

Continuous Meta-Learning without Tasks

Traditional meta-learning frameworks typically rely on clearly defined task boundaries to facilitate learning across multiple tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to meta-learning that operates in continuous environments without explicit task delineation. Our framework, Continuous Task-Free Meta-Learning (CTML), leverages temporal coherence and latent context identification to adapt to gradually changing data distributions without requiring discrete task definitions. We formulate the problem as a continual learning process where the model must simultaneously infer the current context and adapt its parameters accordingly. Through extensive experimentation on both synthetic and real-world continuously varying datasets, we demonstrate that CTML outperforms conventional meta-learning approaches that depend on task boundaries. Our method shows particular strength in environments with smooth distributional shifts, achieving up to 23% improvement in predictive performance compared to task-based alternatives. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of our approach under certain conditions. These results suggest that explicitly modeling task boundaries may be unnecessary and potentially limiting in many real-world applications where environmental changes occur gradually rather than discretely.

Exploring Data Aggregation and Transformations to Generalize across Visual Domains

This paper investigates novel approaches to enhance cross-domain generalization in computer vision tasks by focusing on data aggregation strategies and transformations. We propose a framework that systematically combines diverse visual domains while applying targeted transformations to bridge domain gaps. Our method leverages statistical properties of different domains to identify and reduce domain-specific biases through adaptive feature normalization and augmentation techniques. Experiments conducted across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms standard domain generalization methods, achieving 12.3% improvement in classification accuracy on unseen target domains. We analyze how different aggregation strategies affect model robustness and find that carefully balanced representation of source domains, combined with our proposed transformation pipeline, leads to more domain-invariant feature learning. Furthermore, we introduce a domain similarity metric that effectively predicts generalization performance on novel domains. Our findings provide important insights into how data curation and transformation can be leveraged to build vision systems that generalize more reliably across visual domains without requiring target domain data during training.

Finding the most similar textual documents using Case-Based Reasoning

This paper presents a novel approach to textual document similarity detection using Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) techniques. The increasing volume of digital text documents creates challenges for information retrieval systems to efficiently identify semantically similar content. Our research explores how CBR's problem-solving paradigm—which retrieves, reuses, revises, and retains solutions from past cases—can be adapted to enhance document similarity detection. We propose a framework that represents documents as cases with feature vectors incorporating both lexical and semantic characteristics. The approach combines traditional term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) metrics with modern embedding techniques and implements a multi-level similarity function that considers structural, contextual, and conceptual aspects of text. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets demonstrates that our CBR-based approach outperforms conventional vector space models and basic embedding methods, achieving a 17% improvement in precision and 12% in recall for similar document retrieval tasks. The system also exhibits efficient adaptation to domain-specific terminology through its case retention mechanism. These findings suggest that CBR offers a promising framework for document similarity applications, particularly in specialized domains where contextual understanding is crucial.

Instance Segmentation with the Number of Clusters Incorporated in Embedding Learning

Instance segmentation remains a challenging task in computer vision, particularly when the number of instances is unknown prior to inference. This paper presents a novel approach that explicitly incorporates the number of clusters into the embedding learning process for instance segmentation. Our method learns discriminative pixel embeddings while simultaneously estimating the optimal number of instances present in an image. We propose a dual-branch architecture where the main branch learns pixel-wise embeddings and the auxiliary branch predicts the instance count, with a joint optimization objective that ensures consistency between the two tasks. By incorporating this count information during training, our embeddings become more discriminative for the specific clustering task they will face during inference. Experiments on challenging datasets including COCO, Cityscapes, and cell nuclei segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art embedding-based instance segmentation methods, improving mean Average Precision by 3.2% and reducing over-segmentation errors by 27%. Our method is particularly effective in scenarios with densely packed objects and varying instance counts. The code and pre-trained models are publicly available.

What Synthesis is Missing: Depth Adaptation Integrated with Weak Supervision for Indoor Scene Parsing

Indoor scene parsing remains a challenging computer vision task due to the complexity and diversity of indoor environments. While synthetic data has been used to address the scarcity of labeled real-world data, models trained on synthetic domains often fail to generalize well to real-world scenarios due to the domain gap. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that addresses the limitations of synthetic-to-real adaptation by integrating depth adaptation with weak supervision for indoor scene parsing. Our approach leverages depth information as a domain-invariant geometric cue to bridge the synthetic-real domain gap, while simultaneously incorporating weak labels from real environments to enhance semantic understanding. We introduce a Depth-Guided Adaptation Module (DGAM) that aligns feature distributions in the depth space, and a Weak Supervision Consistency Network (WSCN) that effectively utilizes sparse annotations to improve segmentation accuracy. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including NYUv2 and ScanNet demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation approaches, achieving up to 8.2% improvement in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU). Our analysis reveals that the integration of depth adaptation with weak supervision provides complementary benefits that address the fundamental limitations of using synthetic data alone. The proposed framework offers a practical solution for indoor scene parsing that reduces the dependency on fully-annotated real-world data while maintaining high performance.

Train, Diagnose and Fix: Interpretable Approach for Fine-grained Action Recognition

Fine-grained action recognition remains challenging due to subtle differences between similar action categories and the complex temporal dynamics of human movements. In this paper, we introduce a novel interpretable framework—Train, Diagnose and Fix (TDF)—that not only improves recognition performance but also provides transparent insights into model decision-making processes. Our approach first trains a baseline deep neural network on fine-grained action data, then employs a diagnostic module that identifies critical spatiotemporal regions where the model struggles to differentiate between confusing action classes. The diagnostic outputs generate visual attention maps highlighting discriminative features the model fails to capture. Our fixing stage then implements targeted regularization techniques that guide the model to focus on these previously overlooked discriminative regions. Experiments on three challenging fine-grained action datasets (FineGym, MPII Cooking, and Something-Something-V2) demonstrate that our TDF framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving accuracy by 3.2-5.7% over strong baselines. More importantly, our approach provides human-interpretable explanations for model predictions and errors, bridging the gap between performance and explainability in fine-grained action recognition systems. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component in our framework and its potential for application to other fine-grained visual recognition tasks.

Product Knowledge Graph Embedding for E-commerce

This paper introduces a novel approach to product knowledge graph embedding specifically designed for e-commerce applications. Knowledge graphs have emerged as powerful tools for organizing product information, but traditional embedding techniques often fail to capture the unique characteristics of e-commerce data, such as seasonal trends, customer preferences, and complex product relationships. Our proposed framework integrates multi-modal product attributes (textual descriptions, visual features, price points, and user interaction patterns) into a unified embedding space that preserves both structural and semantic relationships between products. Through extensive experiments on large-scale e-commerce datasets, we demonstrate that our embedding technique significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in key e-commerce tasks including product recommendation (+18.7% in NDCG), query understanding (+12.3% in relevance scores), and product categorization (+9.5% in F1-score). Additionally, our approach shows remarkable efficiency in handling cold-start products by effectively transferring knowledge from established product nodes. The resulting embeddings enable more intuitive product exploration and enhance search relevance, ultimately improving customer satisfaction and conversion rates in real-world e-commerce platforms.

Dataset Culling: Towards Efficient Training Of Distillation-Based Domain Specific Models

Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for creating compact, domain-specific models that maintain much of the performance of larger foundation models. However, the process remains computationally expensive, particularly when training on large datasets. This paper introduces "Dataset Culling," a systematic approach to identify and retain only the most informative training examples for knowledge distillation in domain-specific contexts. Our method employs a multi-stage filtering process that analyzes feature representations, prediction confidence, and example diversity to reduce training data while preserving critical information for student model learning. Experiments across five specialized domains demonstrate that models distilled on culled datasets (reduced by 40-70%) achieve comparable or superior performance to those trained on complete datasets, while significantly decreasing computational requirements. We provide theoretical insights into why certain examples contribute disproportionately to effective knowledge transfer and propose practical guidelines for implementing dataset culling in various distillation scenarios. Our approach addresses a critical efficiency bottleneck in model distillation workflows, enabling more sustainable development of specialized AI models.

A Semi-Supervised Classification Method of Apicomplexan Parasites and Host Cell Using Contrastive Learning Strategy

The accurate classification of apicomplexan parasites and their host cells remains a significant challenge in biomedical imaging analysis due to limited labeled data and morphological complexity. This study presents a novel semi-supervised classification approach leveraging contrastive learning strategies to address these limitations. Our method employs a two-stage framework: first, a contrastive learning pre-training phase that learns discriminative features from unlabeled microscopy images; second, a fine-tuning phase using a small set of labeled samples. We evaluated our approach on diverse microscopy datasets containing Toxoplasma gondii, Plasmodium spp., and Cryptosporidium parasites within various host cell environments. Results demonstrate that our contrastive learning strategy achieves 92.7% classification accuracy, outperforming traditional supervised approaches by 15.3% when using limited labeled data (10% of full dataset). Furthermore, the method shows robust generalization across different imaging conditions and parasite life stages. The proposed approach significantly reduces annotation burden while maintaining high classification performance, offering a practical solution for parasite-host classification in resource-constrained research settings. This work contributes to both the methodological advancement of semi-supervised learning in biomedical imaging and practical applications in parasitology research.

Cross-Global Attention Graph Kernel Network Prediction of Drug Prescription

The accurate prediction of drug prescriptions remains a significant challenge in healthcare systems, requiring models that can effectively capture complex relationships between patient data, disease patterns, and pharmaceutical properties. This paper introduces the Cross-Global Attention Graph Kernel Network (CGA-GKN), a novel deep learning architecture designed specifically for drug prescription prediction. Our approach leverages both local and global graph structures to model intricate interactions between drugs, diseases, and patient characteristics through a dual-attention mechanism that operates across multiple scales of medical data. The CGA-GKN incorporates specialized graph kernels that capture pharmacological similarities while maintaining interpretability of the prediction process. We evaluate our model on a comprehensive dataset comprising over 2 million prescriptions from 15 major healthcare institutions, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods with a 17.3% increase in prediction accuracy and a 22.8% reduction in inappropriate prescription recommendations. Furthermore, our model exhibits robust performance in scenarios with limited patient history and provides meaningful explanations for its predictions, facilitating clinical decision support. These results suggest that the CGA-GKN can serve as a valuable tool for healthcare providers in optimizing medication management and improving patient outcomes.

Relation-weighted Link Prediction for Disease Gene Identification

Identifying disease-associated genes is crucial for understanding disease mechanisms and developing effective therapeutic strategies. In this study, we propose a novel computational approach called Relation-weighted Link Prediction (RWLP) for disease gene identification. Our method leverages heterogeneous biological networks by incorporating weighted relationships between genes, proteins, and diseases to predict previously unknown disease-gene associations. RWLP integrates multiple biological data sources, including protein-protein interaction networks, gene expression profiles, functional annotations, and known disease-gene associations, while assigning different weights to various types of relationships based on their reliability and relevance. We evaluated RWLP on benchmark datasets spanning multiple disease categories and demonstrated its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher precision, recall, and area under the ROC curve. Case studies on Alzheimer's disease and type 2 diabetes revealed biologically plausible candidate genes, several of which were subsequently validated through literature evidence and experimental studies. The RWLP framework provides a powerful tool for prioritizing disease gene candidates, potentially accelerating biomarker discovery and therapeutic target identification for complex diseases.

Equivariant Graph Neural Networks for 3D Macromolecular Structure

Understanding the three-dimensional structure of macromolecules is crucial for elucidating their biological functions and developing therapeutic interventions. This paper introduces a novel equivariant graph neural network (EGNN) framework specifically designed for analyzing and predicting 3D macromolecular structures. Our approach leverages the inherent symmetries in macromolecular systems by employing SE(3)-equivariant neural networks that respect rotational and translational invariances of 3D structures. Unlike previous methods that often lose critical spatial information during feature extraction, our EGNN preserves geometric relationships while learning representations from atomic coordinates and chemical features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on multiple tasks including protein structure quality assessment, protein-protein interaction interface prediction, and RNA 3D structure modeling. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across these applications, showing a 15% improvement in structure quality prediction and 23% enhancement in binding site identification compared to non-equivariant architectures. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into how equivariance constraints guide the model to discover physically meaningful structural patterns. These results highlight the potential of equivariant representations for advancing computational structural biology and drug discovery.

Are You Imitating Me? Unsupervised Sparse Modeling for Group Activity Analysis from a Single Video

This paper introduces a novel unsupervised approach for analyzing group activities and identifying imitation behaviors from a single video sequence. We propose a sparse modeling framework that captures the temporal and spatial relationships between individuals without requiring labeled training data or multiple video examples. Our method decomposes human movements into a dictionary of basic motion primitives and identifies patterns of imitation by analyzing the sparse activation coefficients across different subjects. By leveraging techniques from compressive sensing and manifold learning, we develop a robust representation that can detect leader-follower dynamics, synchronization patterns, and mimicry behaviors even in challenging scenarios with occlusions and varying group sizes. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms supervised methods in identifying imitation patterns while requiring significantly less computational resources. The proposed framework enables new applications in social behavior analysis, crowd monitoring, and human-robot interaction by providing interpretable models of group dynamics from limited visual data.

$O(n)$ Connections are Expressive Enough: Universal Approximability of Sparse Transformers

This paper investigates the theoretical expressivity of sparse attention mechanisms in Transformer architectures. While standard Transformers employ dense attention with quadratic complexity in sequence length, we prove that sparse attention patterns with only linear ($O(n)$) connections per token are sufficient for universal function approximation. We establish this result by constructing a sparse attention mechanism that can simulate arbitrary computations while maintaining linear connection density. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that carefully designed sparse attention patterns preserve the representational power of full attention while significantly reducing computational and memory requirements. We provide formal proofs showing that these sparse Transformers can approximate any continuous function on compact domains with arbitrary precision, matching the expressivity guarantees of dense attention models. Additionally, we characterize the minimal sparsity patterns required for this universal approximation property and analyze the trade-offs between sparsity, expressivity, and computational efficiency. These findings have important implications for scaling Transformer models to longer sequences and larger architectures, suggesting that the quadratic complexity of standard attention is not a fundamental requirement for powerful sequence modeling.

Deepzzle: Solving Visual Jigsaw Puzzles with Deep Learning and Shortest Path Optimization

This paper introduces Deepzzle, a novel hybrid approach to solving visual jigsaw puzzles that combines deep learning techniques with shortest path optimization algorithms. Visual jigsaw puzzles present a significant computational challenge, requiring both pattern recognition and complex spatial reasoning. Our framework employs a two-stage methodology: first, a convolutional neural network architecture trained on diverse puzzle datasets learns to predict pairwise compatibility between puzzle pieces based on visual features; second, these compatibility scores are transformed into a weighted graph representation where nodes represent puzzle pieces and edge weights indicate connection probabilities. We then apply a modified Dijkstra's algorithm to determine the optimal assembly sequence that minimizes the global reconstruction error. Experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that Deepzzle achieves state-of-the-art performance, successfully reconstructing puzzles with up to 1000 pieces and showing particular robustness to challenging conditions including image noise, lighting variations, and non-standard piece shapes. Our approach outperforms existing methods by an average of 18% in reconstruction accuracy while reducing computational time by 35%. These results highlight the potential of combining deep learning with classical optimization techniques for solving complex visual reasoning tasks.

Oracle-Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Factored MDPs with Unknown Structure

This paper addresses the challenge of reinforcement learning in factored Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) when the underlying factorization structure is unknown. Factored MDPs offer a compact representation for environments with high-dimensional state spaces, but most existing algorithms assume prior knowledge of the state factors and their dependencies. We introduce a novel oracle-efficient algorithm that simultaneously learns the factorization structure while optimizing a policy. Our approach leverages statistical techniques to identify conditional independence relationships among state variables and dynamically constructs a factored representation of the environment. We prove that our algorithm achieves regret bounds that depend only polynomially on the number of relevant factors rather than the full state space dimension, while requiring only polynomial sample complexity. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic benchmarks and practical domains demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms structure-agnostic approaches and competes favorably with algorithms that have access to the true factorization. These results represent an important step toward making reinforcement learning practical in complex environments where domain knowledge about structural properties may be limited or unavailable.

Patch-Ordering as a Regularization for Inverse Problems in Image Processing

This paper introduces a novel regularization approach for inverse problems in image processing based on patch ordering. While traditional regularization methods often rely on global image priors or local patch statistics, our approach leverages the inherent structure formed by ordering similar patches. We demonstrate that arranging image patches according to their mutual similarities creates a smooth and regular signal that can be effectively exploited as a powerful prior. This patch-ordering framework transforms the high-dimensional image space into a one-dimensional ordered sequence where regularization becomes more tractable. We formulate this approach mathematically and develop efficient algorithms to incorporate it into various inverse problems including denoising, deblurring, and inpainting. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world images demonstrate that our method outperforms several state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in preserving fine details and textures while effectively removing artifacts. The proposed approach is computationally efficient and can be readily integrated with existing optimization frameworks. Our results suggest that patch-ordering regularization provides a promising direction for solving challenging inverse problems in image processing.

CASSOD-Net: Cascaded and Separable Structures of Dilated Convolution for Embedded Vision Systems and Applications

This paper presents CASSOD-Net, a novel deep learning architecture designed specifically for resource-constrained embedded vision systems. We introduce a lightweight network that leverages cascaded and separable structures of dilated convolutions to achieve an optimal balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. The proposed architecture systematically decomposes standard convolution operations into depth-wise separable components combined with strategically placed dilated convolutions, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining receptive field size. Our experimental results demonstrate that CASSOD-Net achieves competitive accuracy on standard computer vision benchmarks while requiring up to 85% fewer parameters and 73% less computational overhead compared to conventional architectures. We evaluate the model across multiple embedded platforms, including FPGA, mobile SoCs, and microcontrollers, demonstrating real-time performance for critical vision tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and instance recognition. The architecture's cascading structure enables effective feature reuse and creates multiple paths for gradient flow, improving both training stability and inference performance. CASSOD-Net represents a significant advancement for deploying sophisticated computer vision capabilities on resource-limited edge devices across various applications including surveillance, autonomous systems, and IoT devices.

Multi-Level Feature Fusion Mechanism for Single Image Super-Resolution

This paper presents a novel Multi-Level Feature Fusion (MLFF) mechanism for Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR), addressing the challenge of reconstructing high-resolution images from their low-resolution counterparts. Unlike conventional approaches that primarily focus on shallow feature extraction or deep hierarchical architectures, our proposed method leverages information across multiple feature levels through a sophisticated fusion framework. The MLFF mechanism systematically integrates local textural details with global semantic information by establishing dense connections between different network depths. Our architecture incorporates parallel feature extraction pathways with varying receptive fields, followed by adaptive fusion modules that dynamically weight features based on their contribution to reconstruction quality. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of up to 0.45dB in PSNR and 0.023 in SSIM metrics. Visual assessments confirm superior restoration of fine textures and structural details, particularly in challenging scenarios with complex patterns. The proposed MLFF mechanism maintains computational efficiency while significantly enhancing super-resolution performance, making it suitable for practical applications requiring high-quality image upscaling.

Active Learning for Deep Neural Networks on Edge Devices

This paper presents a novel framework for implementing active learning strategies on resource-constrained edge devices to optimize deep neural network (DNN) training. As DNNs continue to permeate edge computing applications, the challenges of limited computational resources, energy constraints, and restricted access to labeled data become increasingly significant. Our approach enables edge devices to intelligently select the most informative samples for labeling, thereby reducing annotation costs while maintaining model performance. We introduce a lightweight uncertainty sampling technique that identifies informative samples with minimal computational overhead, and propose an adaptive batch selection mechanism that dynamically adjusts based on resource availability. Experimental results across various edge platforms (including smartphones, IoT devices, and embedded systems) demonstrate that our active learning framework reduces labeling requirements by up to 60% while achieving comparable accuracy to fully-supervised approaches. Additionally, our method decreases energy consumption by 45% and memory usage by 30% compared to traditional training methods. These findings suggest that active learning provides a promising solution for deploying efficient, high-performing deep learning models in edge computing environments where resources and labeled data are limited.

Extreme Learning Machine Design for Dealing with Unrepresentative Features

This paper addresses a critical challenge in machine learning: the degradation of model performance when training data contains unrepresentative features that fail to generalize to test environments. We propose a novel Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) architecture designed specifically to identify and mitigate the impact of unrepresentative features during training. Our approach introduces a feature importance evaluation mechanism within the ELM framework that dynamically adjusts the influence of input features based on their stability across validation samples. By incorporating a regularization term that penalizes weights associated with highly variable features, our method effectively reduces the model's dependency on potentially unrepresentative patterns. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard ELM implementations by an average of 17% in accuracy when distribution shifts occur between training and testing environments. Furthermore, our modified ELM architecture maintains computational efficiency, preserving the rapid training characteristic of traditional ELMs while significantly improving robustness to feature distribution shifts. These results suggest that our approach offers a promising solution for deploying ELMs in dynamic real-world environments where data distributions may evolve over time.

Video Saliency Prediction Using Enhanced Spatiotemporal Alignment Network

This paper introduces a novel approach to video saliency prediction through an Enhanced Spatiotemporal Alignment Network (ESTAN). Predicting human visual attention in dynamic scenes requires effective modeling of both spatial features and temporal dependencies across video frames. Our proposed ESTAN architecture addresses this challenge by implementing a dual-stream framework that processes spatial and temporal information in parallel before aligning and fusing them through a dedicated alignment module. The spatial stream extracts hierarchical visual features using a modified convolutional backbone, while the temporal stream captures motion patterns and frame-to-frame dependencies via a recurrent mechanism enhanced with 3D convolutions. Our key contribution lies in the spatiotemporal alignment module, which dynamically weights and aligns features from both streams using cross-attention mechanisms. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including DHF1K, Hollywood-2, and UCF-Sports demonstrate that ESTAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 5.2% in NSS, 3.8% in AUC-J, and 4.7% in sAUC metrics. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our alignment module, while visualization results illustrate the model's ability to accurately predict human fixations even in challenging scenarios with complex motion patterns and multiple salient objects. The proposed approach offers a promising direction for video saliency modeling with potential applications in video compression, autonomous systems, and computational cinematography.

A Targeted Universal Attack on Graph Convolutional Network

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as powerful deep learning models for graph-structured data analysis across numerous applications. However, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks raises significant security concerns. In this paper, we introduce a novel targeted universal attack framework specifically designed to compromise GCN models. Unlike existing methods that craft instance-specific perturbations, our approach generates a single universal perturbation pattern capable of causing targeted misclassification across multiple graph instances. We formulate this as a bi-level optimization problem that jointly optimizes for attack transferability and effectiveness while maintaining perturbation imperceptibility. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed, we demonstrate that our attack achieves high success rates (>85%) with minimal perturbations to the graph structure, even when transferring to different GCN architectures. Furthermore, we analyze the topological properties that make certain nodes particularly vulnerable to our attack. Our findings highlight critical security vulnerabilities in GCN models and emphasize the need for robust defense mechanisms against universal adversarial attacks in graph-based learning systems.

Exploiting Context for Robustness to Label Noise in Active Learning

Active learning strategies aim to reduce annotation costs by selecting the most informative samples for labeling. However, these approaches often suffer from performance degradation when annotators provide noisy or incorrect labels, a common occurrence in real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a novel context-aware active learning framework that enhances robustness against label noise. Our approach leverages contextual information surrounding data points to identify potential annotation errors and adjust the learning process accordingly. By incorporating a context-sensitive uncertainty estimation method, we can better distinguish between truly ambiguous samples and those likely to receive noisy labels. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional active learning approaches in the presence of various noise levels. When subjected to 30% random label noise, our approach maintains up to 15% higher classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we show that exploiting contextual relationships enables more effective sample selection strategies that prioritize both informativeness and label reliability. These results highlight the importance of context-awareness in developing robust active learning systems for real-world applications where perfect annotations cannot be guaranteed.

Large-Scale Automatic Labeling of Video Events with Verbs Based on Event-Participant Interaction

This paper presents a novel framework for automatically labeling events in video data using verbs that accurately describe the interactions between participants. We address the challenge of large-scale video understanding by focusing on event-participant relationships as the primary semantic unit for analysis. Our approach combines computer vision techniques with natural language processing to identify participants in video segments and characterize their interactions through appropriate verb assignments. We introduce a hierarchical interaction model that captures both fine-grained motion patterns and high-level semantic relationships between entities. Experiments conducted on a diverse dataset of 250,000 video clips demonstrate that our method achieves 78.3% accuracy in verb assignment, significantly outperforming existing approaches by 12.7%. The resulting labeled dataset, which we make publicly available, contains over 1.2 million event-verb annotations across 3,400 distinct verb categories. Our work enables more nuanced video search, retrieval, and understanding by providing a semantically rich representation of video content based on actions and interactions rather than merely objects and scenes. This approach shows particular promise for applications in surveillance, human behavior analysis, and content-based video retrieval.

Extrapolating Beyond Suboptimal Demonstrations via Inverse Reinforcement Learning from Observations

Learning from demonstrations is a powerful paradigm for training artificial agents, but is often limited by the quality of available demonstrations, which may be suboptimal or incomplete. In this paper, we present a novel approach to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) that enables agents to extrapolate beyond the capabilities demonstrated in suboptimal examples. Our method learns reward functions solely from observations without requiring action labels, making it applicable to scenarios where only state trajectories are available. We introduce a comparative preference framework that identifies which portions of demonstrations are more likely to be optimal, allowing the agent to selectively learn from the most instructive segments while discounting suboptimal behaviors. Through theoretical analysis, we establish convergence guarantees for our approach and characterize the conditions under which extrapolation beyond demonstration quality is possible. Experiments across diverse environments, including robotic manipulation tasks and simulated navigation problems, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms both behavioral cloning and existing IRL approaches when learning from suboptimal data. Notably, agents trained with our approach achieve performance levels that exceed those of the demonstrators themselves, effectively learning what the demonstrator was trying to accomplish rather than merely mimicking observed behavior.

Learning Granularity-Aware Convolutional Neural Network for Fine-Grained Visual Classification
