Pyramidal Edge-maps and Attention based Guided Thermal Super-resolution

This paper presents a novel approach to thermal image super-resolution using pyramidal edge-maps and attention mechanisms guided by visible spectrum information. Thermal imaging, while valuable for numerous applications including surveillance, medical diagnostics, and autonomous systems, often suffers from limited spatial resolution due to hardware constraints. We propose a deep learning framework that leverages the complementary high-frequency details present in visible images to enhance the resolution of corresponding thermal imagery. Our method introduces a pyramidal edge-map extraction module that captures multi-scale structural information from visible images, which is then integrated into the thermal super-resolution process through a custom attention mechanism. This attention-based guidance allows the network to selectively transfer relevant structural details while preserving the thermal characteristics of the original image. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art thermal super-resolution methods, achieving improvements of up to 2.3dB in PSNR and 0.08 in SSIM for 4× upscaling tasks. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of both the pyramidal edge-map representation and the attention guidance mechanism. The proposed method maintains thermal fidelity while substantially enhancing fine details, making it particularly suitable for applications requiring both high spatial resolution and accurate thermal information.

Evaluation of Spectral Learning for the Identification of Hidden Markov Models

This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of spectral learning algorithms for the identification of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). While traditional approaches like Expectation-Maximization suffer from local optima issues and computational inefficiency for large datasets, spectral methods offer a promising alternative with theoretical guarantees of global optimality. We systematically compare several spectral learning variants against established methods across synthetic and real-world datasets of varying complexity and scale. Our experiments demonstrate that spectral methods achieve comparable or superior accuracy to traditional approaches while requiring significantly less computational time, particularly for models with high-dimensional latent spaces. Furthermore, we analyze the sensitivity of spectral algorithms to sample size, noise levels, and model misspecification. Our findings indicate that spectral learning represents a robust and efficient approach for HMM identification, though certain modifications are necessary to ensure stability in low-sample regimes. We also provide practical guidelines for algorithm selection and parameter tuning based on data characteristics and application requirements.

Revisiting 2D Convolutional Neural Networks for Graph-based Applications

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the predominant architecture for learning on graph-structured data. However, their widespread adoption has overshadowed the potential of adapting traditional 2D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for graph-based tasks. In this paper, we revisit and reevaluate the application of 2D CNNs to graph problems through novel graph-to-grid transformation techniques. We propose a framework that effectively preserves topological information while projecting graphs onto 2D grid structures, enabling the direct application of well-established CNN architectures. Our extensive experiments across multiple domains—including molecular property prediction, social network analysis, and citation networks—demonstrate that properly adapted 2D CNNs can achieve competitive or superior performance compared to specialized GNN variants, while offering significant computational efficiency advantages. Furthermore, we show that these models benefit from the extensive optimization and hardware acceleration available for traditional CNNs. This work challenges the notion that specialized graph architectures are always necessary and opens new research directions for leveraging the mature CNN ecosystem in graph-based applications.

Realistic Image Generation using Region-phrase Attention

This paper introduces a novel approach to image generation that leverages region-phrase attention mechanisms to produce highly realistic images with precise spatial control. Our method, which we call Region-Phrase Attention Network (RPAN), bridges the gap between text-to-image generation and fine-grained spatial composition by enabling explicit mapping between textual phrases and specific regions in the generated image. Unlike previous approaches that treat text prompts as holistic descriptions, RPAN decomposes text into semantic phrases and establishes direct attention pathways to corresponding spatial regions during the generation process. Through a multi-stage training procedure, our model learns to maintain global coherence while respecting local semantic constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RPAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks, achieving a 27% improvement in region-specific fidelity and a 19% enhancement in overall image quality as measured by FID scores. Human evaluation studies further confirm that images generated by our approach exhibit superior realism and adherence to spatial specifications. The proposed region-phrase attention mechanism represents a significant advancement in controllable image synthesis, with potential applications in creative design, content creation, and virtual environment development.

Polylidar3D -- Fast Polygon Extraction from 3D Data

This paper presents Polylidar3D, a novel algorithm for efficient polygon extraction from various 3D data representations including point clouds, depth images, and triangular meshes. Our approach addresses the challenging problem of identifying and extracting planar segments and their corresponding boundary polygons in complex 3D environments. Polylidar3D employs a multi-stage pipeline that includes dominant plane detection, mesh construction when necessary, efficient planar segmentation using a region-growing approach, and robust boundary extraction with hole identification. The algorithm incorporates configurable filtering mechanisms to handle noise and outliers commonly present in real-world sensor data. Experimental evaluation across diverse datasets demonstrates that Polylidar3D achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both computational efficiency and extraction accuracy. Processing times of a few milliseconds for typical indoor scenes make it suitable for real-time applications in robotics, augmented reality, and 3D scene understanding. We provide comprehensive benchmarks comparing Polylidar3D against existing methods and offer the implementation as an open-source library with Python bindings to facilitate adoption by the research community.

Graph Attention Networks with Positional Embeddings

Graph Attention Networks (GATs) have emerged as powerful architectures for graph-structured data, allowing nodes to attend differentially to their neighbors. However, standard GATs lack the ability to capture structural and positional information within graphs, which limits their expressiveness on tasks where node positioning is crucial. In this paper, we introduce Graph Attention Networks with Positional Embeddings (GAT-PE), a novel framework that enhances traditional GATs by incorporating explicit positional information. Our approach leverages Laplacian eigenvector-based positional encodings that capture the global graph structure while preserving the inductive capabilities of attention mechanisms. Through extensive experiments on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks across diverse domains, we demonstrate that GAT-PE consistently outperforms standard GATs and other state-of-the-art graph neural networks. Notably, our model achieves significant improvements on tasks with strong structural dependencies, where positional information proves essential. Further analysis reveals that the learned attention weights effectively integrate both feature-based and position-based information, resulting in more informative node representations. Our work provides a principled approach to incorporating structural inductive biases into graph attention mechanisms, addressing a fundamental limitation in existing graph neural network architectures.

Uniform State Abstraction For Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework for state abstraction in reinforcement learning (RL) that emphasizes uniformity across the state space. While traditional abstraction methods often create representations of varying quality across different regions of the state space, our uniform state abstraction approach ensures consistent fidelity throughout the environment. We formalize the notion of uniformity in abstraction and prove that it provides theoretical guarantees on worst-case approximation error. Through extensive experiments on benchmark RL tasks, we demonstrate that our uniform abstraction method significantly improves learning efficiency and policy robustness compared to non-uniform approaches, particularly in environments with sparse rewards or deceptive features. The uniformity principle enables more reliable transfer learning and generalization by preventing the abstraction from overfitting to specific regions of the state space. Our results suggest that prioritizing uniformity in state representation is a promising direction for developing more reliable and sample-efficient reinforcement learning algorithms.

Generative Hierarchical Features from Synthesizing Images

This paper introduces a novel approach to learning hierarchical visual representations through image synthesis. We propose a framework that leverages generative modeling to extract multi-scale features that capture both local details and global semantic structures in images. Unlike traditional discriminative methods that rely solely on classification or regression tasks, our approach learns representations by reconstructing and synthesizing images across different levels of abstraction. By training our model to generate images from latent representations at varying hierarchical levels, we enforce the learning of features that preserve information necessary for synthesis while organizing visual concepts in a hierarchically meaningful way. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that these generatively learned hierarchical features outperform conventional approaches on various downstream tasks including classification, segmentation, and few-shot learning. Furthermore, we show that our representation enables intuitive manipulation of visual attributes across different semantic levels. Our findings suggest that image synthesis provides a powerful self-supervised signal for learning rich hierarchical representations that generalize well across visual understanding tasks.

A Survey on Machine Learning Techniques for Auto Labeling of Video, Audio, and Text Data

This survey provides a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art machine learning techniques for automatic labeling of multimodal data across video, audio, and text domains. As the volume of unlabeled multimedia data continues to grow exponentially, efficient and accurate auto-labeling methods have become essential for developing robust AI systems. We systematically categorize approaches based on learning paradigms—supervised, semi-supervised, weakly-supervised, and unsupervised—and examine their applications across modalities. For video data, we review techniques spanning object detection, action recognition, and scene understanding. In the audio domain, we explore speech recognition, speaker identification, and acoustic event detection methods. For text data, we analyze named entity recognition, sentiment classification, and topic modeling approaches. Our analysis reveals that while modality-specific techniques remain important, recent advances in cross-modal learning and foundation models have enabled significant improvements in auto-labeling performance. We identify key challenges including domain adaptation, data imbalance, temporal coherence, and computational efficiency. Finally, we discuss emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, multimodal transformers, and human-in-the-loop labeling systems, providing directions for future research in this rapidly evolving field.

Abstract: Coarse-to-Fine Searching for Efficient Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper presents a novel architecture search framework for Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that balances computational efficiency with generative quality. We propose a coarse-to-fine search strategy that progressively refines network architectures through a hierarchical optimization process. Our approach begins with a broad exploration of the architectural search space using lightweight proxy models, then iteratively narrows the focus to promising regions while increasing model fidelity. We introduce an adaptive resource allocation mechanism that dynamically adjusts computational budgets during the search process based on architecture performance. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method discovers GAN architectures that achieve comparable or superior Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores while requiring significantly fewer parameters and reduced inference time compared to manually designed state-of-the-art models. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our coarse-to-fine strategy over traditional one-shot search methods. The discovered architectures reveal interesting structural patterns that challenge conventional GAN design principles, suggesting new directions for efficient generative model development.

Unsupervised Hierarchical Concept Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework for unsupervised hierarchical concept learning, addressing the challenge of automatically discovering and organizing conceptual knowledge without labeled data. Our approach leverages recent advances in self-supervised representation learning to identify latent concepts from unstructured data and arrange them in meaningful hierarchical structures. We propose a two-phase methodology: first, a concept discovery phase employing clustering techniques with information-theoretic regularization to identify coherent concept groups; second, a hierarchy induction phase that establishes parent-child relationships between concepts based on semantic abstraction levels. Experiments across diverse domains—including images, text, and multimodal data—demonstrate that our method successfully recovers interpretable concept hierarchies that align with human categorization. Quantitative evaluation shows our approach outperforms existing unsupervised concept learning methods by 18% on hierarchy quality metrics and 12% on concept coherence measures. The resulting hierarchical structures not only facilitate improved knowledge organization but also enhance downstream tasks such as zero-shot learning and explainable AI. Our work provides new insights into how machines can autonomously develop structured conceptual knowledge that mirrors human cognitive organization.

Conditioning of Reinforcement Learning Agents and its Policy Regularization Application

This paper introduces a novel framework for conditioning reinforcement learning (RL) agents on auxiliary information and demonstrates its effectiveness as a policy regularization technique. We formalize a conditioning mechanism that enables RL agents to incorporate diverse forms of contextual information—such as task specifications, demonstrations, or environmental constraints—directly into the policy learning process. Our approach creates a unified architecture where conditioning signals guide exploration and exploitation while maintaining robustness to variations in the input conditioning. Through theoretical analysis, we establish that this conditioning framework serves as an implicit regularizer, preventing overfitting and promoting generalization across task variations. Empirical evaluations across continuous control benchmarks and complex navigation tasks demonstrate that conditioned policies consistently outperform their unconditioned counterparts in sample efficiency, asymptotic performance, and transfer learning capabilities. Additionally, we show that our method can effectively leverage heterogeneous conditioning sources, including human preferences and symbolic constraints, without architectural modifications. These results suggest that explicit conditioning provides a versatile approach to policy regularization that enhances both performance and generalization in reinforcement learning systems.

CoAtNet: Marrying Convolution and Attention for All Data Sizes

This paper introduces CoAtNet (Convolution and Attention Network), a novel hybrid architecture that effectively combines the strengths of convolution and self-attention to create a more powerful and efficient backbone for computer vision tasks. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at capturing local patterns and maintaining translation equivariance, and transformers with self-attention mechanisms demonstrate superior global modeling capabilities, each approach has inherent limitations. We propose a principled integration of these complementary paradigms that preserves their respective advantages while addressing their individual shortcomings. Through extensive empirical studies, we identify key design principles for successfully fusing convolution and attention layers. Our CoAtNet architecture demonstrates remarkable scalability across varying data regimes, from limited to abundant training samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that CoAtNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming both pure CNN and transformer-based approaches. Notably, on ImageNet, our model attains 86.0% top-1 accuracy without extra data, and 89.1% when pre-trained on larger datasets, while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. These results highlight the effectiveness of our hybrid approach and suggest a promising direction for future vision backbone design.

The Immersion of Directed Multi-graphs in Embedding Fields: Generalisations

This paper explores novel approaches to embedding directed multi-graphs within continuous vector fields, extending classical graph embedding techniques to accommodate more complex structures. We present a generalized theoretical framework that addresses the unique challenges posed by directed edges and multiple connections between node pairs. Our approach leverages differential geometry and topological field theory to construct embedding spaces that preserve both local and global graph properties. We demonstrate that conventional embedding methods can be extended through the introduction of orientation-preserving mappings and multi-dimensional tensors that capture edge multiplicity. The theoretical results are accompanied by algorithmic implementations that achieve significant improvements in representation fidelity compared to traditional methods. We validate our approach on synthetic datasets and real-world networks from various domains, showing particular efficacy for biological networks, citation graphs, and communication patterns. These generalizations open new avenues for analyzing complex relational data while maintaining computational tractability. Our findings suggest that the proposed embedding techniques can be further extended to hypergraphs and time-varying networks.

Optimization of Molecules via Deep Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a novel approach to molecular optimization using deep reinforcement learning (RL) techniques. We formulate the molecular design process as a Markov decision process where molecular modifications serve as actions, and desired chemical properties define the reward function. Our framework employs a graph-based representation of molecules combined with a deep Q-network architecture that learns to navigate the vast chemical space efficiently. The agent is trained to optimize multiple objectives simultaneously, including drug-likeness, synthetic accessibility, and target biological activity. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional optimization methods and previous machine learning approaches, discovering novel molecules with improved properties while maintaining structural validity. We observe a 37% improvement in identifying molecules with desired properties compared to established baselines. Additionally, we provide extensive ablation studies analyzing the impact of different reward formulations and neural network architectures. This work establishes a promising direction for computer-aided drug discovery and materials design by enabling efficient exploration of chemical space guided by reinforcement learning.

Explaining Away Attacks Against Neural Networks

Neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse domains, yet their vulnerability to adversarial attacks remains a significant concern for deployment in security-critical applications. In this paper, we introduce the concept of "explaining away attacks," a novel framework for understanding and mitigating adversarial vulnerabilities through the lens of Bayesian inference. We demonstrate how adversaries can exploit the explaining away phenomenon—where the presence of one explanation for observed data reduces the need for alternative explanations—to manipulate neural network predictions while maintaining stealth. Our analysis reveals that conventional neural architectures implicitly encode explaining away relationships that can be systematically targeted. We empirically evaluate our framework across image classification, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning domains, showing that explaining away attacks can bypass existing defenses with minimal perturbations. To counter these vulnerabilities, we propose architectural modifications and training procedures that explicitly account for explaining away effects, demonstrating improved robustness on benchmark datasets. Our findings provide theoretical insights into the fundamental nature of adversarial examples and offer practical approaches to developing more secure neural systems.

Learning Transferable Cooperative Behavior in Multi-Agent Teams

This paper presents a novel framework for developing transferable cooperative behaviors in multi-agent systems. We address the fundamental challenge of enabling agents to learn collaborative strategies that can be effectively applied across different tasks and team compositions without requiring complete retraining. Our approach combines hierarchical reinforcement learning with a modular policy architecture that decouples task-specific skills from general coordination mechanisms. Through extensive experiments in diverse simulated environments—including resource allocation, collective navigation, and collaborative manipulation tasks—we demonstrate that agents trained using our framework can successfully transfer their cooperative behaviors to previously unseen scenarios, team sizes, and even partially novel tasks. Results show that our method achieves up to 78% of optimal performance on new tasks with minimal adaptation, significantly outperforming baseline approaches that struggle with generalization. Furthermore, we identify key representational factors that enable successful transfer of cooperative behaviors and provide theoretical insights into the conditions under which such transfer is possible. This work represents an important step toward creating flexible multi-agent systems capable of adapting their collaborative strategies to dynamic real-world scenarios.

UNISURF: Unifying Neural Implicit Surfaces and Radiance Fields for Multi-View Reconstruction

In this paper, we present UNISURF, a novel approach that unifies neural implicit surfaces and radiance fields for multi-view 3D reconstruction. Recent advances in neural rendering have shown impressive results in novel view synthesis through Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), while implicit surface methods have demonstrated high-quality surface reconstruction capabilities. However, these approaches have largely remained separate, with NeRF-based methods often struggling to recover accurate surfaces and implicit surface techniques lacking the view-dependent appearance modeling needed for photorealistic rendering. UNISURF bridges this gap by introducing a hybrid representation that combines the strengths of both paradigms. Our method employs a continuous neural signed distance function to model geometry while simultaneously learning view-dependent appearance. Through a carefully designed training strategy that transitions from volume rendering to surface rendering, UNISURF effectively disentangles geometry and appearance while maintaining high rendering quality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms both specialized neural surface reconstruction methods and neural radiance fields in terms of reconstruction accuracy and rendering quality. UNISURF requires no additional supervision beyond multi-view images and provides a unified framework that advances the state-of-the-art in neural 3D reconstruction.

Doubly Robust Off-Policy Actor-Critic: Convergence and Optimality

This paper introduces a novel doubly robust approach to off-policy actor-critic reinforcement learning that addresses fundamental challenges in sample efficiency and convergence guarantees. We develop a theoretical framework that combines importance sampling with doubly robust estimators to mitigate the variance issues typically encountered in off-policy learning while maintaining unbiased gradient estimates. Our method leverages data collected from a behavior policy to efficiently learn an optimal target policy without requiring additional environment interactions. We provide rigorous convergence analysis under function approximation settings and establish finite-sample bounds that characterize the algorithm's performance. Theoretical results demonstrate that our approach achieves optimal asymptotic variance among a broad class of off-policy actor-critic methods. Empirical evaluations across continuous control benchmarks show that the proposed doubly robust actor-critic consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art off-policy algorithms in terms of sample efficiency and final performance. This work bridges important theoretical gaps in understanding the convergence properties of actor-critic methods while providing a practical algorithm for real-world reinforcement learning applications.

Generalizable Representation Learning for Mixture Domain Face Anti-Spoofing

Face anti-spoofing (FAS) systems are critical for securing facial recognition technologies against presentation attacks, but they often struggle when deployed in novel domains not represented in training data. This paper addresses the challenging problem of domain generalization in FAS scenarios involving mixture domains—where test environments combine multiple unknown domain characteristics. We propose a novel Generalizable Representation Learning framework (GRL-FAS) that effectively disentangles domain-specific features from domain-invariant spoof cues. Our approach incorporates three key components: (1) a domain-invariant feature extractor that leverages adversarial learning to capture generalizable spoofing patterns, (2) a mixture domain simulator that synthesizes complex domain combinations to enhance robustness, and (3) a contrastive regularization mechanism that enforces consistent representations across domain variations while maintaining discrimination between real and spoof samples. Extensive experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art domain generalization approaches, achieving an average 28.3% reduction in Equal Error Rate on cross-dataset evaluations. Further analysis reveals that our learned representations maintain effectiveness even under challenging mixture domain scenarios not encountered during training. The proposed framework offers a promising solution for real-world deployment of FAS systems across diverse and unpredictable environmental conditions.

A Very Compact Embedded CNN Processor Design Based on Logarithmic Computing

This paper presents a novel embedded processor architecture specifically designed for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that leverages logarithmic computing to achieve significant reductions in hardware complexity and power consumption. By transforming multiplication operations into additions in the logarithmic domain, our design substantially decreases the silicon area required for computational units while maintaining acceptable inference accuracy. The proposed architecture incorporates a custom logarithmic number system (LNS) with optimized bit-width and error compensation techniques to mitigate precision loss inherent to logarithmic approximations. Our implementation achieves a 78% reduction in area compared to conventional fixed-point multiplier-based designs, while consuming only 42mW of power when fabricated in a 28nm process. Experimental results on common CNN benchmarks demonstrate that the processor maintains inference accuracy within 1.2% of floating-point implementations while offering a 3.4× improvement in energy efficiency over state-of-the-art embedded CNN accelerators. This compact design is particularly suitable for resource-constrained edge devices requiring real-time inference capabilities.

Adaptive Confidence Thresholding for Monocular Depth Estimation

This paper presents a novel approach to improving the reliability of monocular depth estimation through adaptive confidence thresholding. While monocular depth estimation has shown promising results in various computer vision applications, existing methods often produce unreliable depth predictions in challenging regions such as object boundaries, reflective surfaces, and areas with complex geometries. We propose a learning-based framework that automatically generates pixel-wise confidence maps alongside depth predictions and adaptively applies thresholds based on scene context. Our method incorporates a dual-stream architecture that jointly optimizes for depth accuracy and confidence estimation, enabling the system to effectively identify and filter unreliable predictions. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including NYU Depth v2, KITTI, and Make3D demonstrate that our adaptive confidence thresholding significantly improves depth estimation metrics, particularly in challenging scenes. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our approach reduces relative error by 12.5% and improves boundary precision by 18.7%. Furthermore, we show that our confidence maps can be leveraged in downstream tasks such as 3D reconstruction and autonomous navigation, providing a more robust foundation for safety-critical applications.

PI-RCNN: An Efficient Multi-sensor 3D Object Detector with Point-based Attentive Cont-conv Fusion Module

This paper presents PI-RCNN, a novel and efficient multi-sensor 3D object detection framework that effectively fuses LiDAR point clouds and camera imagery for autonomous driving applications. Unlike existing approaches that rely on computationally expensive voxelization or bird's-eye-view projection methods, PI-RCNN introduces a Point-based Attentive Continuous Convolution (PACC) fusion module that directly operates on raw point clouds while incorporating image features. Our approach leverages continuous convolution to handle the irregular distribution of LiDAR points and employs an attention mechanism to dynamically weight the importance of multi-modal features. Experimental results on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that PI-RCNN achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining lower computational complexity compared to existing methods. The proposed architecture shows significant improvements in detecting challenging objects with partial occlusion and at long distances. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm that the PACC fusion module effectively captures complementary information from different sensor modalities, resulting in more robust 3D object detection. PI-RCNN provides a promising direction for real-time multi-sensor perception systems in autonomous vehicles.

Optimality-based Analysis of XCSF Compaction in Discrete Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of compaction methods for the eXtended Classifier System for Function approximation (XCSF) in discrete reinforcement learning domains. While XCSF has demonstrated impressive performance in reinforcement learning tasks, the resulting rule sets often contain redundancies that impact both interpretability and computational efficiency. We introduce a novel optimality-based framework for evaluating compaction techniques that considers both the preservation of the learned policy and the minimization of rule set size. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark environments, we identify key trade-offs between approximation accuracy and rule set complexity. Our results demonstrate that strategic compaction can reduce rule set size by up to 75% while maintaining near-optimal performance in most domains. We further propose an adaptive compaction approach that dynamically balances accuracy and parsimony based on problem characteristics. This work provides important insights into the effective deployment of XCSF in resource-constrained applications and enhances our understanding of knowledge representation in learning classifier systems.

SalSum: Saliency-based Video Summarization using Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper introduces SalSum, a novel approach to automatic video summarization that leverages visual saliency detection and generative adversarial networks (GANs). The proposed framework addresses the challenge of creating concise, representative video summaries by identifying visually salient frames and segments that capture the essence of the original content. Our method employs a two-stage architecture: first, a saliency detection network identifies perceptually important regions and frames based on human attention patterns; second, a GAN-based framework learns to generate summaries that preserve these salient elements while maintaining temporal coherence. The adversarial training process enables the model to produce summaries that are both concise and representative, as the discriminator learns to distinguish between human-created and machine-generated summaries. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including TVSum and SumMe demonstrate that SalSum outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 7.2% and 5.8% in F1-score, respectively. Qualitative analysis further reveals that our saliency-guided approach produces summaries that better align with human preferences by focusing on semantically meaningful content. SalSum offers a promising direction for automated video summarization in applications ranging from content recommendation to video surveillance and archiving.

An Interpretable Approach to Hateful Meme Detection

Hateful meme detection presents unique challenges in content moderation due to the multimodal nature of memes, which combine visual elements with text to convey meaning that may not be apparent from either modality alone. While deep learning approaches have shown promise in this domain, they often function as black boxes, offering little insight into their decision-making processes. This paper presents an interpretable approach to hateful meme detection that not only achieves competitive performance but also provides transparent reasoning for its classifications. Our framework decomposes the detection process into explainable components: visual concept extraction, text sentiment analysis, and multimodal context interpretation. We introduce a novel attention mechanism that highlights which elements of the image and text contribute most significantly to the hateful classification, enabling human moderators to understand the model's decisions. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art black-box models while providing meaningful explanations that align with human reasoning. Furthermore, our interpretable system helps identify common patterns in hateful content, potentially informing more effective content moderation strategies. This work represents an important step toward responsible AI deployment in sensitive content moderation applications.

Large Scale Font Independent Urdu Text Recognition System

This paper presents a novel approach for developing a robust, font-independent Urdu text recognition system capable of operating at scale. Urdu text recognition presents unique challenges due to its cursive nature, context-sensitive character shapes, and diverse font styles. Our system employs a hybrid architecture that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for feature extraction with bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to capture the sequential dependencies in Urdu script. We introduce a new preprocessing pipeline specifically designed to handle the complexities of Urdu text, including character connections, diacritics, and ligature formations. To address the font variability challenge, we created a comprehensive dataset comprising over 50,000 text samples spanning 15 commonly used Urdu fonts with diverse stylistic variations. Experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves 94.7% character recognition accuracy across multiple fonts without requiring font-specific training. The system maintains robust performance even with degraded text quality and shows particular improvement in recognizing complex ligatures compared to previous approaches. This work represents a significant advancement toward practical, large-scale Urdu optical character recognition (OCR) systems that can be deployed in real-world applications such as document digitization, content indexing, and heritage preservation.

Consistent Representation Learning for High Dimensional Data Analysis

This paper addresses the challenge of learning robust and consistent representations for high-dimensional data analysis. As datasets grow in complexity and dimensionality, traditional analysis methods often suffer from the curse of dimensionality, computational inefficiency, and inconsistent feature representations across different modalities or conditions. We propose a novel framework that leverages recent advances in representation learning to extract low-dimensional, semantically meaningful embeddings that remain consistent across different data transformations, perturbations, and sampling conditions. Our approach combines contrastive learning techniques with theoretical guarantees on representation stability, ensuring that the learned embeddings preserve essential structural information while being resilient to noise and variations in the data collection process. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world high-dimensional datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing dimensionality reduction and representation learning approaches in terms of downstream task performance, computational efficiency, and representation consistency. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis establishing the statistical consistency of our learned representations under mild assumptions. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for reliable analysis of complex, high-dimensional data in various domains including genomics, neuroimaging, and large-scale sensor networks.

Material Based Object Tracking in Hyperspectral Videos: Benchmark and Algorithms

This paper introduces a novel framework for object tracking in hyperspectral video sequences that leverages the rich spectral information to identify and track objects based on their material composition. Unlike traditional RGB-based tracking approaches that rely primarily on spatial features and appearance models, our method exploits the discriminative spectral signatures captured across hundreds of contiguous narrow bands to achieve robust tracking even under challenging conditions such as occlusion, illumination changes, and low spatial resolution. We present the first comprehensive hyperspectral video tracking benchmark dataset, comprising 50 sequences spanning indoor and outdoor environments, with diverse objects and varying complexity levels. Each sequence is meticulously annotated with ground truth bounding boxes and material classifications. We propose three tracking algorithms specifically designed for hyperspectral data: SpectralTrack, a material-aware correlation filter approach; DeepHSITrack, which employs deep learning to jointly model spatial-spectral features; and AdaptiveSpectralTrack, which dynamically selects optimal spectral bands during tracking. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our material-based tracking approaches significantly outperform state-of-the-art RGB and multispectral trackers, achieving up to 27% improvement in tracking precision and 18% in success rate on challenging sequences. This work establishes a foundation for future research in hyperspectral video analysis and demonstrates the potential of material-based tracking for applications in remote sensing, precision agriculture, security surveillance, and biomedical imaging.

Learning Dynamics of Linear Denoising Autoencoders

This paper provides a theoretical analysis of the learning dynamics of linear denoising autoencoders (DAEs). While DAEs have demonstrated impressive performance in various representation learning tasks, their theoretical properties and training dynamics remain insufficiently understood. We develop a mathematical framework to analyze how linear DAEs evolve during training when optimized with gradient descent. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to standard autoencoders, denoising autoencoders implicitly perform a form of spectral filtering on the input data, progressively emphasizing directions of high variance while suppressing noise. We derive closed-form expressions for the learning trajectories and equilibrium solutions, showing that the noise level acts as a regularization parameter controlling the effective dimensionality of learned representations. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm our theoretical predictions and demonstrate how the noise-to-data ratio influences convergence rates and representation quality. These insights provide a principled approach to hyperparameter selection and shed light on why denoising autoencoders often learn more robust and useful representations than their non-denoising counterparts.

Abstract: A Local Active Contour Model for Image Segmentation with Intensity Inhomogeneity

This paper presents a novel local active contour model for image segmentation that effectively addresses the challenge of intensity inhomogeneity in images. Traditional active contour models often fail to accurately segment images with non-uniform intensity distributions, which are common in real-world applications such as medical imaging. Our proposed approach incorporates local image statistics into the energy functional of the active contour framework, enabling the model to adapt to spatial variations in intensity. By defining a local fitting energy with a kernel function that emphasizes the contribution of local intensities, our method can identify object boundaries despite significant intensity variations across the image domain. We formulate the model within a level set framework and derive the corresponding evolution equation. Experimental results on synthetic images and real medical images with severe intensity inhomogeneity demonstrate that our method achieves superior segmentation accuracy compared to global active contour models and other state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed model is particularly effective for segmenting images from MRI and ultrasound modalities, where intensity inhomogeneity is prevalent. Furthermore, our method exhibits robustness to initialization and noise, making it suitable for automated image analysis applications.

For Manifold Learning, Deep Neural Networks can be Locality Sensitive Hash Functions

This paper explores the intriguing connection between deep neural networks (DNNs) and locality sensitive hashing (LSH) in the context of manifold learning. We demonstrate that DNNs, when appropriately trained, can function as effective LSH functions by mapping similar data points on high-dimensional manifolds to nearby locations in the embedding space while preserving local neighborhood structures. Through theoretical analysis and empirical validation, we show that the internal representations learned by DNNs naturally implement a form of data-dependent hashing that adapts to the intrinsic geometry of the data manifold. Our experiments across diverse datasets reveal that this LSH-like behavior emerges organically during training and contributes significantly to the networks' ability to capture meaningful semantic relationships. We provide quantitative metrics comparing DNN-based embeddings with traditional LSH methods, showing superior performance in preserving similarities within complex manifolds while offering computational advantages. These findings not only deepen our understanding of how neural networks process high-dimensional data but also suggest novel approaches for designing more efficient manifold learning algorithms by explicitly incorporating LSH principles into neural architectures.

Deep Anomaly Detection with Deviation Networks

Anomaly detection remains a significant challenge in machine learning, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data. In this paper, we propose Deviation Networks (DevNet), a novel deep learning approach for anomaly detection that directly optimizes a deviation loss to distinguish between normal and anomalous data points. Unlike conventional methods that rely on surrogate objectives such as reconstruction error or one-class classification, DevNet learns to predict anomaly scores that conform to a predefined probability distribution for normal instances while pushing anomalous samples toward the distribution's tail. Our framework leverages a small number of labeled anomalies during training to anchor the anomaly scoring function, addressing the common challenge of threshold selection in unsupervised approaches. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DevNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including deep autoencoder-based and one-class classification approaches, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled anomalies. Furthermore, we show that DevNet exhibits strong generalization capabilities to detect previously unseen anomaly types, making it applicable to real-world settings where anomalies are diverse and evolving. The proposed method offers both theoretical guarantees and practical advantages, providing a significant advancement in deep anomaly detection.

From Unbiased MDI Feature Importance to Explainable AI for Trees

This paper addresses critical limitations in traditional Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) feature importance methods for tree-based models and proposes a novel framework to enhance explainability in AI systems. We first demonstrate that conventional MDI implementations exhibit systematic bias toward high-cardinality features and fail to account for feature correlations, potentially leading to misleading interpretations. To overcome these shortcomings, we introduce an unbiased MDI methodology that normalizes importance scores based on feature characteristics and correlation structures. Building upon this foundation, we develop a comprehensive explainable AI (XAI) framework specifically designed for tree ensemble models that combines our unbiased MDI approach with local explanation techniques. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets across various domains, we demonstrate that our approach provides more reliable feature rankings compared to standard MDI and other popular feature importance methods. Additionally, we show how our framework can generate consistent explanations at both global and local levels, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness in tree-based models. This work contributes to the growing field of interpretable machine learning by offering practitioners more accurate tools for model understanding and explanation.

An Introduction to Conditional Random Fields

This paper presents a comprehensive introduction to Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), a powerful statistical modeling framework widely used for structured prediction tasks in machine learning. We begin by establishing the theoretical foundations of CRFs as discriminative undirected graphical models that directly model the conditional probability of output sequences given input observations, avoiding the need to model complex input dependencies. The paper systematically explores the mathematical formulation of CRFs, contrasting them with related models such as Hidden Markov Models and Maximum Entropy Markov Models, highlighting their advantages in addressing the label bias problem. We discuss various CRF architectures including linear-chain CRFs for sequence labeling and general CRFs for more complex structured data. Training and inference algorithms are examined in detail, covering gradient-based parameter estimation, dynamic programming for exact inference, and approximate methods for complex structures. The paper concludes with a survey of successful applications across domains including natural language processing, computer vision, and bioinformatics, providing practical insights into implementation considerations and recent advancements in the field. This introduction serves as an accessible entry point for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand and apply CRFs to structured prediction problems.

Bayesian Reinforcement Learning via Deep, Sparse Sampling

This paper introduces a novel approach to Bayesian reinforcement learning that combines deep learning architectures with sparse sampling techniques to address the exploration-exploitation dilemma in complex environments. Our method, Deep Sparse Bayesian Sampling (DSBS), maintains a posterior distribution over possible environment dynamics and uses a hierarchical sampling strategy to efficiently explore the solution space while avoiding the computational burden of exhaustive tree search. By leveraging uncertainty estimates from Bayesian neural networks, DSBS adaptively allocates computational resources to promising regions of the state-action space. We provide theoretical guarantees on regret bounds and demonstrate that our approach achieves near-optimal Bayesian regret with significantly reduced computational complexity compared to existing methods. Empirical evaluations on both benchmark and high-dimensional continuous control tasks show that DSBS outperforms state-of-the-art model-based and model-free reinforcement learning algorithms, particularly in environments with sparse rewards and complex dynamics. Our results suggest that combining Bayesian principles with strategic sampling and deep function approximation offers a powerful framework for efficient reinforcement learning under uncertainty.

Out-of-Sample Representation Learning for Multi-Relational Graphs

Graph representation learning has emerged as a powerful approach for modeling complex relational data. However, most existing methods face significant limitations when handling out-of-sample entities—nodes that were not observed during training. This paper introduces a novel framework for out-of-sample representation learning on multi-relational graphs, enabling the embedding of previously unseen entities without retraining the entire model. Our approach leverages a dual-encoder architecture that disentangles structural and semantic information, allowing for effective inductive inference on new nodes using only their local neighborhood information and available attributes. We formulate an optimization objective that balances topological preservation with semantic consistency, enabling robust generalization to unseen entities. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing inductive approaches on key tasks including link prediction and node classification for out-of-sample entities. Furthermore, our approach exhibits strong computational efficiency, reducing embedding generation time by orders of magnitude compared to retraining-based alternatives. These results highlight the potential of our framework for real-world applications where graph structures evolve dynamically and rapid adaptation to new entities is essential.

Conditional Mean Embeddings as Regressors - Supplementary

This supplementary document extends our main paper on conditional mean embeddings (CMEs) as regressors in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). We provide detailed proofs of the theoretical results presented in the main paper, including convergence rates and consistency guarantees for CME estimators under various sampling conditions. Additionally, we present expanded empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets that could not be included in the main paper due to space constraints. These experiments further validate the effectiveness of CMEs in capturing complex conditional distributions and their practical utility in regression tasks involving non-Gaussian noise and multimodal output distributions. We also include an analysis of computational complexity and memory requirements for different CME implementations, along with code examples demonstrating practical implementation strategies. This supplementary material offers a more comprehensive understanding of CMEs as flexible non-parametric regressors and provides researchers with the necessary tools to apply these methods in diverse application domains.

Goal-driven text descriptions for images

This paper introduces a novel framework for generating contextually appropriate textual descriptions of images based on specific communicative goals. Unlike traditional image captioning systems that produce generic descriptions, our approach tailors the generated text to serve particular objectives such as visual assistance for the visually impaired, educational content for children, or marketing copy for products. We propose a goal-conditioned architecture that integrates visual features with explicit communicative intents to produce descriptions that vary in vocabulary, detail level, and stylistic elements according to the specified purpose. Through extensive experiments on diverse image datasets, we demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms generic captioning systems on goal-specific metrics while maintaining factual accuracy. User studies confirm that recipients find these tailored descriptions more useful and appropriate for their intended contexts than generic alternatives. Our work advances image captioning toward more pragmatic, human-centered applications by acknowledging that effective visual communication must consider not just what an image contains, but why and for whom the description is being generated.

Covariance-based Dissimilarity Measures Applied to Clustering Wide-sense Stationary Ergodic Processes

This paper introduces novel dissimilarity measures for clustering wide-sense stationary ergodic processes based on their covariance structure. While traditional clustering methods often assume independence between observations, many real-world phenomena exhibit temporal or spatial dependencies that can be characterized through covariance functions. We develop a theoretical framework for comparing and clustering stochastic processes using metrics that quantify differences in their second-order statistics. Our approach extends classical divergence measures to accommodate the infinite-dimensional nature of stationary processes, resulting in computationally tractable algorithms with strong statistical guarantees. We establish consistency properties of the proposed measures and derive convergence rates that depend on the mixing properties of the underlying processes. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic data and real-world applications, including time series from economics, neuroimaging, and climate science, demonstrates that our covariance-based clustering approach outperforms conventional methods when applied to dependent data. The proposed framework provides a principled way to identify structure in complex stochastic systems while accounting for their temporal or spatial correlation patterns.

Traditional Method Inspired Deep Neural Network for Edge Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to edge detection by integrating traditional edge detection principles with deep neural network architectures. While convolutional neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance in various computer vision tasks, they often lack the interpretability and theoretical foundation of classical edge detection methods such as Canny and Sobel operators. Our proposed framework, termed TradEdgeNet, bridges this gap by explicitly encoding gradient-based operations as specialized layers within a deep learning architecture. We design differentiable modules that mimic traditional edge detection stages—gradient computation, non-maximum suppression, and hysteresis thresholding—while allowing end-to-end training. Experimental results on standard benchmarks including BSDS500 and NYUDv2 demonstrate that TradEdgeNet achieves state-of-the-art performance with improved boundary localization and reduced sensitivity to noise. Furthermore, our approach requires significantly fewer parameters than comparable deep learning methods while maintaining interpretability. Ablation studies confirm that the incorporation of traditional edge detection principles provides a strong inductive bias, enabling better generalization with limited training data. This work demonstrates the value of combining classical computer vision techniques with modern deep learning approaches for robust edge detection.

Heterogeneous Representation Learning: A Review

Representation learning has emerged as a critical paradigm in machine learning, enabling models to automatically discover meaningful features from raw data. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of heterogeneous representation learning (HRL), which addresses the significant challenge of learning unified representations from data with diverse modalities, structures, and distributions. We systematically categorize existing HRL approaches into three primary frameworks: fusion-based methods that integrate multiple data types, transfer-based techniques that leverage knowledge across domains, and joint learning approaches that simultaneously model heterogeneous data sources. The review examines key applications across domains including multimodal learning, knowledge graphs, recommender systems, and healthcare analytics. We discuss theoretical foundations underpinning HRL, highlighting advances in addressing the semantic gap, distribution shift, and scalability challenges. Furthermore, we identify critical open problems including interpretability, sample efficiency, and robustness to distribution shifts. This survey serves as a structured resource for researchers and practitioners navigating the rapidly evolving landscape of heterogeneous representation learning, providing insights into both established methodologies and emerging directions.

Correspondence Matrices are Underrated

This paper examines the often overlooked potential of correspondence matrices in computational tasks across multiple domains. While recent advances in machine learning have focused primarily on neural architectures and representation learning, we demonstrate that correspondence matrices—which explicitly model relationships between elements of different sets—offer competitive performance with significantly lower computational requirements. Through extensive experiments on tasks including image matching, document alignment, knowledge graph completion, and cross-modal retrieval, we show that properly regularized correspondence matrices consistently outperform more complex approaches on both accuracy and inference speed metrics. We identify key theoretical properties that explain their effectiveness, particularly for problems involving structural alignment and relational reasoning. Additionally, we introduce several novel optimization techniques that address traditional limitations of correspondence-based methods. Our findings suggest that correspondence matrices deserve renewed attention as both standalone solutions and complementary components within modern deep learning frameworks, especially in resource-constrained environments where parameter efficiency is paramount.

Deterministic Policy Gradients With General State Transitions

This paper presents a novel extension of deterministic policy gradient algorithms for reinforcement learning in environments with general state transition dynamics. While traditional deterministic policy gradient methods assume specific forms of state transitions, our approach accommodates a broader class of transition models, including those with discontinuities, mixed discrete-continuous spaces, and non-Markovian dependencies. We derive a generalized deterministic policy gradient theorem that remains valid under these complex transition dynamics, proving convergence guarantees under appropriate regularity conditions. Our theoretical analysis reveals that by reformulating the gradient estimation process through a variational approximation of the transition distribution, we can maintain sample efficiency while handling previously intractable transition models. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments—including those with hybrid state spaces, partial observability, and complex physical dynamics—demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing methods. The proposed approach bridges an important gap in reinforcement learning theory and expands the applicability of deterministic policy gradient methods to a substantially wider range of real-world problems.

Convolutional Oriented Boundaries: From Image Segmentation to High-Level Tasks

This paper presents Convolutional Oriented Boundaries (COB), a novel approach that unifies image segmentation and boundary detection within a single convolutional neural network framework. We demonstrate that leveraging multiscale oriented contours significantly improves boundary detection accuracy while simultaneously generating hierarchical image segmentations at multiple scales. Our architecture efficiently integrates multiscale information through a deep learning approach that predicts oriented boundaries and combines them into a unified framework. The COB method achieves state-of-the-art performance on major benchmarks, including BSDS-500, PASCAL Context, and MS-COCO, surpassing previous approaches by significant margins while maintaining real-time inference speeds. Furthermore, we explore how our boundary-based representations can serve as powerful intermediate features for high-level vision tasks such as object proposal generation, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the rich hierarchical information captured by COB provides superior building blocks for these complex tasks compared to traditional methods. Our unified approach bridges low-level image segmentation with high-level visual understanding, offering a versatile framework applicable across the computer vision pipeline.

Accurate and Lightweight Image Super-Resolution with Model-Guided Deep Unfolding Network

This paper presents a novel approach to single image super-resolution (SISR) that achieves an optimal balance between computational efficiency and reconstruction quality. We propose a Model-Guided Deep Unfolding Network (MGDUN) that integrates model-based optimization principles with deep learning techniques. By unfolding an iterative optimization algorithm into a learnable neural network architecture, our method explicitly incorporates image degradation models while leveraging the representational power of deep networks. The proposed MGDUN employs a lightweight design with parameter sharing across unfolded stages, significantly reducing the model size while maintaining high performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, achieving superior PSNR and SSIM metrics with 40-60% fewer parameters than comparable models. The MGDUN shows particular strength in preserving fine texture details and sharp edges while effectively suppressing artifacts. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates robust generalization to real-world degradations beyond the training distribution. The proposed method offers a promising direction for resource-efficient, high-quality image super-resolution applicable to mobile devices and other compute-constrained environments.

End to End Trainable Active Contours via Differentiable Rendering

Active contour models (snakes) have been fundamental tools in image segmentation for decades, yet their integration into modern deep learning pipelines has been limited by their non-differentiable nature. In this paper, we present a novel framework that enables end-to-end trainable active contours through differentiable rendering techniques. Our approach bridges the gap between traditional energy-based contour models and neural networks by reformulating the contour evolution process as a differentiable operation. By leveraging implicit contour representations and automatic differentiation, we develop a rendering-based loss function that allows gradients to flow from segmentation results back to the contour initialization network. Experiments on medical imaging, aerial photography, and natural image datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms both traditional active contour models and recent deep learning segmentation approaches, particularly in scenarios with limited training data or ambiguous boundaries. The proposed framework maintains the interpretability and topology awareness of classical snakes while harnessing the representational power of deep neural networks. Our approach enables the incorporation of geometric priors into learning-based segmentation systems and opens new avenues for combining classical computer vision techniques with modern deep learning methodologies.

SteReFo: Efficient Image Refocusing with Stereo Vision

This paper introduces SteReFo, a novel computational photography framework that enables efficient post-capture image refocusing using stereo vision. Unlike traditional light field approaches that require specialized hardware, SteReFo leverages conventional stereo camera setups to achieve similar refocusing capabilities with significantly reduced computational and memory requirements. Our method employs a two-stage pipeline: first, a deep learning-based depth estimation from stereo pairs, followed by an efficient refocusing algorithm that simulates variable aperture effects at arbitrary focal planes. We demonstrate that SteReFo can generate high-quality synthetic defocus blur comparable to that of specialized light field cameras while maintaining real-time performance on standard hardware. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of refocusing quality and computational efficiency across diverse scenes and lighting conditions. SteReFo's practical implementation makes advanced computational photography techniques accessible to a wider range of consumer devices without requiring specialized hardware, potentially transforming how photographers approach depth-of-field control in post-processing workflows.

Modeling Feature Representations for Affective Speech using Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper proposes a novel approach to modeling speech emotion recognition (SER) features using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Despite significant advances in affective computing, robust representation of emotional speech features remains challenging due to speaker variability, cultural differences, and limited availability of labeled emotional speech data. We address these limitations by developing a GAN-based framework that learns to generate high-quality emotional speech representations while preserving speaker-independent affective characteristics. Our model consists of a generator network that produces synthetic feature embeddings and a discriminator that distinguishes between real and generated emotional speech features. We introduce an emotion consistency loss to ensure the generated representations maintain emotional saliency. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets including IEMOCAP and RAVDESS demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional feature extraction methods, achieving a 7.3% improvement in emotion classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the generated representations show enhanced robustness to speaker variability and noise conditions. The proposed framework also enables effective data augmentation for emotion recognition systems, particularly beneficial for underrepresented emotional classes. Our findings suggest that adversarial learning provides a promising direction for developing more generalizable and discriminative affective speech representations.

Graph-Embedded Subspace Support Vector Data Description

This paper introduces Graph-Embedded Subspace Support Vector Data Description (GES-SVDD), a novel approach for one-class classification that effectively addresses the challenges of high-dimensional, complex data structures. Our method combines the strengths of Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) with subspace learning techniques while incorporating graph-based manifold regularization to preserve intrinsic data relationships. GES-SVDD simultaneously learns a low-dimensional subspace projection and constructs a minimal enclosing hypersphere in the projected space, allowing for more accurate anomaly detection in real-world datasets where anomalies often lie in specific feature subspaces. 

The proposed framework employs a graph Laplacian regularization term that maintains the local geometric structure of the data during dimensionality reduction, ensuring that similar instances remain close in the embedded subspace. Through an alternating optimization procedure, GES-SVDD iteratively refines both the projection matrix and the SVDD parameters until convergence. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional SVDD and other state-of-the-art one-class classification methods, particularly in scenarios with high-dimensional data and complex manifold structures. Furthermore, the learned subspace provides interpretable insights into the most discriminative features for anomaly detection.

Real-Time Multi-Modal Semantic Fusion on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles

This paper presents a novel framework for real-time semantic fusion of multi-modal sensor data on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). The integration of diverse sensor inputs—including RGB cameras, thermal imaging, LiDAR, and radar—presents significant computational and algorithmic challenges in resource-constrained aerial platforms. We propose a lightweight fusion architecture that efficiently combines complementary information streams while maintaining low latency processing critical for UAV operations. Our approach employs a hierarchical attention mechanism that dynamically weights sensor contributions based on environmental conditions and mission requirements. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves a 37% improvement in object recognition accuracy and a 42% reduction in false positives compared to single-modality approaches, while maintaining a processing rate of 24 frames per second on embedded hardware. Field tests across various weather conditions and lighting scenarios validate the robustness of our fusion methodology. This work addresses critical gaps in UAV perception systems by enabling reliable semantic understanding in challenging and dynamic environments, with applications in search and rescue, infrastructure inspection, and autonomous navigation.

Near-Infrared Coloring via a Contrast-Preserving Mapping Model

This paper presents a novel approach for colorizing near-infrared (NIR) images through a contrast-preserving mapping model. While NIR imaging offers advantages in challenging lighting conditions and material penetration, the resulting grayscale images lack the visual richness of color photographs. Our method addresses this limitation by learning a mapping from NIR to RGB color space while explicitly preserving the structural contrast information inherent in NIR imagery. We introduce a dual-branch neural architecture that simultaneously processes global contextual features and local contrast details, integrating them through an adaptive fusion mechanism. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art colorization methods both quantitatively and qualitatively, achieving more natural color distributions and preserving fine structural details. The proposed contrast-preserving constraint proves particularly effective for maintaining edge definition and texture boundaries in the colorized output. Our method shows robustness across diverse scenes including landscapes, urban environments, and indoor settings, making it applicable for enhancing NIR photography, surveillance footage, and medical imaging applications.

Modeling Multi-Label Action Dependencies for Temporal Action Localization

Temporal action localization (TAL) in untrimmed videos remains challenging, particularly when multiple action categories co-occur or exhibit temporal dependencies. Traditional approaches often treat action categories independently, neglecting the rich contextual relationships between co-occurring actions. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that explicitly models multi-label action dependencies for more accurate temporal action localization. Our approach introduces a graph-based relation modeling module that captures both semantic and temporal dependencies between action categories. We represent actions as nodes in a dynamic graph where edges encode their co-occurrence patterns and temporal relationships. This relational information is leveraged through a multi-head attention mechanism that refines action boundary predictions by conditioning them on related activities. Extensive experiments on challenging multi-label datasets including MultiTHUMOS and Charades demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 4.2% and 3.7% in mAP, respectively. Ablation studies confirm that modeling action dependencies provides substantial benefits for temporally overlapping actions and semantically related categories. Our work highlights the importance of modeling inter-action relationships for advancing temporal action localization in complex, real-world scenarios.

The EPIC-KITCHENS Dataset: Collection, Challenges and Baselines

We present EPIC-KITCHENS, a large-scale egocentric video dataset captured in real-world kitchen environments. Consisting of over 55 hours of recording from 32 participants in their native kitchen settings, this dataset provides unscripted, naturalistic first-person views of daily cooking activities. The dataset features fine-grained annotations of 39,596 action segments, comprising 125 verb and 331 noun classes. We detail our collection methodology, which prioritized ecological validity through minimal intervention in participants' environments and behaviors. The paper discusses several challenges inherent to egocentric vision in unconstrained environments, including object occlusion, camera motion, and the fine-grained nature of hand-object interactions. We establish baseline performance for action recognition, anticipation, and object detection tasks using state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating the dataset's utility while highlighting the significant room for improvement in egocentric action understanding. EPIC-KITCHENS aims to advance research in first-person vision by providing a realistic testbed for developing algorithms that can understand complex human-object interactions in daily activities.

An Efficient Image Retrieval Based on Fusion of Low-Level Visual Features

This paper presents a novel approach to content-based image retrieval (CBIR) that leverages the fusion of multiple low-level visual features to enhance retrieval accuracy and efficiency. Our method combines color, texture, shape, and spatial information through a weighted feature fusion framework that dynamically adjusts feature importance based on query characteristics. We introduce a two-stage retrieval process that first employs a fast filtering mechanism using dominant features, followed by a refined ranking using the complete feature set. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets including Corel-5K and WANG demonstrates that our approach outperforms single-feature methods and several state-of-the-art CBIR systems, achieving 23% improvement in precision and 18% in recall. The computational overhead of our fusion technique is minimal, with retrieval times comparable to single-feature approaches. Additionally, we propose an adaptive feedback mechanism that further optimizes feature weights based on user interactions. The results confirm that intelligent fusion of low-level visual features provides a promising direction for developing more effective and efficient image retrieval systems.

Robust Image Segmentation Quality Assessment

Image segmentation plays a critical role in numerous computer vision applications, yet evaluating segmentation quality remains challenging, particularly in the absence of ground truth data. This paper introduces a novel framework for Robust Image Segmentation Quality Assessment (RISQA) that operates without reference annotations. Our approach combines boundary coherence metrics, region homogeneity analysis, and perceptual consistency measures to provide comprehensive quality evaluation across diverse image domains. We propose a new adaptive weighting mechanism that adjusts quality criteria based on image content characteristics, making our assessment robust to variations in image complexity, noise levels, and segmentation algorithm peculiarities. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method achieves strong correlation with human visual assessment and outperforms existing no-reference quality metrics by an average of 17%. Furthermore, we show that RISQA can effectively guide parameter optimization in segmentation algorithms and detect failure cases in real-time applications. The proposed framework offers a reliable solution for segmentation quality evaluation in practical scenarios where ground truth is unavailable or prohibitively expensive to obtain.

Inductive Link Prediction for Nodes Having Only Attribute Information
