This work contributes to the growing field of synthetic data generation by providing a robust framework for creating high-quality tabular data with conditional control, which has significant implications for data sharing, augmentation, and privacy-preserving analytics.

Node-Centric Graph Learning from Data for Brain State Identification

This paper presents a novel node-centric approach to graph learning for identifying brain states from neuroimaging data. While traditional graph-based methods for brain connectivity analysis often rely on predefined graph structures or global graph properties, our method learns optimized node representations that capture both local and global connectivity patterns directly from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. We introduce a framework that combines graph neural networks with attention mechanisms to prioritize relevant brain regions and their interactions during different cognitive states. The model autonomously identifies discriminative subnetworks without requiring explicit graph construction priors, addressing a significant limitation in current brain connectivity analysis. Experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior classification accuracy for various brain states compared to conventional graph-based methods and deep learning baselines. Furthermore, the learned node representations provide interpretable insights into the functional organization of brain networks across different cognitive conditions. This work bridges the gap between data-driven deep learning approaches and neuroscientifically meaningful graph representations, offering a powerful tool for understanding brain function through the lens of network neuroscience.

Signature Features with the Visibility Transformation

This paper introduces a novel approach to feature extraction in sequential data using the visibility transformation coupled with signature methods from rough path theory. By representing time series as visibility graphs, where data points are connected based on mutual visibility criteria, we capture both local and global topological properties of the underlying data. The transformation maps temporal data into a geometric space where signature features—systematic polynomial representations of path data—can be effectively computed. Our method demonstrates superior performance in capturing nonlinear dependencies and structural patterns compared to traditional feature extraction techniques. Experiments across multiple domains, including financial time series, physiological signals, and motion capture data, show that visibility-signature features significantly improve classification and forecasting accuracy while maintaining interpretability. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees regarding the information preservation properties of this transformation pipeline. This approach bridges graph-theoretic representations with path-based learning frameworks, offering a robust tool for complex sequential data analysis with particular strengths in detecting regime changes and multi-scale patterns.

PoET-BiN: Power Efficient Tiny Binary Neurons

This paper introduces PoET-BiN, a novel architecture for implementing highly power-efficient neural networks using binary neurons. By constraining neural activations and weights to binary values (−1, +1), our approach dramatically reduces computational complexity and memory requirements while maintaining competitive accuracy on resource-constrained devices. PoET-BiN replaces power-hungry multiply-accumulate operations with simple XNOR and bit-counting operations, resulting in up to 58× reduction in energy consumption compared to conventional floating-point implementations. We propose a specialized training methodology that addresses the challenges of binary gradient approximation and achieves accuracy within 2.5% of full-precision counterparts on benchmark datasets. Our hardware implementation demonstrates that PoET-BiN can operate effectively on microcontroller-class devices with sub-milliwatt power budgets, enabling real-time inference for IoT and edge computing applications. Extensive evaluations across multiple tasks show that PoET-BiN offers an optimal balance between model accuracy, inference latency, and energy efficiency for deployment in severely power-constrained environments.

Exploring Online Ad Images Using a Deep Convolutional Neural Network Approach

This study presents a novel application of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for analyzing and classifying online advertisement images. With the exponential growth of digital advertising, understanding the visual elements that drive consumer engagement has become increasingly important. We developed a multi-layered CNN architecture to extract high-dimensional features from a diverse dataset of 50,000 online ad images collected across various platforms and industries. Our model achieved 87.3% accuracy in classifying ads by industry category and identified key visual patterns associated with higher click-through rates. Feature visualization techniques revealed that color schemes, text-to-image ratios, and the presence of human faces significantly influenced ad performance. Additionally, we demonstrate how transfer learning from our pre-trained model can be effectively applied to smaller advertising datasets with limited labeled examples. These findings provide actionable insights for digital marketers and contribute to the growing body of research on computational advertising. Our approach offers a scalable framework for automated visual content analysis that can adapt to evolving advertising trends and consumer preferences.

On the mapping between Hopfield networks and Restricted Boltzmann Machines

This paper explores the theoretical connections between Hopfield networks and Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), two fundamental neural network architectures with significant implications for both computational neuroscience and machine learning. We establish a formal mapping between the energy functions of these models, demonstrating that under specific parametric constraints, an RBM can be transformed into an equivalent Hopfield network. Our analysis reveals that while both models minimize energy functions during their dynamics, the hidden layer in RBMs provides additional representational capacity that extends beyond the direct pairwise connections in Hopfield networks. We derive the precise mathematical conditions under which this mapping holds and examine the implications for memory capacity, pattern completion, and learning dynamics. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings, showing that properly configured RBMs can reproduce the associative memory capabilities of Hopfield networks while offering enhanced feature extraction. This work provides a unifying framework for understanding these seemingly distinct neural network paradigms and suggests new hybrid architectures that leverage the strengths of both approaches.

Spectral Clustering on Spherical Coordinates under the Degree-Corrected Stochastic Blockmodel

This paper investigates a novel approach to community detection through spectral clustering by transforming network data into spherical coordinates under the degree-corrected stochastic blockmodel (DCSBM). While traditional spectral methods often struggle with degree heterogeneity in real-world networks, we demonstrate that projecting the spectral embeddings onto a unit hypersphere effectively normalizes the influence of node degrees, leading to improved clustering performance. We provide theoretical guarantees for the consistency of our approach, establishing error bounds that scale with the square root of the maximum expected degree. Through extensive simulations and applications to real-world networks, we show that our spherical spectral clustering algorithm significantly outperforms conventional spectral methods, particularly in networks with highly skewed degree distributions. The proposed method maintains computational efficiency while being robust to degree variations, making it well-suited for analyzing complex networks across diverse domains. Our findings suggest that geometric transformations of spectral embeddings offer a promising direction for addressing fundamental challenges in network clustering.

CognitiveCNN: Mimicking Human Cognitive Models to resolve Texture-Shape Bias

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in image classification tasks, yet they exhibit a concerning tendency to prioritize texture over shape—a phenomenon known as texture bias. This stands in stark contrast to human visual cognition, which primarily relies on shape for object recognition. This paper introduces CognitiveCNN, a novel neural architecture that incorporates principles from human cognitive models to address the texture-shape bias problem. By integrating hierarchical shape processing pathways inspired by the ventral visual stream and implementing attention mechanisms that mimic human visual attention, our model achieves a more balanced utilization of both shape and texture features. Through extensive experimentation on modified datasets designed to decouple texture and shape cues, we demonstrate that CognitiveCNN achieves superior performance on shape-based classification tasks while maintaining competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks. Our approach reduces texture bias by 37% compared to traditional CNNs while improving robustness to adversarial attacks and domain shifts. These findings suggest that incorporating cognitive science principles into deep learning architectures can yield more human-like visual processing systems with enhanced generalization capabilities.

Dissecting Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning by Deep Visualization

Catastrophic forgetting remains a significant challenge in continual learning, where neural networks tend to abruptly lose previously acquired knowledge when learning new tasks. This paper introduces a novel approach to understanding this phenomenon through advanced visualization techniques that reveal the internal representational dynamics of neural networks during sequential task learning. By developing a suite of deep visualization methods, we expose how feature representations evolve, compete, and interfere across tasks. Our analysis reveals that catastrophic forgetting manifests differently across network layers: lower layers exhibit gradual drift in feature detectors, while higher layers show more abrupt changes in decision boundaries. We quantify these effects through representational similarity metrics and feature importance mapping, demonstrating that forgetting correlates with the degree of representation overlap between sequential tasks. Based on these insights, we propose targeted regularization strategies that selectively preserve critical features for previous tasks while allowing flexibility for new learning. Experiments across multiple architectures and benchmark datasets demonstrate that our visualization-informed approach leads to significant reductions in forgetting while maintaining comparable learning capacity for new tasks. This work not only advances our theoretical understanding of catastrophic forgetting but also provides practical design principles for more effective continual learning systems.

Neural Input Search for Large Scale Recommendation Models

Recommendation systems are increasingly relying on large-scale neural networks to model complex user-item interactions across diverse feature sets. However, determining the optimal feature representations and input transformations for these models remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce Neural Input Search (NIS), an automated framework that systematically explores and optimizes input representations for large-scale recommendation models. NIS employs a differentiable search strategy to discover effective feature transformations, embeddings, and input processing techniques while considering computational constraints specific to production recommendation systems. Our approach jointly optimizes both the input representation space and model architecture, enabling more effective feature interactions. Experiments on several large-scale industrial datasets demonstrate that NIS consistently outperforms manually designed input pipelines, achieving 4.2% improvement in click-through rate prediction and 3.7% improvement in conversion rate tasks. Furthermore, NIS discovers non-intuitive input transformations that human experts had overlooked. We also analyze the transferability of discovered input representations across different recommendation tasks and model architectures. The computational overhead of NIS is minimal during inference, making it suitable for deployment in production environments with strict latency requirements.

code2seq: Generating Sequences from Structured Representations of Code

We present code2seq, a novel approach for generating natural language sequences from source code representations. Unlike previous methods that rely on flat, sequential representations of code, our model leverages the rich structural information inherent in programming languages by operating directly on abstract syntax trees (ASTs). We introduce a path-based attention mechanism that learns to aggregate multiple syntactic paths in the AST, capturing both local and global code semantics. Our neural architecture encodes these paths using bi-directional LSTMs and employs an attention-based decoder to generate coherent and contextually appropriate sequences. We evaluate code2seq on multiple code-to-sequence tasks, including code summarization and method name prediction across various programming languages. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving BLEU scores by 7.9% on code summarization and achieving 12.5% higher precision in method name prediction. Further analysis reveals that code2seq produces more accurate and informative descriptions, particularly for complex code structures where sequential models struggle. Our work provides a foundation for improved code understanding tools and demonstrates the importance of structural representations in bridging the gap between programming languages and natural language.

Learning to Maximize Influence

This paper investigates computational approaches for learning optimal strategies to maximize influence in complex social networks. We formulate the influence maximization problem within a reinforcement learning framework, where an agent learns to identify key nodes that, when activated, lead to maximum information diffusion across the network. Our approach addresses limitations of traditional greedy algorithms by adapting to changing network dynamics and incorporating feedback from previous influence campaigns. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world social network datasets, we demonstrate that our learning-based method outperforms classical heuristic approaches by 18-27% in terms of influence spread, while requiring significantly less computational overhead for large-scale networks. We further analyze the transferability of learned policies across different network topologies and propose a novel attention-based architecture that captures structural properties of influential node configurations. Our findings contribute to both theoretical understanding of influence dynamics and practical applications in viral marketing, public health interventions, and information dissemination strategies.

BeCAPTCHA-Mouse: Synthetic Mouse Trajectories and Improved Bot Detection

This paper introduces BeCAPTCHA-Mouse, a novel behavioral CAPTCHA system that distinguishes between human and automated users by analyzing mouse movement trajectories. Unlike traditional CAPTCHAs that rely on visual challenges, our approach leverages the inherent characteristics of human mouse movements that are difficult for bots to replicate. We present a two-fold contribution: first, a generative adversarial network capable of synthesizing realistic human-like mouse trajectories for training purposes; second, an enhanced detection framework that achieves significantly improved bot identification accuracy. Our system was evaluated using a dataset of over 10,000 mouse trajectories collected from both human users and various bot implementations. Results demonstrate that BeCAPTCHA-Mouse achieves 96.4% detection accuracy with a false positive rate of only 1.2%, outperforming existing behavioral CAPTCHA solutions by an average of 18.7%. Furthermore, the system maintains robustness against adversarial attacks specifically designed to mimic human mouse behavior. This work represents a significant advancement in non-intrusive, accessible CAPTCHA technology that minimizes user friction while maintaining strong security guarantees against automated attacks.

HySTER: A Hybrid Spatio-Temporal Event Reasoner

This paper introduces HySTER, a novel hybrid framework for reasoning about complex spatio-temporal events across diverse domains. HySTER integrates symbolic reasoning with neural methods to address the challenges of event understanding in both structured and unstructured environments. Our approach combines formal logical representations of spatial and temporal relationships with deep learning techniques capable of handling uncertainty and incomplete information. The framework supports multi-modal input, including video, sensor data, and textual descriptions, enabling comprehensive event analysis across varying granularities of time and space. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets spanning urban mobility, human activity recognition, and environmental monitoring demonstrates that HySTER outperforms existing methods by 17-23% on complex event detection tasks while providing interpretable reasoning traces. Additionally, the system's hybrid architecture reduces computational requirements by 40% compared to purely neural approaches while maintaining robustness to noisy real-world data. HySTER advances the state-of-the-art in spatio-temporal reasoning by bridging the gap between symbolic AI's interpretability and neural networks' pattern recognition capabilities, offering a promising direction for next-generation event understanding systems.

A new nature inspired modularity function adapted for unsupervised learning involving spatially embedded networks: A comparative analysis

This paper introduces a novel modularity function inspired by natural systems for unsupervised learning in spatially embedded networks. Traditional modularity-based community detection algorithms often struggle with spatial networks due to their inherent resolution limit and tendency to overlook spatial constraints. Our approach, which we call Spatial-BioCom, incorporates principles observed in biological collective systems—such as bird flocking, ant colonies, and neural networks—to address these limitations. The proposed function integrates spatial distance metrics with topological information, creating a more balanced evaluation of community structures in networks where physical embedding is significant. We conduct extensive comparative analyses against established algorithms including Louvain, Infomap, and spatially-aware variants across multiple domains: transportation networks, brain connectomes, power grids, and social mobility patterns. Results demonstrate that Spatial-BioCom achieves 18-27% improvement in normalized mutual information scores and 12-23% better Adjusted Rand Index values when compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, the communities identified exhibit greater spatial coherence while maintaining topological significance. This work provides new methodological insights for unsupervised learning in the growing field of spatial network analysis, with potential applications in urban planning, neuroscience, and infrastructure resilience assessment.

Overcoming Multi-Model Forgetting

The deployment of multiple machine learning models in production environments often leads to a phenomenon known as multi-model forgetting, where models trained sequentially on different tasks experience catastrophic forgetting of previously learned information. This paper presents a novel framework to address this challenge by introducing adaptive knowledge distillation techniques that preserve critical information across model iterations. Our approach incorporates a dynamic memory module that selectively retains task-specific representations while facilitating knowledge transfer between models. Extensive experiments across diverse domains—including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning—demonstrate that our method reduces forgetting by an average of 68% compared to traditional fine-tuning approaches while maintaining competitive performance on new tasks. Additionally, we propose a computational efficiency metric that quantifies the trade-off between memory requirements and inference speed. Our findings suggest that strategic knowledge preservation across multiple models can significantly improve the stability and performance of machine learning systems in continual learning scenarios, with important implications for real-world applications where computational resources are limited and task distributions evolve over time.

The reinforcement learning-based multi-agent cooperative approach for the adaptive speed regulation on a metallurgical pickling line

This paper presents a novel reinforcement learning-based multi-agent cooperative approach for adaptive speed regulation in metallurgical pickling lines. Pickling lines, critical in metal processing for removing surface oxides, face significant challenges in maintaining optimal production speeds while balancing quality requirements and operational constraints. Traditional control methods often fail to adapt to changing conditions, resulting in suboptimal performance. Our approach employs a distributed multi-agent reinforcement learning framework where autonomous agents collaboratively optimize strip speed throughout different sections of the pickling line. Each agent learns optimal control policies through interaction with its local environment while sharing critical information with neighboring agents. The proposed system dynamically adjusts strip speed based on multiple factors including acid concentration, temperature variations, strip thickness, surface conditions, and production targets. Experimental results from both simulation and implementation on an industrial pickling line demonstrate significant improvements: a 12.3% increase in throughput, 8.7% reduction in energy consumption, and 15.2% decrease in quality defects compared to conventional control methods. The system's ability to adapt to varying operational conditions without explicit reprogramming represents a significant advancement in metallurgical process control, offering a promising solution for smart manufacturing in the steel industry.

Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Unconstrained Monotonic Neural Networks

This paper introduces a novel approach to distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) using unconstrained monotonic neural networks. While traditional reinforcement learning methods focus on learning expected returns, distributional RL aims to learn the entire distribution of returns, providing richer representations of uncertainty and risk. However, existing DRL algorithms often face challenges in maintaining proper probability distributions during learning. We propose a framework that leverages unconstrained monotonic neural networks to directly parameterize cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) without explicit constraints, ensuring valid probability distributions by design. Our approach eliminates the need for distribution projections or quantile regression tricks commonly used in previous methods. Through theoretical analysis, we prove that our method converges to the true return distribution under standard assumptions. Empirical evaluations across a diverse set of environments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in environments characterized by high stochasticity and multi-modal reward structures. Additionally, we show that the learned distributions provide valuable uncertainty estimates that can be effectively utilized for exploration and risk-sensitive decision-making. Our work presents a principled and efficient approach to distributional reinforcement learning that addresses fundamental limitations of existing methods.

Learning Discrete Structures for Graph Neural Networks

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful architectures for learning representations of graph-structured data. However, most existing GNN approaches assume that the input graph structure is fixed and accurately represents the relationships between entities. In this paper, we challenge this assumption and propose a framework for jointly learning the discrete graph structure and the parameters of GNNs. We introduce a differentiable approach to discrete structure learning by developing a novel parameterization of the graph adjacency matrix using a stochastic sampling process with a temperature-controlled Gumbel-Softmax distribution. This allows for end-to-end training while maintaining the interpretability of the learned structures. Our method adaptively discovers task-relevant graph structures that may significantly differ from the input graph or infer latent structures when no initial graph is available. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets spanning node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks, we demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN methods that rely on fixed graph structures. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the representational capacity of our structure learning mechanism and analyze the interpretability of the learned graphs. Our findings suggest that learning discrete structures can significantly enhance the expressive power of GNNs and provide valuable insights into the underlying relationships in the data.

Text-to-Image Generation Grounded by Fine-Grained User Attention

Text-to-image generation models have made remarkable progress in creating high-quality images from natural language descriptions. However, these models often struggle with precisely controlling which parts of the text prompt influence specific regions of the generated image. This paper introduces a novel approach that grounds the generation process using fine-grained user attention signals. Our method allows users to specify attention weights for different parts of the input text, creating an explicit mapping between textual concepts and spatial regions in the output image. We propose a modified diffusion architecture that incorporates these attention signals during both the training and inference stages. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our approach significantly improves spatial layout control, attribute binding, and compositional accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. User studies confirm that our generated images more faithfully reflect the intended emphasis in the text descriptions. Additionally, we show that our attention-grounded generation enables new interactive applications where users can iteratively refine images by adjusting their attention weights. This work represents an important step toward more controllable and interpretable text-to-image generation systems that better align with user intent.

Missingness as Stability: Understanding the Structure of Missingness in Longitudinal EHR data and its Impact on Reinforcement Learning in Healthcare

Electronic Health Records (EHR) provide a rich source of longitudinal patient data that could potentially transform healthcare decision-making through reinforcement learning (RL) applications. However, missingness in EHR data presents a significant challenge that is often overlooked or handled through simplistic imputation methods. This study proposes a novel conceptual framework—"missingness as stability"—which posits that patterns of missing values in longitudinal EHR data contain meaningful clinical information about patient states. We analyze a large-scale, multi-institutional EHR dataset (n=1.2M patients) to characterize the structure of missingness across different clinical variables and demonstrate that missing patterns are non-random and clinically informative. Our findings reveal that periods of measurement stability often correspond to clinical stability, while changes in measurement frequency typically coincide with changes in patient condition. We develop and evaluate several RL algorithms that explicitly incorporate missingness patterns into state representations and reward functions. Results show that models accounting for the informative nature of missingness outperform conventional approaches by 18.3% in policy evaluation metrics and lead to treatment recommendations more aligned with clinical practice. This work challenges the traditional view of missing data as merely a technical limitation and demonstrates how the structure of missingness can be leveraged to enhance the performance and clinical relevance of reinforcement learning applications in healthcare.

New Benchmarks for Learning on Non-Homophilous Graphs

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various graph-based machine learning tasks. However, their performance has been primarily evaluated on homophilous graph benchmarks, where connected nodes tend to share similar properties. In this work, we address the critical gap in the evaluation of GNN models on non-homophilous (heterophilous) graphs, where connected nodes often have dissimilar characteristics. We introduce a suite of new challenging benchmark datasets specifically designed to evaluate learning on non-homophilous graphs across diverse domains including social networks, citation networks, biological networks, and synthetic graphs with controllable heterophily levels. Our comprehensive empirical analysis reveals significant limitations of traditional GNN architectures in these settings and highlights the performance of recent architectural innovations designed for heterophilous graphs. We provide detailed characterizations of each benchmark's structural and feature properties, establishing standardized evaluation protocols to facilitate fair comparisons. Additionally, we identify key research directions for improving GNN performance on non-homophilous graphs. These benchmarks offer a robust foundation for advancing graph representation learning beyond the conventional homophily assumption, enabling the development of more versatile and powerful graph learning algorithms.

FAIM -- A ConvNet Method for Unsupervised 3D Medical Image Registration

Medical image registration is a fundamental task in medical image analysis, yet traditional optimization-based methods remain computationally intensive and often require manual parameter tuning. In this paper, we present FAIM (Fully Automated Image Matching), a novel convolutional neural network approach for unsupervised 3D medical image registration. Unlike supervised methods that require ground truth deformation fields, FAIM learns to predict spatial transformations directly from image pairs without explicit supervision. Our framework consists of a registration network that generates a deformation field, coupled with a spatial transformation layer that warps the moving image, and a similarity metric that provides feedback for network optimization. We evaluate FAIM on multiple public datasets including brain MRI, chest CT, and abdominal CT scans. Experimental results demonstrate that FAIM achieves comparable or superior accuracy to state-of-the-art methods while offering significantly faster registration times (under 1 second per volume pair). Additionally, FAIM demonstrates robust performance across different imaging modalities and anatomical regions without requiring dataset-specific parameter adjustments. The proposed method's combination of accuracy, speed, and generalizability makes it particularly suitable for clinical applications where rapid and reliable image registration is essential.

Cold Start Similar Artists Ranking with Gravity-Inspired Graph Autoencoders

This paper addresses the challenging cold start problem in music recommendation systems, specifically focusing on ranking similar artists for newly added musicians with minimal interaction data. We introduce a novel approach called Gravity-Inspired Graph Autoencoder (GIGAE), which leverages both the structural properties of the artist similarity graph and the gravitational principle that similar entities attract each other in embedding space. Our model combines a graph autoencoder architecture with a physics-inspired loss function that emulates gravitational forces between artist nodes based on their similarity relationships. Experiments conducted on large-scale music streaming datasets demonstrate that GIGAE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 17.3% improvement in Mean Average Precision (MAP) and a 15.8% gain in Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) for cold start artists. The model's ability to effectively infer latent representations for new artists with limited connections enables more accurate similar artist rankings, thereby improving user experience during exploration of unfamiliar music. Additionally, we provide an analysis of the model's sensitivity to different graph sparsity levels, showing robust performance even with extremely limited connectivity information.

Learning Structural Edits via Incremental Tree Transformations

This paper introduces a novel approach to learning and applying structural edits in tree-based representations through incremental transformations. We present a framework that models complex structural modifications as sequences of elementary tree operations, enabling more interpretable and controllable editing processes. Our method leverages a neural architecture that combines attention mechanisms with tree-structured encoders to predict appropriate transformation sequences for a given editing task. Unlike previous approaches that operate on flat representations or generate entire structures from scratch, our incremental transformation model preserves structural integrity while allowing for targeted modifications. Experiments across diverse domains—including code refactoring, document restructuring, and abstract syntax tree manipulation—demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in accuracy and generalization. Additionally, we show that the learned transformations capture meaningful edit patterns that can be transferred across different contexts, enabling applications in automated program repair, document formatting, and assisted editing tools. Our work contributes to the growing field of structure-aware editing systems by providing a more fine-grained, interpretable approach to learning structural modifications.

Refined Continuous Control of DDPG Actors via Parametrised Activation

Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithms have emerged as powerful approaches for continuous control tasks in reinforcement learning. However, their performance often suffers from limited expressivity in the actor network's final activation functions, which can restrict the action space exploration and exploitation capabilities. This paper introduces a novel parametrised activation framework for DDPG actors that adaptively refines the mapping between neural network outputs and control actions. Our approach, which we call Parametrised Activation DDPG (PA-DDPG), incorporates learnable parameters within the activation functions themselves, allowing for more nuanced control policies that better capture the underlying action distributions required for complex tasks. Through extensive experiments across multiple continuous control benchmarks including MuJoCo environments and robotic manipulation tasks, we demonstrate that PA-DDPG consistently outperforms standard DDPG and several state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 27% improvement in cumulative reward and significantly faster convergence rates. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis establishing the representational advantages of our parametrised activation approach. These results suggest that refining the expressivity of policy networks through parametrised activations represents a promising direction for advancing continuous control in reinforcement learning.

Mining Cross-Image Semantics for Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation

Semantic segmentation traditionally requires dense pixel-level annotations, which are time-consuming and expensive to obtain. Weakly supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS) aims to alleviate this burden by learning from image-level labels alone. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that mines cross-image semantic relationships to improve WSSS performance. Our approach leverages the observation that semantically similar regions across different images should share consistent feature representations, even when they appear in varied contexts or visual conditions. We introduce a Cross-Image Semantic Mining (CISM) module that establishes correspondences between regions with similar semantic meanings across the training dataset. This module aggregates and transfers semantic knowledge between images, effectively enriching the localization cues derived from image-level labels. Additionally, we develop a semantic consistency regularization mechanism that enforces coherent predictions for visually diverse but semantically equivalent regions. Extensive experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing weakly supervised methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance with mIoU scores of 68.4% and 39.2% respectively. Our method effectively bridges the gap between weakly supervised and fully supervised semantic segmentation, while requiring only image-level annotations during training.

Common Spatial Generative Adversarial Networks based EEG Data Augmentation for Cross-Subject Brain-Computer Interface

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) face significant challenges in cross-subject applications due to the high variability of electroencephalography (EEG) signals across individuals. This paper introduces a novel data augmentation approach using Common Spatial Generative Adversarial Networks (CS-GANs) to address the limited availability of subject-specific training data. Our proposed framework combines common spatial patterns (CSP) with conditional GANs to generate synthetic EEG data that preserves subject-specific spatial features while enhancing cross-subject transferability. We evaluated our approach on two publicly available motor imagery EEG datasets, comparing classification performance between traditional methods and our CS-GAN augmented datasets. Results demonstrate that the CS-GAN approach significantly improves cross-subject classification accuracy by an average of 11.3% compared to baseline methods, with particularly notable improvements for subjects with initially poor performance. The generated synthetic data exhibited high similarity to real EEG signals based on time-frequency analysis and topographic distribution. Our findings suggest that CS-GAN based data augmentation can effectively reduce calibration requirements while enhancing the robustness and generalizability of BCI systems across different users, representing a promising direction for practical BCI applications.

Interpretable Machine Learning for COVID-19: An Empirical Study on Severity Prediction Task

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the need for reliable predictive models to assist healthcare professionals in resource allocation and patient management. This study presents an interpretable machine learning framework for predicting COVID-19 severity, addressing the critical balance between model performance and clinical interpretability. We developed and evaluated various interpretable models using a multi-center dataset of 6,842 COVID-19 patients, incorporating demographic information, comorbidities, vital signs, and laboratory findings. Our gradient boosting-based approach achieved high predictive accuracy (AUC 0.89, 95% CI: 0.87-0.91) while maintaining transparency through SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and partial dependence plots. Key predictors of disease severity included lymphocyte count, C-reactive protein levels, age, and oxygen saturation. Unlike black-box models, our approach provides clinicians with patient-specific risk factors and their relative contributions to predicted outcomes. External validation across three independent hospitals demonstrated robust generalizability (AUC 0.85-0.88). This work demonstrates that interpretable machine learning can effectively support clinical decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks while maintaining the transparency necessary for healthcare applications.

Dimensionality Reduction for Stationary Time Series via Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization

This paper presents a novel approach to dimensionality reduction for stationary time series data using stochastic nonconvex optimization techniques. We address the fundamental challenge of preserving temporal dependencies while reducing dimensionality, which traditional methods often fail to accomplish effectively. Our proposed framework formulates dimensionality reduction as a nonconvex optimization problem that explicitly accounts for autocorrelation structures and stationarity properties inherent in time series data. By leveraging recent advances in stochastic optimization algorithms, we develop an efficient solution that scales to large datasets while providing theoretical guarantees on convergence and solution quality. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world time series demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms conventional dimensionality reduction techniques, including PCA, t-SNE, and autoencoder-based approaches, particularly in preserving forecasting accuracy and detecting anomalies in the reduced space. Furthermore, we establish theoretical bounds on the approximation error and provide conditions under which stationarity properties are preserved after dimensionality reduction. These results contribute to both the theoretical understanding of time series representation and practical applications in time series analysis, forecasting, and anomaly detection.

BERT2DNN: BERT Distillation with Massive Unlabeled Data for Online E-Commerce Search

Pre-trained language models like BERT have demonstrated remarkable performance in various natural language processing tasks. However, their computational complexity makes them challenging to deploy in high-throughput, low-latency environments such as e-commerce search systems. In this paper, we present BERT2DNN, a knowledge distillation framework that transfers the semantic understanding capabilities of BERT to a lightweight deep neural network architecture suitable for online e-commerce search. Our approach leverages massive unlabeled query-product pairs harvested from search logs to create a rich training signal for the student model. We introduce a novel distillation methodology that captures both the relevance predictions and the semantic representations of BERT, enabling the student model to approximate BERT's performance while achieving inference speeds orders of magnitude faster. Extensive experiments on a large-scale e-commerce search dataset demonstrate that BERT2DNN significantly outperforms traditional information retrieval methods and approaches the quality of the teacher BERT model while meeting the strict latency requirements of production environments. Our deployment in a major e-commerce platform resulted in substantial improvements in key business metrics, including click-through rate (+3.2%) and conversion rate (+2.7%). This work provides valuable insights into effectively distilling complex language models for practical, large-scale search applications.

2nd Place Solutions in the HC-STVG track of Person in Context Challenge 2021

This paper presents our approach that secured the 2nd place in the Human-Centric Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (HC-STVG) track of the Person in Context (PIC) Challenge 2021. The HC-STVG task requires localizing a person in a video and identifying the specific temporal segments based on a natural language query. Our solution employs a multi-modal framework that effectively bridges visual and textual information. We propose a two-stage approach: first, a person detection module identifies potential candidates across video frames; second, a cross-modal matching network aligns the language query with spatio-temporal person features to determine the correct subject and temporal boundaries. Our method incorporates temporal context modeling through a transformer-based architecture that captures long-range dependencies across video frames. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance with a temporal IoU of 0.47 and a spatial IoU of 0.54 on the challenge test set, outperforming most competing methods. We conduct extensive ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of each component in our framework, revealing that the integration of fine-grained visual-linguistic alignment and temporal reasoning significantly contributes to the overall performance.

Cascaded Diffusion Models for High Fidelity Image Generation

This paper introduces a novel architecture for high-fidelity image synthesis through cascaded diffusion models. While diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities, they often struggle with producing fine details at high resolutions. Our approach addresses this limitation by implementing a multi-stage cascade of diffusion models, where each stage operates at progressively higher resolutions and conditions on outputs from previous stages. The cascade begins with a base diffusion model generating low-resolution images that capture global structure, followed by a series of super-resolution diffusion models that incrementally refine details. We demonstrate that this cascaded approach effectively decomposes the challenging high-resolution generation task into more manageable sub-problems, leading to improved sample quality and diversity. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art FID scores and generates images with exceptional detail and realism at resolutions up to 1024×1024 pixels. Additionally, we analyze the computational efficiency of our approach and propose optimization techniques that make high-resolution generation more practical. Our cascaded architecture presents a promising direction for scaling diffusion models to generate increasingly high-fidelity images.

Batch Reinforcement Learning with a Nonparametric Off-Policy Policy Gradient

This paper introduces a novel nonparametric approach for off-policy policy gradient estimation in batch reinforcement learning settings. Unlike traditional methods that rely on parametric function approximators, our approach leverages kernel-based density estimation techniques to directly estimate policy gradients from fixed offline datasets without requiring explicit models of the environment dynamics or value functions. We demonstrate that our method effectively addresses the distribution shift problem inherent in off-policy learning through importance sampling with adaptive kernel bandwidth selection. Theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees and sample complexity bounds under mild assumptions. Empirical evaluations on continuous control benchmarks show that our nonparametric policy gradient approach outperforms existing off-policy algorithms, particularly in scenarios with limited or biased batch data. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our method can be integrated with existing batch reinforcement learning frameworks to enhance policy optimization when working with fixed datasets. Our contributions expand the applicability of policy gradient methods to offline settings where exploration is not possible, making reinforcement learning more practical for real-world applications with safety or cost constraints.

Asymmetric Distributions from Constrained Mixtures

This paper introduces a novel framework for generating flexible asymmetric probability distributions through constrained mixture models. We develop a theoretical foundation for constructing distributions with controlled skewness and tail behavior by imposing specific constraints on the parameters of component distributions within a mixture. Our approach allows for systematic manipulation of distributional properties while maintaining mathematical tractability. We demonstrate that many well-known asymmetric distributions can be represented as special cases of our constrained mixture framework, providing a unifying perspective on seemingly disparate distributional families. Simulation studies validate the flexibility of our approach in modeling diverse asymmetric patterns in data. We further establish theoretical properties including moment calculations, maximum likelihood estimation procedures, and asymptotic behavior. Applications to financial returns data, environmental measurements, and biomedical outcomes illustrate the practical utility of constrained mixture distributions in capturing complex asymmetric phenomena. This work contributes to both the theoretical understanding of asymmetric distributions and provides practitioners with a versatile modeling tool for asymmetric data.

Modelling of Directional Data Using Kent Distributions

This paper explores the application of Kent distributions for modeling directional data on the sphere. The Kent distribution, also known as the Fisher-Bingham five-parameter distribution, provides a flexible framework for analyzing non-symmetrical directional data with elliptical contours. We present the theoretical foundations of Kent distributions, highlighting their ability to capture both the concentration and elliptical shape of directional data distributions. The methodology includes parameter estimation techniques, with particular emphasis on maximum likelihood estimation and moment-based approaches. We demonstrate the practical utility of Kent distributions through applications to various domains, including geoscience, biomechanics, and astronomy, where directional data naturally arise. Comparative analyses with other directional distributions, such as the von Mises-Fisher and Bingham distributions, reveal the advantages of Kent distributions in modeling data with both location and correlation structure. Simulation studies assess the robustness and efficiency of the estimation procedures under different sample sizes and concentration parameters. Our results indicate that Kent distributions provide superior fits for elliptically distributed directional data, particularly when the data exhibit asymmetry around the mean direction. The paper concludes with recommendations for practical implementation and suggestions for future research directions in directional statistics.

Generalization of Reinforcement Learners with Working and Episodic Memory

This paper investigates the generalization capabilities of reinforcement learning agents equipped with working and episodic memory systems. While deep reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in various domains, the ability to transfer knowledge to novel environments remains a significant challenge. We propose a dual-memory architecture that integrates a capacity-limited working memory for immediate task execution with an episodic memory system that stores and retrieves relevant past experiences. Through extensive experiments across diverse environments with systematic distribution shifts, we demonstrate that this memory integration substantially improves generalization performance compared to traditional memory-free approaches and single-memory systems. Our results indicate that working memory facilitates rapid adaptation to new scenarios by maintaining task-relevant information, while episodic memory enables the agent to recognize and leverage similarities with previously encountered situations. We provide theoretical analysis of the complementary roles these memory systems play in generalization and empirically validate our approach on navigation, puzzle-solving, and strategic decision-making tasks. This work contributes to our understanding of how memory mechanisms support generalization in reinforcement learning and offers insights for developing more adaptable artificial agents.

Boosting Few-Shot Classification with View-Learnable Contrastive Learning

Few-shot classification remains a challenging problem in machine learning, where models must learn to recognize new classes from very limited examples. This paper introduces View-Learnable Contrastive Learning (VLCL), a novel approach that significantly improves few-shot classification performance by dynamically learning optimal data augmentation strategies during the representation learning phase. Unlike traditional contrastive learning methods that rely on fixed, hand-crafted augmentations, our approach employs a learnable view generator that produces task-specific transformations tailored to enhance discriminative feature learning. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and CIFAR-FS, we demonstrate that VLCL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods, achieving 2-4% accuracy improvements across various N-way K-shot settings. Further analysis reveals that our learned views capture semantically meaningful transformations that preserve class-relevant features while introducing variations that strengthen the model's generalization capabilities. Our approach requires minimal computational overhead during inference and can be readily integrated with existing few-shot learning frameworks, making it a practical solution for real-world applications where labeled data is scarce.

A Comparative Study of the Clinical use of Motion Analysis from Kinect Skeleton Data

This study evaluates the efficacy of Microsoft Kinect-based skeleton tracking technology for clinical motion analysis applications. We compared Kinect-derived motion data with gold-standard optical motion capture systems across multiple clinical contexts, including gait analysis, rehabilitation assessment, and neurological disorder evaluation. Twenty-five participants with various movement disorders and twenty-five healthy controls were assessed using both Kinect and laboratory-grade motion capture systems simultaneously. Results indicate that while the Kinect demonstrates acceptable accuracy for gross movement patterns (average error: 2.8±1.2cm), with correlation coefficients of 0.82-0.94 compared to reference systems, it shows limitations in capturing fine motor movements and complex joint rotations. The technology performed best in controlled environments with frontal positioning and demonstrated clinical utility for remote monitoring, rehabilitation progress tracking, and preliminary screening. Cost-benefit analysis revealed the Kinect-based approach costs approximately 8% of traditional systems while maintaining clinical relevance for specific applications. This study provides evidence-based recommendations for appropriate clinical implementation of Kinect skeleton data analysis, highlighting both its potential as an accessible motion analysis tool and its technical limitations in specialized clinical assessments.

Real-Time Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework for Real-Time Reinforcement Learning (RTRL) that addresses the fundamental challenge of decision-making under strict timing constraints. Traditional reinforcement learning algorithms often assume unlimited computational resources and time for policy optimization, making them impractical for applications requiring rapid responses such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and high-frequency trading. Our approach reformulates the reinforcement learning paradigm by explicitly incorporating time as a constrained resource in both the learning process and decision execution. We propose a time-aware value function that balances solution quality with computational demands, alongside an adaptive computation allocation mechanism that dynamically adjusts processing time based on environmental complexity. Experimental results across simulated and real-world tasks demonstrate that RTRL achieves near-optimal performance while adhering to hard real-time constraints, outperforming conventional algorithms when operating under time pressure. The framework provides theoretical guarantees on bounded response times while maintaining convergence properties, establishing a foundation for deploying reinforcement learning in time-critical systems where reliability and predictable execution are paramount.

IR2VI: Enhanced Night Environmental Perception by Unsupervised Thermal Image Translation

This paper introduces IR2VI, a novel unsupervised learning framework for translating thermal infrared (IR) images to visible-spectrum (VI) images to enhance environmental perception capabilities in low-light and nighttime conditions. Unlike supervised approaches that require paired training data, our method leverages unpaired IR-VI image sets through a cycle-consistent adversarial network architecture specifically optimized for the thermal-to-visible domain gap. We propose a thermal-aware content preservation module that maintains critical structural and semantic information during translation while a multi-scale perceptual consistency loss ensures realistic visible spectrum characteristics. Extensive experiments on diverse nighttime datasets demonstrate that IR2VI outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both qualitative visual quality and quantitative metrics. When integrated with standard computer vision pipelines, our translated images significantly improve performance in downstream tasks including object detection, semantic segmentation, and scene recognition under challenging nighttime conditions, with an average improvement of 18.7% in detection accuracy over raw thermal inputs. The unsupervised nature of IR2VI makes it particularly valuable for autonomous driving and surveillance applications where paired training data is scarce or unavailable.

Sparse-to-dense Feature Matching: Intra and Inter domain Cross-modal Learning in Domain Adaptation for 3D Semantic Segmentation

This paper introduces a novel approach to domain adaptation for 3D semantic segmentation that addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge between sparse source domains (e.g., LiDAR point clouds) and dense target domains (e.g., depth images). We propose a Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching (SDFM) framework that leverages both intra-domain and inter-domain cross-modal learning to bridge the representation gap between different 3D data modalities and domains. Our approach employs a dual-branch architecture that simultaneously learns domain-invariant features while preserving the unique structural characteristics of each modality. The SDFM framework incorporates three key components: (1) a sparse-to-dense feature alignment module that maps between different density representations, (2) an intra-domain consistency regularization that enforces semantic coherence within each domain, and (3) an inter-domain adaptation mechanism that aligns feature distributions across domains through adversarial learning and mutual information maximization. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including SemanticKITTI, nuScenes, and ScanNet demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing domain adaptation techniques, achieving up to 12.3% improvement in mIoU over state-of-the-art approaches. Our framework provides a robust solution for real-world applications where training data modalities differ from deployment scenarios, enabling more effective transfer learning for 3D semantic segmentation tasks.

Bidirectional Recursive Neural Networks for Token-Level Labeling with Structure

This paper introduces a novel bidirectional recursive neural network (Bi-RNN) architecture designed for token-level labeling tasks that benefit from structural information. Unlike traditional sequential models that process text in a linear fashion, our approach explicitly incorporates syntactic and hierarchical structure into the learning process. The Bi-RNN model processes information both bottom-up and top-down through parse trees, allowing each token to be represented by contextual features from its entire structural neighborhood. We evaluate our approach on several challenging NLP tasks including named entity recognition, opinion target extraction, and semantic role labeling. Experimental results demonstrate that the Bi-RNN consistently outperforms strong sequential baselines such as bidirectional LSTMs, particularly for linguistically complex instances where structural information provides crucial disambiguation cues. Additionally, we present an analysis showing that our model's performance gains correlate with parse tree depth and structural complexity, confirming the value of recursive architectures for capturing long-distance dependencies in hierarchical data. The proposed approach provides a general framework for incorporating structural biases into neural sequence labeling while maintaining computational efficiency during both training and inference.

Group-Wise Semantic Mining for Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation

This paper presents a novel approach to weakly supervised semantic segmentation that addresses the fundamental challenge of generating accurate pixel-level predictions using only image-level labels. We introduce Group-Wise Semantic Mining (GWSM), a framework that leverages the inherent semantic relationships between object categories to enhance segmentation performance. Our method divides object categories into semantically coherent groups and exploits inter-group and intra-group relationships to refine initial class activation maps. GWSM employs a dual-branch architecture: one branch focuses on mining group-level semantic features while the other extracts category-specific details. Through an iterative refinement process, our approach progressively improves localization accuracy and boundary delineation. Extensive experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO datasets demonstrate that GWSM outperforms existing weakly supervised methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance with mIoU improvements of 2.3% and 1.8% respectively. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our semantic grouping strategy and highlight its ability to handle complex scenes with multiple object categories. Our approach significantly narrows the performance gap between weakly supervised and fully supervised semantic segmentation while maintaining computational efficiency.

Learning Bodily and Temporal Attention in Protective Movement Behavior Detection

Protective movement behaviors (PMBs) are altered movement patterns exhibited by individuals with musculoskeletal pain, characterized by movement adaptations intended to avoid discomfort or perceived harm. This paper presents a novel deep learning framework that simultaneously captures both bodily and temporal attention patterns for automated PMB detection from motion capture data. Our approach employs a dual-attention mechanism: a spatial attention module that identifies the most salient body segments contributing to protective behaviors, and a temporal attention layer that focuses on critical movement phases where protective strategies are most evident. Using a dataset of 200 participants performing standardized movement tasks, our model achieved 87.3% accuracy in PMB classification, outperforming previous methods by 9.2%. Visualization of the attention weights revealed consistent patterns of guarding and bracing behaviors primarily manifested in the lower back and lower extremities during transitional movement phases. The proposed architecture not only advances automated PMB detection but also provides clinically interpretable insights into movement adaptations, potentially enhancing assessment and rehabilitation strategies for individuals with chronic pain. Our findings demonstrate the value of attention-based approaches for understanding the complex spatiotemporal nature of protective movement behaviors.

On the Arbitrary-Oriented Object Detection: Classification based Approaches Revisited

This paper revisits classification-based approaches for arbitrary-oriented object detection, a challenging task in computer vision that requires identifying objects with unrestricted rotational angles. While regression-based methods have dominated recent research in this field, we demonstrate that classification-based approaches, when properly designed, can achieve competitive or superior performance. We analyze the limitations of previous classification-based methods, particularly their inefficiency in angle discretization and representation learning. To address these issues, we propose a novel angle-adaptive classification framework that dynamically adjusts the granularity of angle prediction based on object characteristics and context. Our approach incorporates a hierarchical classification scheme coupled with a feature enhancement module that captures rotation-invariant features. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including DOTA, HRSC2016, and UCAS-AOD demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art regression-based approaches by 2.3% mAP while maintaining comparable inference speed. Furthermore, our approach shows particular strength in handling small objects and densely packed scenes with complex orientations. This work challenges the prevailing view that regression is inherently superior for arbitrary-oriented object detection and opens new research directions for classification-based methods in this domain.

Generative One-Class Models for Text-based Person Retrieval in Forensic Applications

This paper introduces a novel approach to text-based person retrieval for forensic applications using generative one-class models. Traditional person retrieval systems often struggle with the unique challenges presented in forensic contexts, including limited reference data, unstructured textual descriptions, and the absence of negative examples. Our framework leverages recent advances in generative AI to develop one-class models specifically designed to operate with only positive instances of person descriptions. We propose a transformer-based architecture that learns to encode the distinctive characteristics of individuals from textual descriptions while being robust to the linguistic variations common in witness statements and investigative reports. Experiments conducted on a forensically relevant dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves 78% retrieval accuracy, outperforming conventional binary and multi-class classification methods by 12-18%. Additionally, the generative capabilities of our model enable it to synthesize plausible textual descriptions that can aid in suspect identification when only partial information is available. The interpretability features built into our system provide investigators with explanation traces for retrieval decisions, addressing critical transparency requirements in forensic applications. This work represents a significant advancement in applying AI to forensic person retrieval while maintaining the standards of reliability and accountability essential in legal contexts.

Segmentation for Radar Images Based on Active Contour

This paper presents a novel approach to radar image segmentation using active contour models. Radar imagery presents unique challenges for segmentation due to speckle noise, low contrast, and complex scattering phenomena. We propose an enhanced active contour framework specifically tailored for radar data that incorporates speckle statistics into the energy functional. Our method combines a region-based term that models the statistical properties of radar backscatter with an edge-based term that adapts to the gradient characteristics of radar imagery. The proposed algorithm demonstrates robustness to speckle noise without requiring pre-filtering steps that might compromise image resolution. Experimental results on synthetic aperture radar (SAR), weather radar, and ground-penetrating radar datasets show significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to conventional methods. Quantitative evaluation reveals our approach achieves an average improvement of 18% in boundary delineation precision and 23% in region homogeneity metrics over traditional active contour implementations. The method shows particular promise for applications including land cover classification, target detection, and change monitoring in radar remote sensing.

DH3D: Deep Hierarchical 3D Descriptors for Robust Large-Scale 6DoF Relocalization

This paper presents DH3D, a novel hierarchical learning framework for extracting discriminative 3D descriptors that enable robust camera relocalization in large-scale environments. Our approach addresses the fundamental challenge of accurately determining 6DoF camera pose in complex, dynamic scenes with limited computational resources. DH3D employs a multi-resolution architecture that processes raw point cloud data through a series of hierarchical feature extraction modules, progressively capturing both fine geometric details and global contextual information. Unlike previous methods that rely heavily on RGB data or dense point representations, our descriptor framework operates efficiently on sparse 3D structure while maintaining high discriminative power. Experimental results on challenging benchmarks including Oxford RobotCar, KITTI, and our newly introduced large-scale dataset demonstrate that DH3D significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 87% recall at precision thresholds where competing approaches fall below 65%. The system maintains real-time performance on standard hardware and exhibits remarkable robustness to environmental variations including seasonal changes, lighting differences, and scene dynamics. Our approach enables practical relocalization applications in autonomous navigation, augmented reality, and robotic systems operating in unconstrained environments.

Abstract: Graph Decoupling Attention Markov Networks for Semi-supervised Graph Node Classification

We present Graph Decoupling Attention Markov Networks (GDAMN), a novel approach for semi-supervised node classification in graph-structured data. Our method addresses key limitations of existing graph neural networks by introducing a decoupling mechanism that separately models feature propagation and structural dependencies through a specialized attention framework. GDAMN incorporates a Markov random field component that effectively captures higher-order neighborhood relationships while maintaining computational efficiency. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our approach mitigates the over-smoothing and over-squashing problems common in deep graph architectures. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Cora, Citeseer, PubMed, and protein interaction networks show that GDAMN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 3-5% improvement in classification accuracy while requiring fewer parameters. The model exhibits particular strength in scenarios with limited labeled data and heterogeneous graph structures. Our ablation studies confirm the importance of each component in the architecture and validate the effectiveness of the decoupling strategy. GDAMN provides a powerful framework for learning node representations that balance local feature preservation with global structural awareness.

Impact of Low-bitwidth Quantization on the Adversarial Robustness for Embedded Neural Networks

This study investigates the relationship between low-bitwidth quantization techniques and adversarial robustness in neural networks deployed on resource-constrained embedded systems. While quantization is widely used to reduce model size and computational requirements for embedded applications, its effects on vulnerability to adversarial attacks remain poorly understood. We conduct comprehensive experiments across multiple network architectures (CNNs, MobileNets, and EfficientNets) quantized to various bitwidths (8-bit, 4-bit, and 2-bit) and evaluate their resilience against common adversarial attacks including FGSM, PGD, and CW methods. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship: moderate quantization (8-bit) often enhances adversarial robustness by up to 17% compared to full-precision models, likely due to the gradient masking effect and reduced sensitivity to small perturbations. However, extreme quantization (2-bit) significantly degrades both standard accuracy and adversarial robustness. We further propose a novel quantization-aware adversarial training framework that achieves better robustness-efficiency trade-offs than standard approaches. These findings provide important insights for designing secure embedded neural networks and demonstrate that properly calibrated quantization can simultaneously address resource constraints and security concerns in edge AI applications.

Abstract: Lossless Compression of Structured Convolutional Models via Lifting

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success across various computer vision tasks, but their computational and storage requirements often limit deployment on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel lossless compression technique for structured convolutional models through a mathematical framework we call "lifting." Our approach exploits inherent redundancies in convolutional filter structures by mapping them to a higher-dimensional space where their essential characteristics can be represented more compactly. Unlike traditional pruning or quantization methods that sacrifice accuracy, our lifting-based compression preserves the model's functional behavior exactly, ensuring truly lossless compression. We formalize the theoretical foundations of the lifting transformation and derive optimal compression bounds for common CNN architectures. Experimental results demonstrate compression ratios of 3-5× on modern architectures like ResNet and MobileNet without any degradation in accuracy across image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks. The compressed models maintain identical inference results while requiring significantly less storage and achieving faster inference times due to reduced memory bandwidth requirements. Our method is complementary to existing compression techniques and can be combined with them for enhanced efficiency. The proposed approach opens new possibilities for deploying sophisticated deep learning models in memory-constrained environments.

ConvNets for Counting: Object Detection of Transient Phenomena in Steelpan Drums

This study explores the application of convolutional neural networks (ConvNets) for detecting and quantifying transient acoustic phenomena in steelpan drums. We present a novel approach that adapts object detection architectures to identify, localize, and count short-lived vibrational events that characterize the unique timbre of these instruments. Using high-speed imaging and spectral analysis, we generated a dataset of labeled transient phenomena occurring on the drum's surface during performance. Our model, based on a modified Faster R-CNN architecture, achieved 93.7% accuracy in detecting these events with a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.91. The system successfully differentiated between multiple classes of transients, including note onsets, modal coupling effects, and harmonic interactions. This computational approach provides new insights into the complex acoustical behavior of steelpan drums that traditional signal processing methods struggle to capture. The methodology developed has implications beyond musical acoustics, offering potential applications in structural analysis, manufacturing quality control, and the preservation of traditional instrument-making knowledge.

Abstract: Deep Machine Learning Based Egyptian Vehicle License Plate Recognition Systems

This research presents a comprehensive deep machine learning framework for Egyptian vehicle license plate recognition, addressing the unique challenges posed by Egypt's diverse plate formats, Arabic characters, and varying environmental conditions. Our system employs a two-stage approach: first utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for license plate detection and localization, followed by a sequence-to-sequence model with attention mechanisms for character recognition. The proposed architecture achieves robust performance by integrating transfer learning techniques on a custom dataset of over 5,000 Egyptian license plates collected across different lighting conditions, angles, and distances. Experimental results demonstrate an overall accuracy of 94.7% for plate detection and 92.3% for character recognition, significantly outperforming traditional computer vision methods. The system maintains real-time processing capabilities (24 fps) while handling complex scenarios including partial occlusions and varying illumination. This work contributes to intelligent transportation systems in Egypt by providing a scalable solution that accommodates both legacy and modern license plate formats, with potential applications in traffic management, security systems, and automated toll collection.

Foreground-Background Segmentation Based on Codebook and Edge Detector

This paper presents a novel approach to foreground-background segmentation that combines codebook modeling with edge detection techniques. The proposed method addresses common challenges in segmentation such as illumination changes, background variations, and noise. Our algorithm employs a two-stage process: first, a codebook model captures the statistical properties of background pixels over time, allowing for adaptive background representation; second, an edge detection mechanism enhances boundary delineation between foreground and background regions. By integrating these complementary techniques, our method achieves more accurate segmentation in complex scenes. Experimental results on standard datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average F1-score improvement of 8.7% and reducing false positives by 12.3% compared to traditional approaches. The method shows particular robustness in challenging scenarios including dynamic backgrounds, shadows, and varying lighting conditions. This work contributes to the field of computer vision by offering an efficient solution for real-time applications such as video surveillance, human-computer interaction, and automated visual inspection systems.

Generator Versus Segmentor: Pseudo-healthy Synthesis

The synthesis of pseudo-healthy medical images—where pathological regions are replaced with healthy-appearing tissue—presents a significant challenge in medical image analysis.
