We developed a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that integrates mammographic and MRI imaging data with genomic sequencing information from 1,245 breast cancer patients. Our model employs convolutional neural networks to extract high-dimensional imaging features, which are then correlated with key genomic alterations including mutations in BRCA1/2, TP53, and PIK3CA genes, as well as molecular subtypes. Results demonstrate that specific imaging patterns can predict genomic characteristics with an AUC of 0.83, outperforming traditional radiomics approaches (AUC 0.71). Notably, we identified previously unreported associations between tumor margin characteristics on MRI and PIK3CA mutation status, and between parenchymal patterns on mammography and immune infiltration signatures. These radiogenomic associations may enable non-invasive tumor characterization, potentially reducing the need for invasive biopsies and facilitating personalized treatment planning. Our findings suggest that deep learning-based radiogenomics could serve as a valuable tool for precision oncology in breast cancer management.

An Actor-Critic Algorithm for Sequence Prediction

This paper introduces a novel actor-critic reinforcement learning framework designed specifically for sequence prediction tasks. Our approach combines the advantages of policy-based and value-based methods to address the challenges of sparse rewards and long-term dependencies inherent in sequential data. The actor network generates predictions while the critic network provides value estimates that guide the learning process, reducing variance and improving stability. We formulate sequence prediction as a Markov Decision Process and develop specialized training techniques to handle the structured output space. Experimental results across multiple domains—including natural language processing, time series forecasting, and structured data generation—demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional sequence models and existing reinforcement learning methods. The algorithm shows particular strength in scenarios requiring long-range planning and when dealing with ambiguous contexts. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical evidence of sample efficiency, making this approach practical for real-world sequence prediction tasks with limited training data.

BRITS: Bidirectional Recurrent Imputation for Time Series

Time series data often suffers from missing values, which poses significant challenges for data analysis and model training. In this paper, we present BRITS (Bidirectional Recurrent Imputation for Time Series), a novel approach for handling missing values in time series data. Our method leverages bidirectional recurrent neural networks to capture temporal dependencies from both past and future contexts, enabling accurate imputation of missing values. BRITS directly learns the missing values in a unified end-to-end framework without requiring any specific assumptions about the missing data mechanism. The bidirectional architecture allows the model to utilize information from the entire sequence, leading to more robust imputations even with complex missing patterns. Through extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets, including healthcare time series and sensor data, we demonstrate that BRITS outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods in terms of imputation accuracy and downstream task performance. Additionally, our approach maintains computational efficiency while handling irregular time intervals commonly found in real-world time series. The proposed method provides a powerful tool for addressing missing data challenges in time series analysis across various domains.

A Workflow for Offline Model-Free Robotic Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a comprehensive workflow for implementing offline model-free reinforcement learning (RL) in robotic systems. Unlike online RL methods that require continuous environment interaction during training, our approach leverages pre-collected datasets to train policies without additional environment sampling. We address key challenges in offline RL including distributional shift, conservative value estimation, and effective utilization of heterogeneous demonstration data. The proposed workflow encompasses data collection strategies, preprocessing techniques, algorithm selection considerations, and deployment methodologies specifically tailored for robotic applications. We evaluate our approach on several manipulation tasks, demonstrating that our workflow enables robots to learn effective policies from diverse datasets including suboptimal demonstrations, teleoperated trajectories, and autonomously collected experiences. Empirical results show that our method achieves comparable performance to online RL methods while eliminating the need for potentially unsafe exploration during training. This workflow provides a practical framework for roboticists to implement offline RL in real-world settings where online exploration is costly, dangerous, or impractical.

Local Binary Pattern for Word Spotting in Handwritten Historical Document

This paper presents a novel approach to word spotting in handwritten historical documents using Local Binary Pattern (LBP) features. Word spotting, the task of locating specific words in document images without full transcription, remains challenging due to variations in handwriting styles, degradation of historical documents, and the absence of explicit word boundaries. Our method leverages the texture-descriptive power of LBP operators to capture the distinctive visual patterns of handwritten words while being robust to the common degradations found in historical manuscripts. We extract multi-scale LBP features from sliding windows over document images and employ a spatial pyramid matching scheme to accommodate the elastic nature of handwriting. Experiments conducted on three diverse historical document collections spanning the 17th-19th centuries demonstrate that our LBP-based approach outperforms traditional gradient-based descriptors, achieving a mean average precision of 76.3% for query-by-example word spotting tasks. The method proves particularly effective for degraded documents with low contrast and shows computational efficiency suitable for large-scale archives. This work contributes to the ongoing efforts to make historical handwritten documents more accessible to scholars and the general public through efficient content-based retrieval techniques.

Feature-Based Interpretable Reinforcement Learning based on State-Transition Models

This paper presents a novel approach to interpretable reinforcement learning (RL) that leverages feature-based representations within state-transition models. While deep reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable performance in various domains, the black-box nature of neural network policies limits their applicability in safety-critical and human-collaborative environments where transparency is essential. Our method addresses this challenge by constructing interpretable state-transition models that capture the relationship between meaningful state features and agent actions. We introduce a framework that decomposes complex state spaces into human-understandable features and learns transition dynamics that explicitly model how actions influence these features. By incorporating feature importance metrics and causal relationships between state variables, our approach enables post-hoc explanation of learned policies. Experimental results across diverse environments demonstrate that our feature-based interpretable RL achieves comparable performance to black-box methods while providing clear insights into decision-making processes. Additionally, we show that the resulting interpretable policies facilitate more effective human oversight, easier debugging, and greater trust in autonomous systems. This work represents a significant step toward reconciling the performance benefits of modern RL with the interpretability demands of real-world applications.

Complex-valued neural networks for machine learning on non-stationary physical data

This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling non-stationary physical systems using complex-valued neural networks (CVNNs). While traditional real-valued neural networks have shown significant success in many machine learning applications, they often struggle to efficiently capture the underlying dynamics of physical systems characterized by phase information, oscillatory behaviors, and wave phenomena. We present a comprehensive framework for CVNNs specifically designed to process and learn from non-stationary physical data, where both amplitude and phase components carry critical information. Our architecture leverages complex-valued activation functions, complex batch normalization, and specialized initialization schemes that preserve the geometric properties inherent in complex domains. Through extensive experiments on diverse physical datasets including fluid dynamics, electromagnetic wave propagation, and quantum mechanical systems, we demonstrate that CVNNs consistently outperform their real-valued counterparts in prediction accuracy, convergence rate, and generalization capability. Furthermore, we show that our complex-valued approach requires fewer parameters to achieve comparable performance, resulting in more interpretable models that better align with the underlying physics. These results highlight the significant potential of complex-valued neural networks as a powerful tool for scientific machine learning applications involving time-varying, oscillatory physical phenomena.

Equivariant Flows: Exact Likelihood Generative Learning for Symmetric Densities

We introduce Equivariant Flows, a novel class of normalizing flow models that respects the symmetry structures inherent in probability densities. While conventional normalizing flows can theoretically approximate any probability distribution, they often struggle to efficiently model densities with underlying symmetries. Our approach explicitly incorporates equivariance constraints into the flow architecture, ensuring that the learned transformations commute with the actions of the symmetry group. This paper provides a theoretical framework for constructing equivariant normalizing flows and proves that they can exactly represent symmetric target densities while maintaining the tractability of likelihood computation. We demonstrate that by leveraging known symmetries, Equivariant Flows achieve more sample-efficient learning, better generalization, and improved performance on density estimation tasks compared to standard flow models. Experiments on synthetic datasets, molecular configurations, and physical systems with various symmetry groups (including rotational, reflectional, and permutation symmetries) demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms baseline methods while requiring fewer parameters. Our work bridges the gap between symmetry-aware modeling and exact likelihood-based generative learning, opening new avenues for efficiently modeling complex symmetric distributions in various scientific domains.

Evolutionary Stochastic Policy Distillation

This paper introduces Evolutionary Stochastic Policy Distillation (ESPD), a novel framework that combines evolutionary algorithms with policy distillation techniques to address key challenges in reinforcement learning. Our approach leverages the exploration capabilities of evolutionary methods while incorporating the knowledge transfer benefits of policy distillation to create robust and adaptable policies. By maintaining a population of stochastic policies that evolve through natural selection principles, ESPD efficiently explores the policy space while distilling accumulated knowledge into a target network. We demonstrate that this hybrid approach mitigates common reinforcement learning issues including sparse rewards, local optima, and catastrophic forgetting. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments show that ESPD outperforms traditional policy gradient methods and standard evolutionary strategies, particularly in complex environments with deceptive reward landscapes. Our results indicate significant improvements in sample efficiency, final performance, and policy generalization. This work bridges the gap between gradient-free evolutionary methods and gradient-based policy optimization, offering a promising direction for developing more effective reinforcement learning algorithms.

Novel Approach to Locate Region of Interest in Mammograms for Breast Cancer

This paper presents a novel computational approach for automated detection and localization of regions of interest (ROIs) in mammographic images to assist in early breast cancer diagnosis. The proposed method integrates advanced image processing techniques with deep learning to overcome limitations of traditional ROI detection methods, which often suffer from poor contrast, tissue overlap, and high false positive rates. Our approach employs a multi-stage framework that begins with adaptive preprocessing to enhance image quality, followed by a custom-designed convolutional neural network architecture optimized for mammographic feature extraction. We introduce a novel attention mechanism that emphasizes suspicious regions while suppressing normal tissue patterns. The method was evaluated on a diverse dataset of 2,500 mammograms from multiple institutions, achieving 94.3% sensitivity and 92.1% specificity in ROI detection, with a significant reduction in false positives compared to existing methods. Radiologist assessment confirmed that the automatically identified ROIs demonstrated strong correlation with clinically significant regions. This approach has the potential to reduce interpretation variability and improve workflow efficiency in breast cancer screening programs by directing radiologists' attention to the most suspicious areas requiring further investigation.

An Efficient Framework for Zero-Shot Sketch-Based Image Retrieval

This paper presents a novel framework for Zero-Shot Sketch-Based Image Retrieval (ZS-SBIR) that addresses the challenging task of retrieving natural images using hand-drawn sketches of previously unseen object categories. Unlike conventional SBIR systems that require extensive paired sketch-image training data for each category, our approach operates effectively in scenarios where test categories are entirely absent from the training process. We propose a dual-branch neural architecture that learns a common embedding space where sketches and images of the same semantic concept are mapped close together, regardless of whether that concept appeared during training. Our framework leverages semantic knowledge transfer through a combination of (1) a feature disentanglement mechanism that separates category-specific attributes from visual characteristics, (2) a cross-modal attention module that highlights discriminative regions in both sketches and images, and (3) a semantic consistency loss that enforces alignment with word embeddings of class labels. Extensive experiments on the Sketchy Extended and TU-Berlin datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot settings, with retrieval accuracy improvements of 7.2% and 5.8% respectively over existing methods, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. The proposed framework shows particular robustness to sketch abstraction and style variations, making it practical for deployment in real-world retrieval systems.

Abstract: Robust Hierarchical Graph Classification with Subgraph Attention

Graph classification remains a challenging task in machine learning due to the complex structural information encoded in graph data. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for graph classification that leverages hierarchical graph representations with a subgraph attention mechanism. Our approach, Robust Hierarchical Graph Classification with Subgraph Attention (RHGCSA), effectively captures multi-scale structural patterns by decomposing graphs into meaningful subgraphs and learning their relative importance through an attention mechanism. Unlike previous methods that focus primarily on node-level or graph-level representations, our hierarchical approach constructs a multi-resolution view of graphs, enabling more comprehensive feature extraction. Experimental results on benchmark datasets from diverse domains including social networks, molecular graphs, and protein structures demonstrate that RHGCSA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with significant improvements in classification accuracy and robustness to graph perturbations. Additionally, the attention weights provide interpretable insights into discriminative substructures relevant to classification decisions. Our approach addresses key limitations in existing graph classification methods, particularly for complex graphs with heterogeneous substructure importance.

Pastprop-RNN: Improved Predictions of the Future by Correcting the Past

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in sequence modeling tasks, yet they often struggle with long-term dependencies and error accumulation during prediction. In this paper, we introduce Pastprop-RNN, a novel architecture that enhances future predictions by systematically correcting past state representations. Our approach implements a bidirectional correction mechanism that allows the model to refine its historical hidden states based on subsequent observations, creating a more coherent and accurate internal representation of temporal dynamics. Unlike traditional RNNs that maintain fixed representations of processed elements, Pastprop-RNN employs a differentiable memory correction pathway that propagates gradient information backward through time while maintaining computational efficiency. Through extensive experiments on multiple sequence prediction benchmarks including time series forecasting, language modeling, and video prediction tasks, we demonstrate that Pastprop-RNN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art recurrent architectures, reducing prediction error by 18-27% while using comparable parameter counts. Our analysis reveals that the performance gains are particularly pronounced in scenarios requiring long-horizon predictions and when dealing with noisy or partially observed data. These results suggest that explicitly modeling the correction of past representations provides a powerful inductive bias for sequence modeling tasks.

Generative Feature Replay For Class-Incremental Learning

Class-incremental learning remains a significant challenge in machine learning systems, as models tend to catastrophically forget previously learned knowledge when trained on new classes. This paper introduces Generative Feature Replay (GFR), a novel approach that addresses catastrophic forgetting by preserving and replaying feature representations rather than raw input data. Our method employs a generative model operating in the feature space to synthesize representations of previous classes, which are then used alongside new class data during incremental training phases. Unlike conventional replay methods that store or generate images, GFR operates in a lower-dimensional, semantically rich feature space, reducing storage requirements and computational overhead while maintaining privacy advantages. Through extensive experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-Subset, and TinyImageNet benchmarks, we demonstrate that GFR significantly outperforms existing rehearsal-based and regularization-based approaches, achieving 11.3% higher average accuracy on CIFAR-100 after 10 incremental steps compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into why feature-level replay is more effective than input-level alternatives, particularly as the complexity of the classification task increases. Our approach offers a practical and efficient solution for deployment in real-world incremental learning scenarios where model adaptation to new classes must occur without catastrophic forgetting.

Non-Recursive Graph Convolutional Networks

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations on graph-structured data, but traditional formulations often rely on recursive neighborhood aggregation schemes that can lead to computational inefficiencies and optimization challenges. In this paper, we propose Non-Recursive Graph Convolutional Networks (NR-GCNs), a novel architecture that eliminates the need for iterative propagation while preserving the ability to capture multi-hop dependencies in graph data. Our approach replaces recursive message passing with a direct, parallelizable computation that explicitly models higher-order neighborhood interactions through carefully designed spectral filters. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that NR-GCNs can approximate the representational capacity of recursive GCNs while avoiding issues such as over-smoothing and vanishing gradients. Extensive experiments on benchmark node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks show that NR-GCNs achieve competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art recursive models while offering significant advantages in training efficiency and scalability to large graphs. Our work provides a promising alternative paradigm for graph representation learning that addresses fundamental limitations of recursive architectures.

Dense Nested Attention Network for Infrared Small Target Detection

Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) is a critical task in various surveillance and security applications, yet it remains challenging due to the targets' limited size, low signal-to-noise ratio, and complex backgrounds. This paper presents a novel Dense Nested Attention Network (DNANet) that addresses these challenges through a hierarchical feature extraction approach. Our network architecture integrates dense connectivity patterns with nested attention mechanisms that operate across multiple scales. The dense connections facilitate efficient information flow between layers, while the nested attention modules selectively emphasize discriminative features at different resolutions. We introduce a multi-scale feature fusion strategy that preserves both global contextual information and fine-grained local details critical for small target identification. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that DNANet outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior detection rates with fewer false alarms, particularly in scenarios with cluttered backgrounds and dim targets. Our approach shows a 15% improvement in detection precision and 12% in recall compared to previous methods, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. The proposed framework provides a robust solution for IRSTD without requiring complex preprocessing or post-processing steps.

Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning for Medical Image Segmentation Based on Multi-Domain Data Aggregation

Medical image segmentation remains a challenging task due to limited annotated data and domain variations across imaging modalities and anatomical structures. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical self-supervised learning framework that leverages multi-domain data aggregation to address these challenges. Our approach employs a two-stage learning paradigm: first, a domain-agnostic feature extractor is pre-trained on diverse unlabeled medical images using contrastive learning with hierarchical feature representation, followed by a domain-specific fine-tuning stage that adapts to target segmentation tasks with minimal supervision. The framework introduces a multi-scale feature aggregation module that captures both local anatomical details and global contextual information across different imaging domains. Extensive experiments on four public datasets spanning various modalities (MRI, CT, ultrasound) and anatomical regions demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation approaches, achieving 4-7% improvement in Dice similarity coefficient while requiring 60% fewer labeled examples. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robust generalization to unseen domains and anatomical structures, making it particularly valuable for real-world clinical applications where annotated data is scarce. The proposed framework provides a promising direction for developing more data-efficient and generalizable medical image segmentation systems.

Reintroducing Straight-Through Estimators as Principled Methods for Stochastic Binary Networks

Binary neural networks offer significant computational and memory advantages, but training them remains challenging due to the non-differentiability of binary activations. This paper revisits Straight-Through Estimators (STEs), widely used but often considered heuristic approaches for training binary networks. We establish a rigorous theoretical framework that reinterprets STEs as principled gradient estimators for stochastic binary networks. By analyzing STEs through the lens of stochastic optimization, we demonstrate that they approximate the expected gradients of binary networks with stochastic neurons. Our theoretical results reveal that popular STE variants correspond to specific distributional assumptions on the binary sampling process. We provide convergence guarantees under mild conditions and introduce a family of theoretically-grounded STE methods that outperform existing approaches. Extensive experiments across image classification, reinforcement learning, and natural language processing tasks demonstrate that our principled STEs consistently improve performance while maintaining the efficiency benefits of binary networks. This work bridges the gap between heuristic practices and theoretical foundations, offering new insights for developing more effective training methods for binary neural networks.

Understanding and Visualizing Deep Visual Saliency Models

Deep neural networks have revolutionized visual saliency prediction, significantly outperforming traditional approaches in estimating where humans direct their attention in images. However, these powerful models often function as black boxes, limiting our understanding of their internal mechanisms. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for interpreting and visualizing deep visual saliency models to bridge this interpretability gap. We introduce a suite of visualization techniques that reveal how different network layers and components contribute to saliency predictions. Through extensive experiments across multiple state-of-the-art architectures, we demonstrate that early layers primarily capture low-level features such as contrast and edges, while deeper layers progressively integrate semantic information including objects and contextual relationships. Our analysis reveals unexpected attention patterns and failure cases that provide insights into model limitations. Additionally, we propose a novel attribution method that quantifies the contribution of specific image regions to final saliency maps. The resulting visualizations not only enhance our theoretical understanding of visual attention mechanisms in deep networks but also provide practical tools for model debugging, comparison, and refinement. This work takes an important step toward more transparent and interpretable deep visual saliency models that can better inform applications in computer vision, human-computer interaction, and cognitive science.

A Statistician Teaches Deep Learning

This paper presents a unique pedagogical approach to deep learning from a statistician's perspective. By bridging traditional statistical methods with modern neural network architectures, we offer insights into how fundamental statistical concepts underpin the theory and practice of deep learning. The work highlights how statistical thinking—including sampling theory, hypothesis testing, and model evaluation—provides a robust framework for understanding neural network behavior, optimization challenges, and generalization capabilities. Through a series of case studies from an advanced undergraduate course, we demonstrate how students with statistical backgrounds can leverage their existing knowledge to develop intuition about complex deep learning systems. Our approach emphasizes the complementary nature of statistical rigor and deep learning flexibility, revealing how concepts like regularization, cross-validation, and uncertainty quantification create natural connections between these fields. This statistical lens not only enhances technical understanding but also cultivates critical thinking about model limitations and appropriate applications, addressing a significant gap in current deep learning education.

Tree Decomposed Graph Neural Network

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, they often struggle with capturing long-range dependencies and higher-order structural information due to their local message-passing mechanisms. In this paper, we introduce the Tree Decomposed Graph Neural Network (TD-GNN), a novel architecture that leverages tree decomposition to enhance the representational power of GNNs. Our approach transforms the original graph into a tree decomposition, where each node represents a subgraph of the original structure, enabling the model to reason about higher-order graph properties. By operating on this hierarchical representation, TD-GNN can effectively capture both local and global graph structures while maintaining computational efficiency. We establish theoretical connections between our approach and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, demonstrating that TD-GNN achieves strictly greater expressive power than standard message-passing GNNs. Extensive experiments on node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks across diverse datasets show that TD-GNN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN architectures, especially on graphs with complex structural patterns. Our results suggest that tree decomposition provides a promising direction for developing more powerful graph neural networks capable of capturing sophisticated graph properties.

Beyond Pixels: A Comprehensive Survey from Bottom-up to Semantic Image Segmentation and Cosegmentation

This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the evolution and current state of image segmentation techniques, spanning from traditional bottom-up approaches to advanced semantic segmentation and cosegmentation methods. We systematically categorize and analyze the progression of segmentation algorithms over the past decades, examining the transition from low-level pixel clustering to high-level semantic understanding. The paper first explores foundational techniques including edge-based, region-based, and graph-based segmentation, before delving into modern deep learning architectures that have revolutionized semantic segmentation. We give special attention to cosegmentation—the simultaneous segmentation of common objects across multiple images—highlighting its unique challenges and applications. For each category, we discuss representative algorithms, evaluation metrics, benchmark datasets, and performance comparisons. Additionally, we identify current limitations and emerging research directions, including weakly supervised learning, efficient network design, and multi-modal integration. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the landscape of image segmentation techniques and their applications across computer vision domains including scene understanding, medical imaging, and computational photography.

RSS-Net: Weakly-Supervised Multi-Class Semantic Segmentation with FMCW Radar

This paper introduces RSS-Net, a novel deep learning framework for multi-class semantic segmentation using Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar data. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on extensive pixel-level annotations, our method employs a weakly-supervised learning paradigm that requires only image-level class labels, significantly reducing annotation costs while maintaining high segmentation performance. RSS-Net leverages the unique properties of FMCW radar, including its ability to operate in adverse weather conditions and provide rich spatial and velocity information. Our architecture incorporates a custom attention mechanism that effectively identifies class-discriminative regions from radar range-Doppler and range-azimuth representations, followed by a refinement module that produces precise segmentation masks. Experimental results on diverse automotive scenarios demonstrate that RSS-Net achieves competitive segmentation performance compared to fully-supervised methods, with mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) scores only 3.2% lower while using substantially less annotation effort. Furthermore, we show that our approach maintains robust performance in challenging environmental conditions where camera-based systems typically fail. The proposed method represents a significant advancement toward practical deployment of radar-based perception systems for autonomous driving and other safety-critical applications.

Advanced Multiple Linear Regression Based Dark Channel Prior Applied on Dehazing Image and Generating Synthetic Haze

This paper presents a novel approach to image dehazing and synthetic haze generation using an advanced multiple linear regression (MLR) technique integrated with the dark channel prior (DCP). While traditional DCP-based dehazing methods often suffer from color distortion and inaccurate transmission map estimation, our proposed framework leverages MLR to optimize the atmospheric light estimation and refine transmission maps. We establish a mathematical relationship between haze density, scene depth, and atmospheric conditions through regression analysis of diverse hazy image datasets. Our bidirectional approach not only enhances dehazing performance but also enables realistic synthetic haze generation—a valuable tool for training deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate superior quantitative performance with average PSNR improvements of 3.2dB and SSIM increases of 0.15 compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed algorithm shows particular robustness in challenging scenarios with non-uniform illumination and varying haze densities. Furthermore, our synthetic haze generation capabilities produce visually consistent results that closely mimic natural atmospheric scattering phenomena, as validated through comprehensive user studies and objective quality metrics.

Synthetic Image Rendering Solves Annotation Problem in Deep Learning Nanoparticle Segmentation

The segmentation of nanoparticles in microscopy images is critical for materials science and nanotechnology research, but suffers from a fundamental limitation: the scarcity of accurately annotated training data for deep learning models. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages synthetic image rendering to overcome this annotation bottleneck. We developed a physics-informed rendering pipeline that generates realistic transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of nanoparticles with perfect ground truth segmentation masks. Our method incorporates variable particle morphologies, imaging artifacts, noise profiles, and contrast variations to create diverse, realistic training datasets. When trained on these synthetic images, our deep learning segmentation models demonstrated remarkable generalization to real TEM images, achieving a 94% Dice coefficient on test data without any manual annotation. Ablation studies confirmed that the physical accuracy of our rendering approach was critical for successful domain transfer. This synthetic data approach not only eliminates the need for labor-intensive manual annotation but also enables the segmentation of challenging nanoparticle configurations that would be difficult to annotate manually. Our findings demonstrate that physics-based synthetic data generation represents a powerful paradigm for specialized computer vision tasks where annotation constraints have previously limited the application of deep learning techniques.

Move2Hear: Active Audio-Visual Source Separation

This paper introduces Move2Hear, a novel active perception framework for audio-visual source separation in complex acoustic environments. Unlike traditional passive approaches that rely on fixed sensor positions, Move2Hear leverages controlled agent motion to dynamically improve separation quality. We formulate the problem as a reinforcement learning task where an embodied agent learns to navigate toward optimal listening positions that maximize source separation performance. Our approach integrates visual scene understanding with binaural audio processing to create a multimodal representation that guides navigation decisions. Extensive experiments in simulated environments with varying acoustic conditions demonstrate that Move2Hear significantly outperforms state-of-the-art passive separation methods, achieving an average 4.2 dB improvement in Signal-to-Interference Ratio (SIR) and 3.7 dB gain in Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SDR). We further validate our approach on a real robotic platform, showing effective generalization to physical environments. This work establishes a foundation for embodied audio-visual intelligence that actively exploits motion to enhance auditory perception, with potential applications in assistive listening technologies, autonomous recording systems, and human-robot interaction.

A Generative Map for Image-based Camera Localization

This paper introduces a novel approach to image-based camera localization through the development of a generative map framework. Our method addresses fundamental challenges in visual localization by representing scenes as continuous generative models rather than discrete feature collections. The proposed generative map encodes both appearance and geometric information of the environment, enabling robust localization across varying conditions. We formulate camera pose estimation as a likelihood maximization problem within our generative framework, which allows for efficient and accurate localization without explicit feature matching or exhaustive pose-space search. Experiments conducted on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in challenging scenarios involving significant appearance changes, viewpoint variations, and partial scene occlusions. The generative nature of our map also facilitates novel applications, including synthetic view generation for localization refinement and uncertainty estimation in pose predictions. Our results suggest that generative scene modeling provides a promising direction for robust visual localization systems in real-world applications such as augmented reality, autonomous navigation, and robotics.

Conditionally Adaptive Multi-Task Learning: Improving Transfer Learning in NLP Using Fewer Parameters & Less Data

This paper introduces Conditionally Adaptive Multi-Task Learning (CAMTL), a novel approach that enhances transfer learning efficiency in Natural Language Processing tasks while significantly reducing computational and data requirements. Our framework dynamically adapts parameter sharing across tasks based on conditional relevance, allowing for selective knowledge transfer that preserves task-specific information while leveraging cross-task similarities. Through extensive experiments across diverse NLP benchmarks including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and question answering, we demonstrate that CAMTL achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art transfer learning methods while using up to 60% fewer parameters and requiring 40% less training data. Our approach shows particular strength in low-resource scenarios, where performance improvements of 7-12% over traditional fine-tuning methods are observed. We provide theoretical analysis explaining why conditional adaptation is more parameter-efficient than full model fine-tuning or fixed parameter sharing approaches. These findings suggest a promising direction for making advanced NLP models more accessible in resource-constrained environments while maintaining high performance standards.

Epitome for Automatic Image Colorization

This paper presents a novel approach to automatic image colorization using epitomes, a generative model that represents image patches in a condensed form. Our method leverages the spatial and structural information encoded in epitomes to predict plausible color distributions for grayscale images without manual intervention. We introduce a two-stage framework: first, constructing an epitome from a diverse training set of colored images that captures color-structure relationships; second, applying this epitome to infer appropriate chrominance values for grayscale input images while preserving their luminance information. Unlike previous colorization techniques that rely heavily on semantic segmentation or extensive user guidance, our epitome-based approach captures the inherent correlation between image structure and color, enabling more coherent and contextually appropriate colorization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces visually compelling colorizations across various image categories, outperforming several state-of-the-art approaches in both quantitative metrics and user preference studies. The proposed technique is particularly effective for natural scenes, historical photographs, and textured images where local structure provides strong cues for color assignment. This work contributes to the growing field of automatic image enhancement by offering an efficient, data-driven solution to the challenging problem of colorization.

Emergence of Compositional Language with Deep Generational Transmission

This paper investigates how compositional language structures emerge through multi-generational transmission in artificial communication systems. We introduce a novel deep generational transmission model where artificial agents develop communication protocols that are passed to subsequent generations through cultural learning. Our experiments demonstrate that while early generations develop partially effective but largely holistic communication systems, compositional structure emerges gradually over generations as language is transmitted through a chain of learners. We observe that pressures for both expressivity and learnability drive this compositional emergence, with languages evolving to systematically recombine discrete elements to convey complex meanings. Compositional languages prove more resistant to transmission errors and more adaptable to novel concepts than their holistic counterparts. Our findings reveal that deep generational dynamics play a crucial role in the emergence of linguistic structure, supporting theories that fundamental properties of human language may arise from cultural evolutionary processes rather than specialized biological adaptations alone. These results have implications for understanding language evolution and for developing more human-like communication systems in artificial intelligence.

Unique Metric for Health Analysis with Optimization of Clustering Activity and Cross Comparison of Results from Different Approach

This study introduces a novel metric for comprehensive health analysis that integrates multiple physiological parameters into a unified framework. We developed a composite health index that captures the multidimensional nature of wellness while addressing the limitations of conventional single-parameter assessments. Using a dataset of 14,753 participants across diverse demographic groups, we applied optimized clustering algorithms to identify distinct health profiles and their associated risk factors. Our methodology employed k-means, hierarchical, and density-based clustering techniques with parameter optimization through silhouette coefficient analysis. The resulting clusters demonstrated strong internal cohesion (average silhouette width: 0.72) and clinically meaningful separation. Cross-comparison of results from these different approaches revealed substantial agreement in identified health patterns (Rand index: 0.84), while highlighting unique insights from each method. The proposed metric demonstrated superior predictive power for adverse health outcomes compared to traditional risk scores (AUC: 0.89 vs. 0.76, p<0.001). This research provides a robust framework for personalized health assessment that can inform targeted interventions and enhance clinical decision-making. The methodology's versatility suggests applications across various healthcare domains, from preventive medicine to chronic disease management.

Pose-guided Visible Part Matching for Occluded Person ReID

Person re-identification (ReID) in occluded scenarios remains a significant challenge for visual surveillance systems. This paper introduces a novel Pose-guided Visible Part Matching (PVPM) framework to address the occlusion problem in person ReID. Our approach leverages human pose estimation to identify visible body parts and focuses the matching process on these unoccluded regions. The proposed framework consists of three key components: (1) a pose-guided visibility predictor that estimates the visibility of different body parts, (2) a part-aligned feature extractor that generates discriminative representations for visible regions, and (3) a visible part matching module that dynamically compares corresponding visible parts between probe and gallery images. Extensive experiments on three challenging occluded person ReID datasets (Occluded-DukeMTMC, Occluded-REID, and Partial-REID) demonstrate that our PVPM framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach achieves improvements of 7.8%, 8.5%, and 9.3% in Rank-1 accuracy on these datasets respectively, while maintaining competitive performance on holistic person ReID benchmarks. The results verify that explicitly modeling visible body parts through pose guidance effectively mitigates the negative impact of occlusions in person ReID.

Image Captioning with Context-Aware Auxiliary Guidance

This paper introduces a novel approach to image captioning that leverages context-aware auxiliary guidance to enhance the quality and relevance of generated descriptions. Our framework, Context-Aware Auxiliary Guidance (CAAG), integrates visual scene understanding with contextual information to produce more comprehensive and accurate image captions. Unlike traditional methods that rely solely on visual features, CAAG incorporates auxiliary information streams—including scene graphs, object relationships, and contextual cues—to guide the caption generation process. We propose a multi-head attention mechanism that dynamically weighs these auxiliary inputs based on their relevance to different aspects of the image. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets MS COCO and Flickr30k demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across standard evaluation metrics, with particularly notable improvements in semantic accuracy and descriptive richness. Human evaluations further confirm that captions generated by our model are more contextually appropriate and informative. Our work highlights the importance of contextual understanding in bridging the semantic gap between visual perception and natural language description, establishing a new direction for context-aware image captioning systems.

Deep Co-Attention Network for Multi-View Subspace Learning

This paper introduces a novel Deep Co-Attention Network (DCAN) for multi-view subspace learning, addressing the challenge of effectively integrating complementary information from multiple data views. Unlike traditional multi-view learning approaches that rely on shallow architectures or simple fusion strategies, our proposed DCAN leverages deep neural networks with a co-attention mechanism to capture complex cross-view relationships. The framework consists of view-specific encoders that extract high-level features from each input view, followed by a co-attention module that dynamically weights feature importance based on cross-view interactions. This allows the model to focus on the most discriminative and complementary information across views when learning a unified subspace representation. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets for clustering, classification, and retrieval tasks demonstrate that DCAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-view learning methods. Notably, our approach shows remarkable robustness to view-specific noise and missing data scenarios. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the co-attention mechanism in capturing meaningful cross-view correlations. The proposed DCAN provides a principled approach to multi-view representation learning that effectively preserves both view-specific characteristics and cross-view semantic relationships.

Clickstream Analysis for Crowd-Based Object Segmentation with Confidence

This paper introduces a novel approach to crowd-based image segmentation that leverages clickstream analysis to improve segmentation accuracy while providing confidence metrics for the resulting annotations. We present a framework that captures and analyzes the temporal sequence of clicks, hesitations, corrections, and interaction patterns from multiple annotators working on object segmentation tasks. By modeling these behavioral signals, our system not only generates high-quality segmentation masks but also estimates confidence maps that highlight regions of uncertainty. Experiments conducted on diverse image datasets demonstrate that our clickstream-based approach achieves 17% higher boundary precision compared to traditional crowd-based segmentation methods, while reducing annotation time by 23%. Furthermore, our confidence metrics show strong correlation (r=0.82) with actual segmentation accuracy, enabling quality control and targeted refinement of ambiguous regions. The proposed method bridges the gap between fully automated and human-in-the-loop segmentation approaches, offering a scalable solution for generating reliable training data for computer vision systems while providing valuable uncertainty quantification.

Distributed and Consistent Multi-Image Feature Matching via QuickMatch

Feature matching across multiple images is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in structure from motion, simultaneous localization and mapping, and image retrieval. Traditional approaches typically match features between pairs of images independently, leading to inconsistencies when considering the entire image collection. In this paper, we present QuickMatch, a novel distributed algorithm for consistent multi-image feature matching. Our approach formulates the matching problem within a density-based clustering framework, ensuring global consistency of correspondences across the entire dataset. QuickMatch scales efficiently with the number of images and features through a distributed implementation that minimizes communication overhead while maintaining matching accuracy. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior matching precision and recall compared to state-of-the-art techniques, while significantly reducing computational time for large image collections. Furthermore, QuickMatch effectively handles challenging scenarios with viewpoint changes, repetitive structures, and illumination variations. The algorithm's ability to produce globally consistent matches improves downstream applications such as 3D reconstruction and visual localization, as validated by our comprehensive evaluation.

Binding via Reconstruction Clustering

This paper introduces Binding via Reconstruction Clustering (BRC), a novel approach to the binding problem in neural networks. We propose a framework that dynamically binds distributed representations through an unsupervised clustering mechanism based on reconstruction error. Unlike traditional binding methods that rely on predefined association rules or specialized architectures, BRC learns to identify and group related features across different modalities or processing streams. Our method operates by projecting representations into a shared latent space where semantically similar elements naturally cluster together, enabling the system to bind related components without explicit supervision. Through extensive experiments on visual-semantic binding tasks, compositional reasoning problems, and cross-modal retrieval benchmarks, we demonstrate that BRC outperforms existing binding approaches while maintaining computational efficiency. The results suggest that reconstruction-based clustering provides a neurally plausible mechanism for solving the binding problem in both artificial neural networks and as a potential model for understanding binding in biological systems. Furthermore, we show that BRC exhibits emergent properties that support generalization to novel combinations of familiar elements, addressing a key challenge in compositional representation learning.

Feature Importance in Gradient Boosting Trees with Cross-Validation Feature Selection

This study investigates the integration of cross-validation feature selection with gradient boosting tree models to enhance feature importance assessment. While gradient boosting algorithms are widely recognized for their predictive power, their native feature importance metrics can be biased and unstable across different data samples. We propose a methodological framework that combines k-fold cross-validation with iterative feature selection to produce more robust importance rankings. Our approach systematically evaluates feature subsets across multiple cross-validation folds, measuring both the stability of feature rankings and the impact on model performance. Experiments conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate that this integrated approach significantly reduces variance in feature importance scores compared to traditional methods. Additionally, we observe improved model generalization and interpretability, particularly in high-dimensional settings with correlated features. The proposed methodology provides practitioners with a more reliable mechanism for feature selection in gradient boosting models, addressing a critical gap between model performance and explainability. Our findings contribute to the broader effort of developing trustworthy machine learning techniques that balance predictive accuracy with interpretable insights.

Semantic and Geometric Modeling with Neural Message Passing in 3D Scene Graphs for Hierarchical Mechanical Search

This paper presents a novel framework for hierarchical mechanical search in complex 3D environments using neural message passing over scene graphs that encode both semantic and geometric information. We introduce a structured representation that models physical environments as hierarchical 3D scene graphs, where nodes represent objects with their geometric and semantic attributes, and edges capture spatial, functional, and mechanical relationships. Our approach leverages graph neural networks to perform message passing across this representation, enabling reasoning about both explicit object properties and implicit mechanical affordances. The framework implements a hierarchical search strategy that progressively narrows down regions of interest by reasoning about mechanical systems at multiple levels of abstraction. Through extensive experiments in simulated household and industrial environments, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in tasks requiring complex mechanical reasoning, such as identifying hidden mechanisms, predicting functional outcomes of interactions, and efficiently localizing operational components. Results show a 37% improvement in search efficiency and a 29% increase in success rate compared to baselines that do not integrate semantic and geometric reasoning. Our work contributes to the development of embodied AI systems that can understand and interact with complex mechanical environments in a human-like manner.

Graph Pattern Mining and Learning through User-defined Relations (Extended Version)

This paper presents a novel framework for graph pattern mining and learning that leverages user-defined relations to enhance both the interpretability and effectiveness of graph analysis. Traditional graph mining approaches often rely on predefined structural patterns or purely data-driven methods, limiting their applicability in domains where domain expertise is crucial. Our approach allows users to explicitly define semantic relations of interest within graphs, which then guide the pattern discovery and learning processes. We formalize a flexible specification language for these user-defined relations and develop efficient algorithms that incorporate these specifications into pattern mining workflows. Experimental evaluation across diverse domains—including social networks, molecular structures, and knowledge graphs—demonstrates that our approach significantly improves pattern relevance, reduces computational overhead, and enhances model performance in downstream machine learning tasks. The extended version of this work provides comprehensive theoretical analysis of the framework's expressiveness, detailed case studies, and additional optimization techniques that further improve scalability. Our results indicate that incorporating domain knowledge through user-defined relations bridges the gap between purely structural graph analysis and semantic interpretation, enabling more meaningful and actionable insights from complex graph data.

Zoom-In-to-Check: Boosting Video Interpolation via Instance-level Discrimination

Video frame interpolation (VFI) aims to synthesize intermediate frames between existing frames, enhancing temporal resolution and visual smoothness. Despite significant progress in recent years, existing methods still struggle with complex motion patterns and fine-grained details, particularly in regions with intricate textures or object boundaries. In this paper, we propose "Zoom-In-to-Check" (ZIC), a novel instance-level discrimination approach that substantially improves VFI performance by focusing on challenging regions that require special attention. Our method dynamically identifies problematic areas in interpolated frames and applies a targeted refinement process that "zooms in" on these regions for detailed correction. The core of our approach is a discriminative network that learns to distinguish between genuine and synthesized content at an instance level, providing localized guidance for the interpolation network. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Vimeo-90K, UCF101, and DAVIS, we demonstrate that our ZIC framework achieves state-of-the-art performance with improvements of up to 0.72dB PSNR over previous methods. Ablation studies confirm that our instance-level discrimination strategy significantly outperforms both global and random patch-based approaches. The proposed method not only enhances overall interpolation quality but also preserves temporal consistency and fine details in challenging scenarios such as occlusions and rapid movements.

Fast Automatic Feature Selection for Multi-Period Sliding Window Aggregate in Time Series

Time series analysis often requires the extraction of informative features through sliding window aggregates, but selecting optimal window parameters remains challenging, particularly when data exhibits multiple underlying periodicities. This paper introduces a novel framework for fast automatic feature selection of multi-period sliding window aggregates in time series data. Our approach leverages spectral analysis to identify dominant frequencies in the data, which guide the automatic selection of relevant window sizes and aggregation functions. We propose an efficient algorithm that reduces the computational complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) compared to exhaustive search methods, while maintaining high feature quality. Experiments on diverse datasets including financial markets, IoT sensor networks, and physiological signals demonstrate that our method not only accelerates feature generation by an average of 87% but also improves downstream model performance by 12-18% compared to fixed-window approaches. The framework adapts to evolving time series characteristics, making it particularly valuable for real-time applications where periodic patterns may shift over time. Our contribution enables practitioners to automatically extract meaningful temporal features without manual parameter tuning, significantly streamlining the time series modeling pipeline.

Self-supervised Auxiliary Learning with Meta-paths for Heterogeneous Graphs

Heterogeneous graphs, which contain multiple types of nodes and edges, have become increasingly important in modeling complex real-world systems across various domains. However, learning effective representations for heterogeneous graphs remains challenging due to their structural complexity and the frequent scarcity of labeled data. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called Meta-path Auxiliary Self-supervised Learning (MASL) that leverages the semantic relationships inherent in heterogeneous graphs through meta-paths to enhance representation learning. Our approach integrates self-supervised auxiliary tasks that capture both local and global structural information guided by meta-path semantics. Specifically, we design three complementary auxiliary tasks: meta-path context prediction, meta-path instance discrimination, and meta-path schema alignment, which collectively preserve the rich semantic relationships in heterogeneous graphs. The framework employs a meta-learning strategy to dynamically adjust the contribution of each auxiliary task to the primary learning objective. Extensive experiments on six real-world heterogeneous graph datasets demonstrate that MASL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on node classification and link prediction tasks, with particularly substantial improvements in low-label regimes. Our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component and reveal that the combination of meta-path-guided auxiliary tasks provides complementary information that enhances the learned representations. The proposed approach offers a promising direction for leveraging self-supervision in heterogeneous graph learning without requiring additional labeled data.

Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Neural Networks

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations on graph-structured data. However, traditional GCNs operate in Euclidean space, which can be suboptimal for capturing the hierarchical and complex relationships inherent in many real-world graphs. In this paper, we introduce Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (HGCNs), a novel architecture that leverages the properties of hyperbolic geometry to better represent hierarchical structures. By embedding graph data in hyperbolic space, our model can capture exponentially more information with the same dimensionality compared to Euclidean GCNs. We reformulate the standard graph convolution operations using gyrovector space mathematics to ensure operations remain within the hyperbolic manifold. Experimental results on benchmark datasets including citation networks, protein interaction graphs, and social networks demonstrate that HGCNs significantly outperform their Euclidean counterparts, particularly on graphs with tree-like structures and power-law degree distributions. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks while requiring fewer parameters. These results highlight the effectiveness of hyperbolic geometry for graph representation learning and open new directions for geometric deep learning approaches.

A Complex KBQA System using Multiple Reasoning Paths

This paper presents a novel Knowledge Base Question Answering (KBQA) system designed to handle complex queries requiring multi-hop reasoning across knowledge graphs. Unlike traditional KBQA approaches that rely on single reasoning paths, our system dynamically explores and integrates multiple reasoning trajectories to address questions with inherent ambiguity or those requiring diverse evidence paths. We introduce a hierarchical reasoning framework that combines neural semantic parsing with graph-based traversal techniques to decompose complex questions into manageable sub-queries. The system employs a path ranking mechanism that evaluates and merges evidence from different reasoning chains based on relevance, consistency, and information gain. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets including WebQuestions, ComplexWebQuestions, and MetaQA demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with a 7.2% increase in F1 score on complex multi-hop questions. Ablation studies confirm that the integration of multiple reasoning paths substantially enhances performance on questions requiring diverse forms of knowledge composition. Our approach offers a more robust solution to complex KBQA tasks while providing interpretable reasoning chains that explain the system's answer derivation process.

Explainable cardiac pathology classification on cine MRI with motion characterization by semi-supervised learning of apparent flow

Cardiac cine Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides valuable insights into cardiac function, yet automated classification of pathologies while maintaining clinical interpretability remains challenging. This study presents a novel semi-supervised learning framework for cardiac pathology classification that leverages motion characterization through apparent flow estimation. Our approach extracts meaningful motion features from cine MRI sequences without requiring explicit motion annotations during training. We employ a two-stage architecture where a self-supervised apparent flow estimation network captures cardiac motion dynamics, followed by a classification network that utilizes these motion representations to identify pathologies. The framework was evaluated on a diverse multi-center dataset of 1,200 cardiac cine MRI studies spanning five common pathologies (dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, abnormal right ventricle, and healthy controls). Our method achieved 89.3% classification accuracy, outperforming conventional deep learning approaches by 7.2%. Importantly, the derived apparent flow maps provide clinically interpretable visualizations of cardiac motion abnormalities, highlighting regions of dyskinesia, hypokinesia, and other motion patterns associated with specific pathologies. The semi-supervised nature of our approach enables effective learning from limited labeled data, requiring only 60% of the labeled examples to achieve comparable performance to fully-supervised baselines. This work demonstrates the potential of motion characterization through apparent flow as an explainable approach for cardiac pathology classification that aligns with clinical diagnostic reasoning.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Deep Learning Models for Face Recognition Against Image Degradations

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of deep learning models for face recognition with a specific focus on their resilience against various image degradations. While deep convolutional neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance in ideal conditions, their reliability in real-world scenarios with degraded images remains challenging. We systematically evaluate several state-of-the-art face recognition architectures against common degradations including blur, noise, compression artifacts, illumination variations, and occlusions. Our experiments reveal that modern architectures exhibit impressive robustness to moderate degradations, particularly those employing attention mechanisms and specialized data augmentation techniques. However, significant performance deterioration occurs under severe degradations, with recognition accuracy dropping by up to 45% in extreme cases. Notably, different model architectures demonstrate varying sensitivity patterns to specific degradation types, with transformer-based models showing superior resilience to occlusions while CNN-based models better handle noise and blur. We also identify that models trained on diverse datasets demonstrate improved generalization across degradation types. These findings highlight the importance of degradation-aware training strategies and architecture selection for robust face recognition systems in practical applications. Our work provides valuable insights for developing more resilient face recognition systems for security, surveillance, and mobile applications where image quality cannot be guaranteed.

Scaling All-Goals Updates in Reinforcement Learning Using Convolutional Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to scaling all-goals updates in reinforcement learning using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning algorithms typically suffer from inefficient learning when the goal space is large or continuous, as they struggle to generalize across different goals. We introduce a CNN-based architecture that effectively parameterizes value functions and policies over continuous goal spaces by exploiting the spatial structure inherent in many goal-directed tasks. Our method enables efficient all-goals updates, where a single experience can be used to update the value estimates for multiple goals simultaneously. We demonstrate that by leveraging the translational equivariance properties of CNNs, our approach significantly reduces sample complexity compared to traditional methods that use separate updates for each goal or standard multi-layer perceptrons. Extensive experiments across various continuous control and navigation tasks show that our method achieves faster convergence, better generalization to unseen goals, and improved sample efficiency. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into why CNNs are particularly well-suited for all-goals updates in reinforcement learning. Our approach scales effectively to high-dimensional goal spaces while maintaining computational efficiency, making it applicable to real-world robotic tasks with continuous goal specifications.

Fingerprint Spoof Detection: Temporal Analysis of Image Sequence

This paper presents a novel approach to fingerprint spoof detection by leveraging temporal information from image sequences captured during the fingerprint acquisition process. While traditional anti-spoofing methods rely primarily on static single-image analysis, our work explores how the subtle temporal dynamics of genuine fingerprints differ from spoofed presentations. We collected a comprehensive dataset of 5,200 authentic and fake fingerprint image sequences, with spoofs created using diverse materials including silicone, gelatin, and play-doh. Our proposed deep learning architecture combines convolutional neural networks with recurrent modules to extract both spatial and temporal features from the image sequences. Experimental results demonstrate that our temporal analysis approach achieves a 97.3% detection accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art single-image methods by 8.7%. Furthermore, we identify distinctive temporal patterns in liveness indicators such as perspiration, elastic deformation, and blood flow that provide robust discriminative features across different spoof materials. The proposed method shows particular strength in detecting sophisticated presentation attacks that successfully mimic static characteristics of genuine fingerprints but fail to replicate their dynamic properties during the acquisition process.

Abstract: Aff-Wild Database and AffWildNet

This paper presents the Aff-Wild database, a novel large-scale dataset of facial expressions captured "in-the-wild," and introduces AffWildNet, a deep neural network architecture designed for continuous affect recognition. The Aff-Wild database contains 298 videos with approximately 1.2 million frames annotated along the valence-arousal dimensional model of affect. To our knowledge, this represents the largest and most diverse publicly available dataset of spontaneous facial expressions recorded in unconstrained conditions. We describe the data collection methodology, annotation process using crowd-sourcing techniques, and statistical properties of the resulting dataset. Building upon this resource, we develop AffWildNet, a deep learning framework combining convolutional and recurrent neural networks specifically optimized for continuous emotion recognition in challenging real-world scenarios. Our experimental results demonstrate that AffWildNet significantly outperforms existing approaches on the Aff-Wild benchmark, achieving concordance correlation coefficients of 0.57 for valence and 0.43 for arousal. Furthermore, we show that models pre-trained on Aff-Wild exhibit superior generalization capabilities when fine-tuned on other affect recognition datasets. The Aff-Wild database and AffWildNet provide valuable resources for advancing affective computing research in naturalistic settings.

Nonparametric Variable Screening with Optimal Decision Stumps

This paper introduces a novel nonparametric approach to variable screening in high-dimensional settings using optimal decision stumps. While traditional variable selection methods often rely on parametric assumptions or complex model specifications, our proposed framework leverages the simplicity and interpretability of decision stumps—single-split decision trees—to identify relevant predictors. We develop a theoretical foundation for optimal decision stump selection that maximizes an information-theoretic criterion, establishing consistency properties under mild conditions. Our method efficiently handles nonlinear relationships and interaction effects without requiring explicit model specification. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing screening techniques across various data-generating processes, particularly in scenarios with complex nonlinear dependencies. When applied to real-world datasets from genomics and finance, our method successfully identifies important variables while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed framework provides a valuable addition to the high-dimensional statistical toolbox, offering robust variable screening capabilities that adapt to underlying data structures without imposing restrictive assumptions.

AttWalk: Attentive Cross-Walks for Deep Mesh Analysis

We present AttWalk, a novel attentive cross-walk mechanism for deep mesh analysis that effectively captures both local and non-local geometric relationships in 3D meshes. Traditional mesh analysis approaches often struggle to model long-range dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency. Our method introduces a hierarchical attention-guided walk strategy that dynamically traverses mesh structures by learning optimal paths between vertices based on geometric and topological features. AttWalk employs a dual-stream architecture that simultaneously processes spatial and spectral representations, enabling it to capture intricate shape characteristics across multiple scales. Through extensive experiments on shape classification, segmentation, and correspondence tasks across standard benchmarks including SHREC, COSEG, and FAUST datasets, we demonstrate that AttWalk consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3-5% while requiring 20% less computational resources. Our approach is particularly effective for meshes with complex topological structures and varying resolutions, making it suitable for real-world applications in computer graphics, vision, and medical imaging. The code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this direction.

Convex Formulation of Overparameterized Deep Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel convex reformulation of overparameterized deep neural networks (DNNs), addressing a fundamental challenge in deep learning optimization. While DNNs have achieved remarkable success across various domains, their non-convex loss landscapes have remained a theoretical obstacle, complicating convergence guarantees and optimization analysis. We demonstrate that in the overparameterized regime, where network width exceeds certain thresholds, the optimization problem can be transformed into an equivalent convex formulation. Our approach leverages techniques from functional analysis and convex geometry to construct a reparameterization that preserves the network's expressivity while enabling access to powerful convex optimization tools. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that global minima of standard DNNs correspond one-to-one with solutions in our convex framework. Empirical evaluations across multiple architectures confirm that our convex formulation achieves comparable performance to traditional training methods while offering improved convergence properties and robustness to initialization. This work bridges the gap between deep learning practice and convex optimization theory, potentially enabling more principled approaches to neural network design, analysis, and training.

Abstract: Weakly- and Semi-Supervised Panoptic Segmentation

Panoptic segmentation, which unifies semantic and instance segmentation tasks, has recently emerged as a comprehensive scene understanding challenge. While fully-supervised approaches have shown impressive results, they require dense pixel-level annotations that are prohibitively expensive and time-consuming to obtain. In this work, we propose a novel framework for weakly- and semi-supervised panoptic segmentation that significantly reduces the annotation burden. Our approach leverages a combination of sparse annotations (box-level and image-level labels) alongside a limited set of fully-annotated images to effectively train panoptic segmentation models. We introduce a multi-stage training pipeline with specialized consistency regularization techniques that enable knowledge transfer between different levels of supervision. Through extensive experiments on COCO and Cityscapes datasets, we demonstrate that our method achieves up to 85% of the performance of fully-supervised approaches while using only 20% of the pixel-level annotations. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the trade-offs between annotation effort and model performance across different supervision settings. Our findings suggest that strategically combining weak and sparse supervision signals offers a promising direction for scaling up panoptic segmentation to real-world applications where annotation resources are limited.

Fast Underwater Image Enhancement for Improved Visual Perception

Underwater imagery suffers from unique degradation factors including wavelength-dependent light absorption, scattering, and color distortion that significantly impair visual perception for both human operators and computer vision systems.
