This paper presents a novel, computationally efficient approach to underwater image enhancement that addresses these challenges while maintaining real-time performance. Our method employs a physics-inspired multi-scale fusion framework that simultaneously corrects color cast, enhances contrast, and reduces haze-like effects without introducing artificial artifacts. Extensive experiments conducted on diverse underwater datasets demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both quantitative metrics and processing speed, achieving enhancement rates of over 30 frames per second on standard hardware. The enhanced images show significant improvements in feature visibility, color fidelity, and overall visual quality, directly benefiting applications such as marine robotics, ecological monitoring, and underwater infrastructure inspection. User studies further confirm that our enhanced imagery leads to improved object detection accuracy and reduced visual fatigue during extended viewing sessions. The proposed method's combination of visual quality and computational efficiency makes it particularly suitable for deployment in resource-constrained underwater vehicles and real-time monitoring systems.

A Comparison of Deep Learning Object Detection Models for Satellite Imagery

This study presents a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art deep learning object detection models applied to satellite imagery analysis. We evaluated multiple architectures including Faster R-CNN, YOLO, RetinaNet, SSD, and EfficientDet across diverse satellite datasets featuring varying spatial resolutions, spectral bands, and object categories. Performance was assessed using precision, recall, mean average precision (mAP), and inference speed metrics. Our experiments revealed that two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN achieved higher accuracy for small object detection, while single-stage models such as YOLOv5 offered superior computational efficiency with competitive accuracy for larger objects. We also investigated the impact of transfer learning, data augmentation techniques, and multi-spectral information integration on model performance. Results demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning and appropriate augmentation strategies significantly improve detection accuracy in satellite imagery. Additionally, we identified key challenges including small object detection, handling varying illumination conditions, and class imbalance. This comparative analysis provides valuable insights for selecting and optimizing deep learning models for remote sensing applications such as urban planning, environmental monitoring, and disaster response.

STOPPAGE: Spatio-temporal Data Driven Cloud-Fog-Edge Computing Framework for Pandemic Monitoring and Management

This paper introduces STOPPAGE, a novel hierarchical computing framework that leverages cloud, fog, and edge computing paradigms to address the critical challenges of pandemic monitoring and management. The framework utilizes spatio-temporal data analysis to process multi-source pandemic-related information across different geographical regions and time periods. STOPPAGE implements a three-tier architecture where edge devices collect real-time health metrics and mobility data, fog nodes perform intermediate processing and regional analytics, and cloud infrastructure handles complex modeling, storage, and global coordination. Through intelligent workload distribution and adaptive resource allocation, the framework minimizes latency for time-sensitive applications while optimizing bandwidth utilization and computational efficiency. Our implementation demonstrates significant improvements in early outbreak detection, contact tracing, resource allocation, and public health decision support compared to traditional centralized approaches. Experimental evaluation across multiple simulated pandemic scenarios shows that STOPPAGE reduces response time by 68%, increases prediction accuracy by 23%, and enhances system scalability while maintaining data privacy compliance. The framework provides a comprehensive technological solution that can be rapidly deployed and adapted for various public health emergencies beyond the current pandemic context.

CTAB-GAN: Effective Table Data Synthesizing

Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution to data privacy concerns and limited data availability in machine learning applications. In this paper, we introduce CTAB-GAN (Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network), a novel approach for synthesizing high-quality tabular data. Our method addresses key challenges in tabular data generation including handling mixed data types, capturing complex column dependencies, and preserving statistical properties of the original data. CTAB-GAN employs a conditional GAN architecture with specialized encoding mechanisms for categorical and numerical features, along with a novel training procedure that incorporates classification and regression loss components. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that CTAB-GAN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of statistical similarity, machine learning efficacy, and privacy preservation. Synthetic data generated by our approach enables downstream models to achieve performance comparable to those trained on real data, while maintaining differential privacy guarantees. CTAB-GAN provides a robust framework for organizations to share and utilize sensitive tabular data without compromising individual privacy, with potential applications in healthcare, finance, and other domains where data privacy is paramount.

Attacking Optical Flow

Optical flow estimation is a fundamental component in modern computer vision systems, with applications ranging from autonomous driving to video analysis. Despite its widespread use, the robustness of optical flow algorithms against adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we systematically investigate the vulnerability of state-of-the-art optical flow networks to adversarial perturbations. We propose a novel attack framework that generates imperceptible perturbations to input image pairs, causing significant errors in the estimated flow fields while maintaining visual similarity to the original inputs. Our experiments across multiple architectures (including PWC-Net, RAFT, and FlowNet2) demonstrate that even small, carefully crafted perturbations can induce flow errors exceeding 50% on standard benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that these attacks transfer across different models, presenting a real-world security concern. We analyze the patterns of vulnerability and propose potential defense mechanisms through adversarial training and input preprocessing. Our findings highlight critical security implications for systems relying on optical flow and suggest directions for developing more robust algorithms for this essential vision task.

Beyond Trees: Classification with Sparse Pairwise Dependencies

Traditional classification models often rely on tree-based structures or assume feature independence, limiting their ability to capture complex relationships between features. This paper introduces a novel classification framework that extends beyond tree structures by incorporating sparse pairwise dependencies between features. Our approach maintains computational efficiency while modeling important feature interactions that tree-based methods may miss. We formalize the sparse pairwise dependency structure as a constrained graphical model and develop an efficient inference algorithm with favorable scaling properties. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms standard tree-based classifiers and competitive baseline methods, particularly in domains where feature interactions are critical. The proposed approach shows significant improvements in classification accuracy (3-7% on benchmark datasets) while maintaining interpretability through the explicit representation of feature dependencies. We also provide theoretical guarantees on the model's expressiveness and generalization capabilities. This work bridges the gap between simple tree models and fully connected graphical structures, offering a practical compromise between model complexity and predictive power.

Multimodal Deep Learning for Mental Disorders Prediction from Audio Speech Samples

This study presents a novel multimodal deep learning framework for predicting mental disorders through the analysis of audio speech samples. Mental health disorders affect millions globally, yet diagnostic challenges persist due to subjective assessment methods and limited biomarkers. Our approach leverages both acoustic features (prosody, rhythm, spectral characteristics) and linguistic content from speech samples to identify subtle patterns associated with various mental health conditions. We developed a hybrid neural architecture combining convolutional neural networks for processing spectrograms with transformer-based models for linguistic analysis, enabling comprehensive feature extraction across modalities. The framework was evaluated on a diverse dataset of 5,000 speech samples from individuals with clinically confirmed diagnoses of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and healthy controls. Results demonstrate superior performance compared to unimodal approaches, achieving 87.3% accuracy in disorder classification with particularly strong performance in depression detection (91.2% sensitivity). Notably, our system identified several previously undocumented speech biomarkers through attention mechanism analysis. This research contributes to the development of objective, accessible screening tools for mental health assessment, potentially enabling earlier intervention and improved patient outcomes in clinical settings.

Kernel Cuts: MRF meets Kernel & Spectral Clustering

This paper introduces Kernel Cuts, a novel framework that unifies Markov Random Field (MRF) optimization and kernel-based spectral clustering. While these methodologies have traditionally been developed separately in computer vision and machine learning, we demonstrate their complementary strengths and propose a principled integration. Our approach leverages kernel representations to capture complex data distributions and non-linear structures, while incorporating the discrete optimization advantages of MRF techniques. We formulate a joint energy function that combines pairwise kernel affinities with standard MRF regional and boundary constraints. Through theoretical analysis, we establish connections between normalized cut criteria in spectral clustering and our kernel-induced MRF potentials. Experimental results on image segmentation, object extraction, and multi-label clustering demonstrate that Kernel Cuts outperforms both standard graph cut methods and spectral clustering approaches when used independently. The framework is particularly effective for heterogeneous data where linear separation is insufficient, and offers improved robustness to initialization compared to traditional MRF optimization. Our work bridges an important gap between discrete and continuous optimization paradigms, opening new directions for combining discriminative kernel learning with MRF-based structured prediction.

Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation

This paper introduces a novel approach to model compression that preserves privacy while maintaining performance through knowledge distillation. As deep learning models grow increasingly complex, the need for efficient deployment on resource-constrained devices becomes critical, yet traditional compression methods often expose sensitive information embedded in model parameters. We propose a privacy-preserving knowledge distillation framework that enables the transfer of knowledge from large teacher models to compact student models while providing formal privacy guarantees. Our method incorporates differential privacy mechanisms during the distillation process, carefully calibrating the noise addition to balance the privacy-utility trade-off. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model architectures demonstrate that our approach achieves compression ratios of up to 10× with minimal accuracy degradation (less than 2% drop) while satisfying ε-differential privacy. We provide theoretical analysis of the privacy bounds and empirically validate our framework's resilience against model inversion and membership inference attacks. This work addresses the growing concern of privacy leakage in deployed AI systems and offers a practical solution for organizations seeking to share or deploy compressed models without compromising sensitive training data.

Metric learning by Similarity Network for Deep Semi-Supervised Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to deep semi-supervised learning through metric learning using a Similarity Network architecture. Semi-supervised learning remains challenging due to the limited availability of labeled data in many real-world applications. Our method addresses this challenge by learning an effective similarity metric that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. The proposed Similarity Network learns embeddings where semantically similar samples are mapped close together while dissimilar ones are pushed apart, regardless of their labeled status. We formulate a joint optimization framework that combines supervised classification loss on labeled data with a consistency regularization term based on similarity relationships in the embedding space. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, particularly when labeled data is extremely scarce. The Similarity Network shows robust performance across various label ratios and network architectures, with an average improvement of 3.7% in classification accuracy compared to previous methods. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into why learning the similarity metric enhances generalization in the semi-supervised setting. Our approach offers a promising direction for effectively utilizing unlabeled data in deep learning systems.

On the Power of Multitask Representation Learning in Linear MDP

This paper investigates the theoretical benefits of multitask representation learning in the context of linear Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). We analyze how shared representations across multiple related tasks can significantly improve sample efficiency and generalization performance compared to single-task learning approaches. By formalizing the notion of task relatedness through a common linear structure in the state-action value functions, we establish finite-sample guarantees that quantify the reduction in sample complexity as a function of the number of tasks and the underlying representation dimension. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that when the number of tasks exceeds the dimension of the shared representation, the per-task sample complexity can decrease linearly with the number of tasks, leading to substantial efficiency gains. We complement our theoretical results with algorithmic innovations that effectively learn these shared representations across tasks and empirical evaluations on both synthetic and benchmark environments. Our findings highlight the fundamental advantages of multitask representation learning in reinforcement learning and provide insights into when and why such approaches outperform single-task learning in linear MDPs.

GazeGAN: Unpaired Adversarial Image Generation for Gaze Estimation

Accurate gaze estimation is crucial for applications spanning human-computer interaction, augmented reality, and driver monitoring systems. However, training robust gaze estimation models requires large, diverse datasets that are expensive and time-consuming to collect and annotate. In this paper, we present GazeGAN, a novel unpaired adversarial framework for generating synthetic eye images with precise gaze directions. Unlike previous approaches that require paired images, our method leverages unpaired data through a cycle-consistent generative adversarial network architecture, enabling the transformation between different gaze directions while preserving subject-specific eye appearance characteristics. GazeGAN incorporates a specialized attention mechanism that focuses on critical eye regions and a gaze-direction consistency loss that ensures accurate angular representation in the synthesized images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that models trained on our synthetic data achieve comparable performance to those trained on real data, with only a 0.4° angular error difference on the MPIIGaze dataset. When used for data augmentation, GazeGAN improves estimation accuracy by 15.7% on challenging cross-dataset scenarios. Our approach significantly reduces the annotation burden while enhancing the generalization capabilities of gaze estimation systems across different environments, head poses, and lighting conditions.

Human Action Recognition in Drone Videos using a Few Aerial Training Examples

This paper addresses the challenging problem of human action recognition in aerial footage captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), where limited training data presents a significant obstacle. We propose a novel few-shot learning framework specifically designed for aerial view action recognition that effectively leverages knowledge from ground-view datasets while adapting to the unique characteristics of drone footage. Our approach employs a dual-stream architecture that combines spatial and temporal information with a cross-view knowledge transfer module to bridge the domain gap between ground and aerial perspectives. Experiments conducted on multiple drone video datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance while requiring only 5-10 labeled examples per action class, representing a 75% reduction in annotation requirements compared to previous approaches. The framework shows particular robustness to challenges inherent in drone footage, including varying altitudes, camera movements, and small subject sizes. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark dataset of annotated aerial human actions to facilitate future research. Our work enables more practical deployment of action recognition systems in drone-based applications such as search and rescue, surveillance, and automated cinematography.

Stabilizing Training of Generative Adversarial Nets via Langevin Stein Variational Gradient Descent

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating realistic data across various domains, yet their training process is often hampered by instability issues such as mode collapse and non-convergence. In this paper, we introduce a novel training framework that leverages Langevin Stein Variational Gradient Descent (LSVGD) to stabilize GAN training dynamics. Our approach combines the particle-based nature of Stein variational methods with Langevin dynamics to create a more robust optimization procedure for the generator-discriminator adversarial game. By reformulating the generator update as a Wasserstein gradient flow in the space of probability measures, we establish theoretical guarantees for convergence under mild assumptions. Empirical evaluations on benchmark image datasets demonstrate that our LSVGD-GAN framework significantly mitigates mode collapse, reduces training oscillations, and improves sample quality compared to traditional GAN training methods. Furthermore, our approach requires minimal additional computational overhead while providing substantial stability benefits, making it a practical enhancement for various GAN architectures. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical properties of our method and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments.

Multimodal Categorization of Crisis Events in Social Media

The proliferation of social media during crisis events has created vast repositories of multimodal data—including text, images, videos, and metadata—that contain critical information for emergency responders and humanitarian organizations. This paper presents a novel framework for the multimodal categorization of crisis events on social media platforms. We develop an integrated approach that leverages both textual content and visual information to classify crisis-related posts across multiple dimensions, including event type, severity, affected infrastructure, and required resources. Our methodology employs a transformer-based architecture that aligns visual and textual representations in a shared semantic space, enabling more robust classification compared to unimodal approaches. Experiments conducted on a diverse dataset spanning multiple crisis events—including hurricanes, earthquakes, wildfires, and flooding—demonstrate that our multimodal approach achieves a 17.3% improvement in classification accuracy over text-only baselines and a 22.6% improvement over image-only methods. Furthermore, we introduce a new attention mechanism specifically designed to identify and prioritize critical information in noisy social media streams. The proposed framework offers significant potential for enhancing situational awareness during emergencies and improving the efficiency of resource allocation in crisis response scenarios.

Image Transformer

This paper introduces the Image Transformer, a novel architecture that extends the self-attention mechanism of Transformers to the domain of image processing. Unlike convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that rely on fixed, local receptive fields, our proposed model employs multi-head self-attention to capture long-range dependencies across the entire image. The Image Transformer treats an image as a sequence of patches and learns contextual relationships between these patches regardless of their spatial distance. Through extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and generation tasks, we demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN-based methods. The Image Transformer is particularly effective for tasks requiring global context understanding and exhibits strong transfer learning capabilities. Additionally, we propose an efficient implementation that addresses the quadratic complexity challenge inherent in self-attention mechanisms when applied to high-resolution images. Our work suggests that self-attention-based architectures present a promising alternative paradigm for computer vision tasks traditionally dominated by convolutional approaches.

In-Vehicle Object Detection in the Wild for Driverless Vehicles

This paper presents a novel approach to in-vehicle object detection for autonomous driving systems operating in unconstrained real-world environments. While significant progress has been made in external environmental perception for driverless vehicles, the detection and classification of objects within the vehicle cabin remains an underexplored yet critical component for fully autonomous operation. We introduce a robust deep learning framework specifically designed to identify and track various objects in the vehicle interior across challenging conditions including variable lighting, occlusions, and diverse passenger behaviors. Our method employs a multi-modal sensor fusion approach combining RGB cameras, depth sensing, and infrared imaging to achieve high detection accuracy in day and night scenarios. Extensive experiments conducted on our newly compiled dataset of over 50,000 annotated in-vehicle scenes demonstrate that our approach achieves 94.7% mean average precision, outperforming existing methods by 8.3%. The proposed system enables critical autonomous vehicle functionalities including passenger safety monitoring, forgotten item detection, and cabin-aware decision making. This work bridges an important gap in autonomous vehicle perception systems by extending robust object detection capabilities to the vehicle interior.

Don't miss the Mismatch: Investigating the Objective Function Mismatch for Unsupervised Representation Learning

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations without human-annotated labels. Despite impressive empirical success, there remains a critical gap in our understanding of why certain objective functions yield more transferable representations than others. In this work, we investigate the phenomenon of "objective function mismatch" - where the optimization target during pre-training differs substantially from downstream evaluation metrics. Through systematic experimentation across diverse architectures and datasets, we demonstrate that this mismatch can significantly impact representation quality. We introduce a theoretical framework that quantifies this discrepancy and propose a novel regularization approach that explicitly minimizes the alignment gap between pretext tasks and anticipated downstream applications. Our method consistently improves performance across multiple benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on several vision tasks. Furthermore, we provide insights into designing better self-supervised objectives by analyzing the geometric properties of learned embedding spaces. These findings challenge conventional wisdom about representation learning objectives and offer practical guidelines for developing more effective self-supervised learning algorithms.

A Thorough View of Exact Inference in Graphs from the Degree-4 Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of exact inference in graphical models through the lens of the degree-4 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) hierarchy. We investigate the power and limitations of this specific level of the SoS hierarchy for solving fundamental inference problems that arise in probabilistic graphical models. Our work establishes several novel theoretical results characterizing when degree-4 SoS relaxations yield exact solutions to otherwise intractable inference tasks. We prove that for a significant class of sparse graphical models with bounded treewidth, the degree-4 SoS hierarchy captures precisely the marginal polytope, enabling exact inference in polynomial time. Furthermore, we identify structural graph properties that serve as sufficient conditions for the tightness of this relaxation. Through rigorous analysis, we demonstrate separation results between degree-2 (equivalent to standard semidefinite programming relaxations) and degree-4 SoS formulations, exhibiting families of inference problems where the higher-degree approach succeeds while lower-degree methods provably fail. Our theoretical contributions are complemented by efficient algorithmic implementations and empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world graph inference problems, confirming the practical advantages of degree-4 SoS for exact inference. These results advance our understanding of the algebraic and geometric landscape of inference problems and provide new insights into the broader question of when convex relaxations can exactly solve combinatorially challenging tasks in machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Learning Slice-Aware Representations with Mixture of Attentions

Machine learning models often perform well on average but struggle with specific data slices that represent important subpopulations or challenging scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called Mixture of Attentions (MoA) that learns slice-aware representations to address this challenge. Our method leverages multiple specialized attention mechanisms, each designed to focus on different data characteristics, and combines them dynamically based on input features. We formulate this as a mixture of experts problem where each attention module serves as an expert for particular data slices. Through extensive experiments on image classification, natural language understanding, and multimodal tasks, we demonstrate that MoA significantly improves performance on underrepresented and challenging slices without compromising overall accuracy. Our approach outperforms existing slice-aware methods by 3-7% on slice-specific metrics while maintaining competitive performance on standard benchmarks. Further analysis reveals that MoA learns more robust representations that generalize better to distribution shifts and provides interpretable insights into model decision-making across different data slices. Our work contributes a flexible framework for developing models that perform reliably across diverse data subpopulations.

Flow-based Anomaly Detection

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for flow-based anomaly detection in network traffic. We propose a novel approach that leverages the temporal and spatial characteristics of network flows to identify abnormal patterns indicative of security threats, performance issues, and operational anomalies. Our method combines statistical analysis, machine learning techniques, and domain-specific heuristics to process high-volume network flow data in near real-time. By analyzing communication patterns between hosts, protocol distributions, and traffic volume variations, our system can detect various anomalies including DDoS attacks, port scans, data exfiltration, and network misconfigurations. Experimental evaluation on multiple datasets, including the CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 benchmarks, demonstrates that our approach achieves 97.3% detection accuracy with a false positive rate of only 0.8%, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, our system shows robust performance in operational environments with concept drift and maintains detection efficacy even when faced with previously unseen attack vectors. The scalable architecture enables deployment in enterprise networks processing up to 100 Gbps of traffic with minimal performance overhead.

Holopix50k: A Large-Scale In-the-wild Stereo Image Dataset

We present Holopix50k, a novel large-scale dataset of 50,000 in-the-wild stereo image pairs captured by users of consumer light field cameras. This dataset addresses the critical shortage of diverse, real-world stereoscopic imagery needed for training and evaluating computational stereo algorithms. Unlike existing stereo datasets that often feature controlled environments or synthetic scenes, Holopix50k encompasses a rich variety of everyday scenes, lighting conditions, camera motions, and subject matter. The dataset includes comprehensive metadata and has been carefully curated to ensure quality and privacy compliance. We demonstrate the utility of Holopix50k through benchmark experiments on stereo matching, depth estimation, and novel view synthesis tasks, showing significant improvements in model generalization compared to models trained on existing datasets. Our analysis reveals that the diversity and scale of Holopix50k enable more robust performance across challenging real-world scenarios. We believe this dataset will serve as a valuable resource for advancing stereoscopic vision research and applications.

Automated Self-Supervised Learning for Graphs

This paper introduces a novel framework for automating the design and optimization of self-supervised learning (SSL) strategies for graph-structured data. While self-supervised learning has shown remarkable success in extracting meaningful representations from unlabeled graph data, the manual design of pretext tasks and training objectives remains largely heuristic and domain-specific. Our proposed approach, AutoGraphSSL, employs a hierarchical search space and efficient optimization algorithm to automatically discover effective self-supervised learning paradigms for diverse graph learning scenarios. The framework systematically explores combinations of graph augmentation techniques, contrastive objectives, and architectural components, adapting to the specific characteristics of the input graph data. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning molecular graphs, social networks, and citation networks, we demonstrate that AutoGraphSSL consistently outperforms hand-crafted SSL methods by 4-7% on downstream tasks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in the discovered SSL strategies, providing insights into the relationship between graph properties and optimal self-supervision mechanisms. The automated approach not only reduces the human effort in designing SSL methods but also enhances the transferability of learned representations across different graph domains and tasks.

Estimation of Warfarin Dosage with Reinforcement Learning

Warfarin remains one of the most widely prescribed oral anticoagulants despite its narrow therapeutic window and high inter-patient variability in dose requirements. This study introduces a novel reinforcement learning (RL) approach for personalizing warfarin dosing regimens. We formulated the dosing problem as a Markov Decision Process where the state space comprises patient characteristics and coagulation measurements, actions represent dosage adjustments, and rewards reflect therapeutic outcomes. Using retrospective data from 2,500 patients, we trained and evaluated several RL algorithms including Deep Q-Networks and Proximal Policy Optimization. Our RL-based dosing strategy achieved 15% higher time in therapeutic range compared to conventional clinical algorithms, with 22% fewer adverse events. The model demonstrated robust performance across diverse patient subgroups, including those with genetic variants affecting warfarin metabolism. Importantly, the RL framework continuously improved its dosing policy through ongoing interaction data, adapting to individual patient responses over time. These findings suggest that reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to optimize warfarin therapy, potentially improving safety and efficacy while reducing the burden of frequent monitoring and dose adjustments.

AdaBins: Depth Estimation using Adaptive Bins

This paper presents AdaBins, a novel approach for monocular depth estimation that addresses the fundamental challenge of continuous depth prediction by reformulating it as a bin-based classification and regression problem. Unlike previous methods that use fixed, uniform bins, our approach dynamically adapts the bin widths for each input image, enabling more precise depth estimation across varying scenes and depth ranges. We introduce an adaptive bin module that learns to partition the depth range into optimal intervals based on scene context, followed by a transformer-based architecture that effectively captures global dependencies critical for accurate depth prediction. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including NYU Depth V2 and KITTI demonstrate that AdaBins significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing absolute relative error by up to 14% while maintaining real-time inference capabilities. Our qualitative results show particularly impressive performance in challenging scenarios with complex geometries and varying depth distributions. The proposed adaptive binning strategy proves especially effective for indoor scenes where depth values are not uniformly distributed, demonstrating the importance of context-aware depth discretization in monocular depth estimation tasks.

Abstract: Learn to Learn Metric Space for Few-Shot Segmentation of 3D Shapes

This paper introduces a novel meta-learning approach for few-shot 3D shape segmentation that addresses the challenge of limited labeled data in 3D domains. We propose a learning-to-learn framework that dynamically constructs an adaptive metric space tailored to each segmentation task. Unlike traditional methods that rely on fixed feature embeddings, our approach meta-learns how to generate task-specific distance metrics that better capture the geometric and topological relationships between shape parts. The framework consists of a meta-embedding network that extracts point-level features and a metric adaptation module that reconfigures the feature space based on the few-shot support examples. Extensive experiments on ShapeNet and PartNet benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation techniques by 6.2% in 1-shot and 4.8% in 5-shot settings. Furthermore, we show that our learned metric space effectively generalizes to unseen shape categories while maintaining segmentation consistency. This work presents a promising direction for reducing annotation requirements in 3D shape analysis through meta-learning of adaptive metric spaces.

Equivariant Wavelets: Fast Rotation and Translation Invariant Wavelet Scattering Transforms

We present a novel approach to constructing rotation and translation invariant wavelet scattering transforms with significantly improved computational efficiency. Our method leverages equivariant wavelet designs that maintain their structural properties under geometric transformations, enabling the extraction of robust features that are invariant to rotations and translations while preserving discriminative information. The proposed framework reduces the computational complexity from O(n³) to O(n log n) compared to traditional approaches, making it feasible for high-dimensional image and signal processing tasks. Through theoretical analysis, we establish stability guarantees and demonstrate that our equivariant wavelet scattering network achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets including rotated MNIST, CIFAR-10, and texture classification tasks. Experimental results show that our method not only accelerates computation but also improves classification accuracy by effectively capturing orientation-independent features. This work bridges the gap between the mathematical elegance of wavelet scattering transforms and their practical applicability to large-scale computer vision and signal processing problems where rotational and translational invariance are critical.

Quaternion Knowledge Graph Embeddings

Knowledge graph embeddings (KGEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for knowledge representation and reasoning in artificial intelligence. This paper introduces Quaternion Knowledge Graph Embeddings (QKGE), a novel approach that leverages quaternion algebra to represent entities and relations in knowledge graphs. Unlike traditional KGE methods that operate in real vector spaces or complex planes, our quaternion-based framework captures multidimensional interactions through the four-dimensional hypercomplex number system. We demonstrate that quaternion representations provide a natural framework for modeling the compositional structure of knowledge graph triples while preserving rotational invariance and hierarchical relationships. The proposed QKGE models achieve state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmark datasets including FB15k-237, WN18RR, and YAGO3-10, showing significant improvements in link prediction tasks. Experimental results reveal that quaternion embeddings effectively capture semantic hierarchies and complex relational patterns while requiring fewer parameters than comparable methods. This work establishes quaternion algebra as a promising mathematical foundation for knowledge graph representation learning.

Grid-to-Graph: Flexible Spatial Relational Inductive Biases for Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces Grid-to-Graph (G2G), a novel framework that bridges the gap between grid-based and graph-based representations in reinforcement learning environments with spatial structure. While grid-based approaches naturally capture spatial relationships, they often struggle with computational efficiency and flexibility in irregular environments. Conversely, graph-based methods offer flexibility but may fail to leverage inherent spatial structure. Our G2G framework dynamically transforms grid-based observations into graph representations that preserve critical spatial relationships while discarding irrelevant information. We formalize this transformation process and demonstrate how it enables the incorporation of flexible spatial relational inductive biases into reinforcement learning algorithms. Through extensive experimentation across navigation, puzzle-solving, and strategy game environments, we show that G2G agents consistently outperform both pure grid-based and graph-based alternatives, particularly in complex scenarios requiring spatial reasoning. Our approach achieves up to 35% improvement in sample efficiency and 28% higher final performance compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis establishing that G2G preserves representational capacity while reducing computational complexity. These results suggest that flexible spatial relational inductive biases are crucial for effective reinforcement learning in spatially structured environments.

Predictive Inequity in Object Detection

Object detection systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet their performance may not be uniform across different demographic groups. This study investigates the presence of predictive inequity in contemporary object detection models, with a particular focus on pedestrian detection across different skin tones. We analyze several state-of-the-art object detection frameworks on diverse datasets and find consistent disparities in detection accuracy, with darker-skinned pedestrians being detected with lower accuracy and higher false negative rates compared to lighter-skinned pedestrians. This performance gap persists across various lighting conditions, occlusion levels, and resolutions, though it is often exacerbated in challenging visual scenarios. Our controlled experiments suggest these disparities stem from both dataset representation imbalances and algorithmic design choices that inadequately address feature extraction for diverse skin tones. We propose evaluation metrics for quantifying predictive inequity and outline potential mitigation strategies, including balanced dataset curation and algorithmic modifications. These findings highlight the critical need to address fairness concerns in computer vision systems, particularly for applications like autonomous vehicles and surveillance where equitable performance is essential for public safety and trust.

Integrating Image Captioning with Rule-based Entity Masking

This paper presents a novel approach that combines image captioning techniques with rule-based entity masking to enhance privacy and security in visual content description systems. Our framework addresses the critical challenge of generating informative image descriptions while systematically protecting sensitive information through intelligent entity detection and selective masking. We introduce a two-stage pipeline where images are first processed by a state-of-the-art captioning model, followed by a rule-based entity recognition system that identifies and masks sensitive entities according to configurable privacy policies. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach maintains comparable BLEU, METEOR, and CIDEr scores to unmasked captioning systems while significantly reducing privacy leakage by up to 94% for personally identifiable information. The proposed method offers a flexible, interpretable solution that balances descriptive accuracy with privacy preservation, making it particularly valuable for applications in healthcare, security, and social media contexts where both informative content description and privacy protection are essential. Our work contributes to the growing field of privacy-preserving AI by offering a practical approach that can be readily integrated with existing image captioning systems.

Spatial-Channel Transformer Network for Trajectory Prediction on the Traffic Scenes

Accurate trajectory prediction of road users is critical for autonomous driving systems to ensure safe and efficient navigation in complex traffic environments. This paper introduces a novel Spatial-Channel Transformer Network (SCTN) that effectively captures both spatial relationships between traffic participants and channel-wise feature dependencies for trajectory prediction. Our approach leverages a dual-attention mechanism: spatial transformers model interactions between agents across the traffic scene, while channel transformers extract meaningful feature representations from heterogeneous input data including historical trajectories, agent attributes, and map information. The proposed architecture incorporates a hierarchical encoding structure that progressively refines trajectory predictions by considering multi-scale temporal dynamics. Extensive experiments on popular benchmarks including Argoverse, nuScenes, and Interaction demonstrate that our SCTN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 19% lower average displacement error and 22% improved final displacement error. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our spatial-channel attention mechanisms and highlight the model's robustness in complex scenarios involving multiple interacting agents. The SCTN framework provides interpretable attention maps that offer insights into the model's decision-making process, enhancing trustworthiness for real-world deployment in autonomous driving systems.

Finding Original Image Of A Sub Image Using CNNs

This paper presents a novel approach for identifying the original image from which a sub-image has been extracted, using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The task of matching image fragments to their source is challenging due to the loss of contextual information, potential transformations, and the vast search space of possible originals. Our method leverages the hierarchical feature extraction capabilities of CNNs to create robust representations of both sub-images and potential parent images. We propose a two-stream architecture that computes similarity scores between the query sub-image and candidate originals through a specialized matching network. Experiments conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves 87.3% accuracy in identifying correct parent images, significantly outperforming traditional feature-matching methods. The system maintains resilience even when sub-images undergo moderate transformations such as rotation, scaling, and illumination changes. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient indexing mechanism that enables rapid retrieval from large image repositories with minimal computational overhead. This work has important applications in digital forensics, content verification, and visual data management systems.

Dynamic Graph-Based Anomaly Detection in the Electrical Grid

This paper presents a novel approach to anomaly detection in electrical grid systems using dynamic graph-based modeling techniques. Modern power grids face increasing vulnerabilities due to growing complexity, integration of renewable energy sources, and evolving cyber threats. Traditional threshold-based monitoring systems often fail to capture subtle, coordinated anomalies that may indicate failures or attacks. Our method represents the electrical grid as a dynamic graph where nodes correspond to generators, substations, and loads, while edges represent transmission lines with time-varying electrical parameters. By leveraging temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) that incorporate both spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, our system can identify anomalous patterns that deviate from normal grid operations. We evaluate our approach using both simulated grid disturbances and real-world data from regional transmission operators, demonstrating significant improvements in detection accuracy (87% vs. 63%) and reduced false positive rates (4.2% vs. 11.7%) compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, our system provides interpretable insights into detected anomalies, facilitating faster response by grid operators. This research contributes to enhancing the reliability and security of critical electrical infrastructure through advanced graph-based analytics.

ConvNets vs. Transformers: Whose Visual Representations are More Transferable?

This study presents a comprehensive empirical investigation comparing the transfer learning capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) and Vision Transformers across diverse downstream visual tasks. While Transformers have demonstrated remarkable performance on many computer vision benchmarks, their representation transferability relative to traditional ConvNets remains incompletely understood. We systematically evaluate architecturally comparable ConvNet and Transformer models pre-trained on ImageNet, measuring their transfer performance on tasks spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, fine-grained classification, and few-shot learning. Our experiments reveal that Transformer-based models generally produce more transferable representations for tasks requiring global context integration and complex scene understanding, while ConvNets maintain advantages in tasks demanding precise spatial localization and computational efficiency. Notably, we observe that the transferability gap narrows with increased model size and pre-training data diversity. We further analyze the attention mechanisms and feature hierarchies that contribute to these differences, providing insights into when practitioners should prefer one architecture over the other. Our findings suggest that hybrid approaches combining the strengths of both architectures may represent a promising direction for maximizing representation transferability across the visual domain spectrum.

PAN++: Towards Efficient and Accurate End-to-End Spotting of Arbitrarily-Shaped Text

Text detection and recognition in natural scenes remains challenging, particularly when dealing with arbitrarily-shaped text such as curved, rotated, or irregularly formatted instances. This paper presents PAN++ (Pixel Aggregation Network++), an enhanced end-to-end framework that simultaneously detects and recognizes text of arbitrary shapes in a single forward pass. Building upon the original PAN architecture, our approach introduces several key improvements: (1) a refined feature pyramid network with attention mechanisms that better captures multi-scale text features, (2) an adaptive text region proposal module that precisely localizes text instances regardless of their geometric configurations, and (3) a lightweight recognition head that efficiently decodes text content while maintaining high accuracy. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Total-Text, CTW-1500, and ICDAR 2015 demonstrate that PAN++ achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining faster inference speeds compared to existing methods. Notably, our model achieves an F-measure of 85.7% on Total-Text and 83.5% on CTW-1500 for end-to-end text spotting, with an inference time of only 8.7ms per image on a single GPU. The proposed framework provides a practical solution for real-world applications requiring efficient and accurate text spotting in complex environments.

Reprogramming Language Models for Molecular Representation Learning

This study presents a novel approach to molecular representation learning by repurposing pre-trained large language models (LLMs) for molecular property prediction and drug discovery tasks. While deep learning has shown promise in computational chemistry, developing specialized architectures for molecular data remains challenging due to the complex, graph-structured nature of molecules and limited labeled datasets. We introduce a technique called "molecular reprogramming" that adapts powerful language models trained on vast text corpora to understand molecular structures without extensive retraining. By developing specialized tokenization schemes that convert molecular structures (SMILES, SELFIES, or graph representations) into language-model-compatible sequences, we enable LLMs to process molecular information within their existing architectural frameworks. Our experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that reprogrammed language models achieve competitive or superior performance compared to specialized graph neural networks and other molecular machine learning approaches, particularly in low-data regimes. This transfer learning approach significantly reduces computational requirements while improving predictive accuracy for properties including binding affinity, toxicity, and solubility. The framework provides a promising direction for leveraging the representational power of language models in scientific domains beyond natural language.

MixRL: Data Mixing Augmentation for Regression using Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces MixRL, a novel data augmentation framework that leverages reinforcement learning to optimize mixing strategies for regression tasks. While data augmentation techniques have shown significant success in classification problems, their application to regression tasks remains challenging due to the continuous nature of target variables. MixRL addresses this gap by formulating the data mixing process as a sequential decision-making problem, where a reinforcement learning agent learns to create synthetic training examples by intelligently combining existing data points. Our approach dynamically adapts the mixing policy based on model performance feedback, effectively exploring the continuous output space to generate informative augmented samples. Extensive experiments across diverse regression benchmarks demonstrate that MixRL consistently outperforms traditional augmentation methods, reducing mean squared error by an average of 18.7% compared to baseline approaches. The framework shows particular effectiveness in low-data regimes and for datasets with imbalanced target distributions. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into why reinforcement learning-guided mixing strategies can improve generalization in regression tasks. MixRL offers a flexible, model-agnostic solution to enhance regression performance through intelligent data augmentation.

Compressing Large-Scale Transformer-Based Models: A Case Study on BERT

This paper investigates efficient compression techniques for large-scale Transformer-based models, focusing specifically on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers). While BERT and its variants have achieved state-of-the-art performance across numerous natural language processing tasks, their substantial computational and memory requirements pose significant deployment challenges, particularly in resource-constrained environments. We present a comprehensive evaluation of multiple compression approaches including knowledge distillation, quantization, pruning, and parameter sharing. Our experiments demonstrate that a combination of task-specific knowledge distillation and structured pruning yields the most favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, reducing model size by 74% and inference time by 68% while maintaining performance within 2.5% of the original model across GLUE benchmark tasks. We further analyze the linguistic capabilities preserved in compressed models through probing tasks, revealing that syntactic knowledge is largely retained while certain types of semantic reasoning degrade more substantially. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying compressed Transformer models and highlight promising directions for future research in efficient natural language processing.

Auxiliary Tasks Speed Up Learning PointGoal Navigation

This paper investigates how auxiliary learning tasks can accelerate the training of embodied agents for PointGoal navigation, where agents must navigate to specific coordinates in unseen environments. We introduce a suite of auxiliary tasks designed to enhance spatial understanding and efficient exploration, including local occupancy prediction, relative position estimation, and scene segmentation. Through extensive experiments in visually complex, photorealistic environments, we demonstrate that our proposed auxiliary tasks lead to significant improvements in both sample efficiency and final performance. Agents trained with our auxiliary objectives learn effective navigation policies with 45% fewer environment interactions compared to baseline methods, while achieving a 23% higher success rate on challenging test environments. Further analysis reveals that the auxiliary tasks particularly benefit learning during the early and middle stages of training by providing richer gradient signals that improve feature representations. Our approach addresses a key challenge in embodied AI by reducing the computational resources required to train navigation agents, making research in this domain more accessible and environmentally sustainable.

Visually Imperceptible Adversarial Patch Attacks on Digital Images

This paper presents a novel approach to creating adversarial patch attacks that remain visually imperceptible to human observers while successfully deceiving state-of-the-art deep learning image classification systems. Unlike traditional adversarial patches that are visibly apparent, our method leverages human visual perception limitations to design patches that blend seamlessly with the target image while maintaining high attack success rates. We introduce a perception-aware optimization framework that jointly minimizes both the visual detectability of the patch and maximizes its adversarial effect. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets including ImageNet and MS-COCO, we demonstrate that our imperceptible patches achieve over 92% attack success rates against leading convolutional neural networks while scoring significantly lower on human detection tests compared to conventional adversarial patches. Further analysis reveals that these attacks remain robust against common defense mechanisms including adversarial training and input preprocessing. Our work highlights critical security vulnerabilities in vision systems by showing that effective adversarial attacks need not be visually apparent, raising important implications for the deployment of machine learning models in security-sensitive applications.

Flexible Log File Parsing using Hidden Markov Models

Log file analysis is crucial for system monitoring, debugging, and security auditing, yet the diversity and evolving nature of log formats present significant challenges for automated parsing. This paper introduces a novel approach to log file parsing using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) that addresses the limitations of traditional rule-based and regular expression methods. Our framework dynamically learns the underlying structure of log entries without requiring predefined templates or extensive manual configuration. By modeling the sequential dependencies between tokens in log messages, the HMM approach can effectively distinguish between static message components and variable parameters, even in previously unseen log formats. Experimental evaluation across diverse log datasets demonstrates that our method achieves 92.7% parsing accuracy while requiring minimal human intervention. The system exhibits robust performance when confronted with format variations, timestamp irregularities, and multi-line entries. Additionally, we present an adaptive learning mechanism that continuously improves parsing accuracy as it processes new log data. This flexible approach significantly reduces the engineering effort required for log analysis systems while improving their resilience to evolving log formats.

Abstract: Learnable Companding Quantization for Accurate Low-bit Neural Networks

This paper introduces a novel learnable companding quantization (LCQ) framework for deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. While quantization reduces model size and computational demands, existing methods struggle to maintain accuracy at extremely low bit-widths (1-4 bits). Our proposed LCQ approach addresses this challenge by employing a non-uniform quantization scheme with learnable companding functions that adaptively compress and expand the dynamic range of network parameters and activations. The companding transformation is optimized end-to-end alongside network weights, allowing the quantization intervals to be distributed according to the statistical properties of each layer. Extensive experiments across multiple architectures (ResNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-10) demonstrate that LCQ significantly outperforms state-of-the-art quantization methods, with particularly notable improvements in ultra-low bit scenarios. For instance, our 2-bit quantized ResNet-18 achieves only a 1.7% accuracy drop compared to full-precision models, while reducing model size by 16×. Ablation studies confirm that the learnable nature of our companding functions is crucial for capturing the complex distributions of weights and activations. The proposed method requires minimal modifications to existing training pipelines and introduces negligible computational overhead during inference, making it a practical solution for real-world deployment of efficient neural networks.

Constructing Multiple Tasks for Augmentation: Improving Neural Image Classification With K-means Features

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance neural image classification through multi-task learning augmented with unsupervised feature representations. We propose a framework that leverages K-means clustering to generate auxiliary tasks that complement the primary classification objective. By extracting cluster-based features from intermediate network representations, we construct supplementary classification tasks that encourage the model to learn more robust and discriminative features. Our method applies K-means clustering to activation maps at various network depths, creating cluster assignments that serve as targets for auxiliary classification heads. These additional tasks act as regularizers during training, improving the network's generalization capabilities without requiring additional labeled data. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms single-task baselines, with accuracy improvements of 2.3-4.1% across different architectures. The performance gains are particularly pronounced in limited data regimes, where our method reduces overfitting and improves sample efficiency. Further analysis reveals that the learned representations capture complementary visual patterns that might be overlooked in standard training paradigms. Our approach is architecture-agnostic, computationally efficient, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep learning pipelines.

Unsupervised Detection of Adversarial Examples with Model Explanations

Deep neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains but remain vulnerable to adversarial examples—subtly perturbed inputs designed to cause misclassification. This paper presents a novel unsupervised approach for detecting adversarial examples by leveraging model explanations. Our method analyzes the attribution patterns generated by explainability techniques such as Integrated Gradients and SHAP to identify inconsistencies characteristic of adversarial inputs. Unlike previous detection methods that require adversarial examples during training, our approach operates without prior exposure to attacks, making it applicable in real-world scenarios where attack strategies are unknown. Through extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and MNIST, we demonstrate that explanation-based features can effectively distinguish between natural and adversarial examples across various attack types (FGSM, PGD, CW, DeepFool). Our method achieves detection rates of up to 96% while maintaining a low false positive rate of 3% on unseen attacks. Additionally, we show that our approach is robust to adaptive adversaries attempting to circumvent the detection mechanism. This work establishes model explanations as powerful tools for unsupervised adversarial detection, offering a promising direction for improving the security of deep learning systems in practice.

Many Paths to Equilibrium: GANs Do Not Need to Decrease a Divergence At Every Step

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as powerful frameworks for learning generative models of complex data distributions. While the training dynamics of GANs are often conceptualized as minimizing a divergence between the model and target distributions, we demonstrate that this perspective is unnecessarily restrictive. In this paper, we analyze the training trajectories of various GAN algorithms and show that successful GAN training does not necessarily correspond to monotonically decreasing a divergence measure at each step. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we establish that non-monotonic paths can still lead to equilibrium, challenging the conventional wisdom about GAN convergence. We introduce a more general framework for understanding GAN dynamics that accommodates these diverse training trajectories and provides insights into why some GAN variants demonstrate greater stability than others. Our findings reveal that the relationship between gradient-based updates and divergence minimization is more nuanced than previously understood, suggesting new approaches for designing and analyzing GAN training algorithms. This broader perspective on GAN dynamics helps explain the practical success of many GAN variants despite their apparent theoretical limitations.

Weight-Sharing Neural Architecture Search: A Battle to Shrink the Optimization Gap

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a promising approach to automate the design of neural networks, yet its computational demands remain prohibitive for many applications. Weight-sharing NAS methods have gained popularity for their efficiency, allowing multiple architectures to share parameters within a single supernet. However, these methods often suffer from an "optimization gap" between the performance of architectures during the search phase and their actual performance after standalone training. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of this optimization gap in weight-sharing NAS frameworks. We identify three primary contributing factors: insufficient training of the supernet, interference between architectures sharing weights, and inconsistent ranking of candidate architectures. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets and search spaces, we propose several techniques to shrink this gap, including progressive training strategies, architectural distance-aware sampling methods, and improved performance estimation protocols. Our approaches demonstrate significant improvements in correlation between search and evaluation accuracy, reducing the optimization gap by up to 45% compared to standard weight-sharing methods while maintaining computational efficiency. These findings provide valuable insights for designing more reliable and effective weight-sharing NAS algorithms that better align search-time proxy metrics with final architecture performance.

Analysis and a Solution of Momentarily Missed Detection for Anchor-based Object Detectors

This paper addresses a critical yet under-explored phenomenon in anchor-based object detection systems: momentarily missed detections (MMDs), where objects clearly visible in video sequences are sporadically undetected in isolated frames despite successful detection in adjacent frames. Through comprehensive analysis across multiple state-of-the-art anchor-based detectors including Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, and YOLO variants, we identify that MMDs primarily stem from anchor assignment failures rather than classification or regression errors. Our investigation reveals that traditional intersection-over-union (IoU) thresholding mechanisms for anchor assignment can fail when objects undergo subtle appearance changes or slight positional shifts, creating temporary misalignments between anchor boxes and ground truth objects. To address this issue, we propose Temporal Anchor Assignment Smoothing (TAAS), a lightweight, training-free solution that leverages temporal consistency across video frames to dynamically adjust anchor assignments. TAAS significantly reduces MMD occurrences by 76.3% on average across benchmark datasets while maintaining or slightly improving overall detection performance. Importantly, our method introduces minimal computational overhead (less than 5ms per frame) and requires no model retraining, making it readily applicable to existing deployment pipelines. Extensive experiments on autonomous driving and surveillance datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing detection stability for safety-critical applications.

Improving Dermoscopic Image Segmentation with Enhanced Convolutional-Deconvolutional Networks

Accurate segmentation of skin lesions in dermoscopic images is a critical preprocessing step for automated melanoma detection systems. This paper presents a novel approach to dermoscopic image segmentation using enhanced convolutional-deconvolutional networks (ECDNs). Our proposed architecture incorporates several key innovations: (1) dense skip connections to preserve fine-grained spatial information, (2) an attention mechanism that emphasizes diagnostically relevant regions, and (3) a hybrid loss function combining focal and boundary-aware components to address class imbalance and improve edge delineation. We evaluated our method on three public datasets: ISIC 2018, PH2, and Derm7pt, achieving mean Jaccard indices of 0.923, 0.941, and 0.917 respectively, representing a statistically significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each proposed enhancement, with the attention mechanism providing the most substantial performance gain. The ECDN model demonstrates particular robustness to challenging cases including low contrast boundaries, irregular shapes, and the presence of artifacts such as hair and ruler markings. These results suggest that our approach can significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of automated skin lesion analysis systems in clinical settings.

Improving GAN Training with Probability Ratio Clipping and Sample Reweighting

Despite their widespread success, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remain notoriously difficult to train, often suffering from training instability, mode collapse, and vanishing gradients. In this paper, we introduce two novel techniques to address these challenges: Probability Ratio Clipping (PRC) and Sample Reweighting (SR). PRC constrains the ratio between the generator and real data distributions, preventing the discriminator from becoming overly confident and maintaining meaningful gradients throughout training. SR dynamically adjusts the importance of training samples based on their contribution to generator learning, focusing computational resources on the most informative examples. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that these methods effectively regularize the training dynamics, leading to more stable convergence. Our extensive experiments across multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet, show that models incorporating PRC and SR achieve state-of-the-art performance as measured by Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS). Additionally, our approach demonstrates enhanced training stability, improved sample diversity, and faster convergence compared to existing GAN variants. The proposed techniques are architecture-agnostic and can be readily integrated into existing GAN frameworks with minimal computational overhead.

Time-Series Representation Learning via Temporal and Contextual Contrasting

This paper introduces a novel self-supervised approach for learning robust representations from time-series data without requiring manual annotations. Our framework, which we call Temporal and Contextual Contrasting (TCC), leverages the inherent temporal structure and contextual relationships within time-series data to create powerful representations that capture both local and global patterns. TCC employs a dual contrastive learning strategy: temporal contrasting, which encourages representations to preserve chronological dependencies by contrasting different temporal segments, and contextual contrasting, which distinguishes between semantically related and unrelated contexts across different time scales. Through extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets spanning healthcare monitoring, industrial sensor readings, and financial forecasting applications, we demonstrate that TCC outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised methods in downstream tasks including classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection. Our representations show remarkable robustness to noise, missing data, and limited labeled examples, making TCC particularly valuable for real-world time-series analysis where high-quality annotations are scarce. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into why the joint optimization of temporal and contextual objectives leads to more discriminative and generalizable representations.

Style Transfer With Adaptation to the Central Objects of the Scene

This paper presents a novel approach to neural style transfer that prioritizes the semantic importance of central objects within a scene. While traditional style transfer methods apply stylistic transformations uniformly across an image, our method introduces an adaptive mechanism that identifies and preserves the visual integrity of central objects while allowing for more aggressive stylization in peripheral regions. We propose a dual-branch architecture that combines object-aware attention maps with a hierarchical feature transformation pipeline. Our approach first employs an object detection module to localize central elements, then applies spatially-varying style transformations that respect object boundaries and semantic importance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior perceptual quality compared to state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in scenarios where central object recognition is crucial to the viewer's interpretation of the scene. User studies confirm that our adaptive approach maintains better object fidelity while still achieving compelling stylistic effects. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric that specifically measures central object preservation in stylized outputs. The proposed method enables more controlled and semantically aware style transfer, making it particularly valuable for applications in creative content generation, computational photography, and mixed reality.

Funnelling: A New Ensemble Method for Heterogeneous Transfer Learning and its Application to Cross-Lingual Text Classification

This paper introduces Funnelling, a novel ensemble methodology designed specifically for heterogeneous transfer learning scenarios where source and target domains differ in feature representation. The approach creates a unified framework that effectively leverages knowledge from multiple source languages to improve performance on target language tasks, particularly for low-resource languages. Unlike traditional transfer learning methods that rely on direct feature mapping or translation, Funnelling employs a two-stage process: first training base classifiers on source languages, then combining their predictions through a meta-classifier that learns optimal weighting patterns. We evaluate our approach on cross-lingual text classification tasks across 15 languages from diverse language families, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Experiments show Funnelling achieves an average performance gain of 13.2% when the target language has limited labeled data, with particularly strong results for languages with distinct linguistic properties from the source languages. Furthermore, the method exhibits robust performance even with heterogeneous feature representations and noisy source data. Our analysis reveals that Funnelling effectively captures complementary information from diverse source languages while mitigating negative transfer effects. The proposed approach offers a flexible, scalable solution for cross-lingual knowledge transfer that can be readily extended to other heterogeneous transfer learning applications.

Microtubule Tracking in Electron Microscopy Volumes

Microtubules are essential cytoskeletal components that play critical roles in cellular structure, intracellular transport, and cell division. Accurate three-dimensional reconstruction and tracking of microtubule networks in electron microscopy (EM) volumes remains challenging due to the complex, densely packed cellular environments and inherent limitations of EM imaging. This study presents a novel computational framework for automated microtubule tracking in electron microscopy volumes. Our approach combines deep learning-based segmentation with a specialized curvilinear structure tracking algorithm to identify and trace individual microtubules through complex cellular environments. The method addresses key challenges including microtubule crossings, image artifacts, and varying signal-to-noise ratios. We validate our approach using both synthetic datasets and real EM volumes from neurons and dividing cells, demonstrating significant improvements in tracking accuracy (92% F1-score) and computational efficiency compared to existing methods. The resulting three-dimensional reconstructions provide unprecedented insights into microtubule organization, enabling quantitative analysis of microtubule length, orientation, and network topology. This framework represents an important advancement for studying microtubule-related cellular processes and pathologies in their native three-dimensional context.

CIDEr: Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation

Automatic evaluation metrics for image description generation have become increasingly important as computer vision and natural language processing systems advance in their ability to generate human-like descriptions of visual content. In this paper, we introduce CIDEr (Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation), a novel evaluation metric designed to assess the quality of generated image descriptions by measuring their similarity to a set of human-generated reference descriptions. Unlike previous metrics that rely primarily on n-gram matching or semantic similarity, CIDEr incorporates the notion of consensus by giving higher weights to n-grams that are commonly used by humans to describe a particular image, while penalizing n-grams that appear frequently across the dataset. Our approach employs a Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) weighting scheme to capture this consensus and implements a robust similarity function that correlates strongly with human judgments. Through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that CIDEr outperforms existing metrics in terms of correlation with human assessments of description quality. Furthermore, we analyze CIDEr's performance across diverse image types and description styles, showing its effectiveness as a general-purpose evaluation metric for image description generation systems. CIDEr provides researchers with a more reliable automated method for evaluating progress in this rapidly evolving field.
