The proposed approach shows particular robustness in challenging scenarios with varying illumination conditions and complex textures, making it suitable for applications in remote sensing, precision agriculture, and environmental monitoring.

Learning to Predict Salient Faces: A Novel Visual-Audio Saliency Model

This paper presents a novel computational model for predicting salient faces in videos by leveraging both visual and audio cues. While traditional visual saliency models focus on generic attention prediction, they often fail to effectively capture the unique attentional properties of human faces, particularly in dynamic audiovisual scenarios. Our proposed Visual-Audio Face Saliency (VAFS) model introduces a multimodal architecture that integrates facial features, motion dynamics, and corresponding audio signals to predict which faces will attract viewer attention in videos containing multiple people. The model employs a two-stream network where visual features are extracted through a modified convolutional neural network optimized for facial analysis, while audio features are processed through a specialized audio encoding branch that captures speech patterns and sonic events. These streams are fused through a cross-modal attention mechanism that learns to weight audiovisual correspondences. We evaluate our approach on a newly collected dataset of 220 videos with eye-tracking data from 35 participants, demonstrating that VAFS outperforms state-of-the-art visual-only saliency models by 17% in terms of AUC metrics and 22% in NSS scores. Our findings highlight the importance of audiovisual integration in face saliency prediction and offer new insights into human attention mechanisms in social scenarios.

Pixel-wise Attentional Gating for Parsimonious Pixel Labeling

Pixel labeling tasks, such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation, typically require dense per-pixel predictions, often leading to redundant computations in regions of low complexity. In this paper, we introduce Pixel-wise Attentional Gating (PAG), a novel approach that dynamically allocates computational resources across the spatial dimensions of an image according to the complexity of local regions. Our method employs a lightweight gating network that learns to predict which pixels require more detailed processing and which can be inferred with minimal computation. By selectively activating deep feature pathways only where needed, PAG significantly reduces the overall computational cost while maintaining high accuracy in critical regions. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art dense prediction networks while reducing computational requirements by up to 30%. Furthermore, we show that PAG naturally focuses computational attention on object boundaries and complex textural regions where precise labeling is most challenging. This parsimonious approach to pixel labeling offers an efficient solution for resource-constrained applications such as autonomous vehicles and mobile devices, where both accuracy and computational efficiency are crucial.

Heterogeneous Face Attribute Estimation: A Deep Multi-Task Learning Approach

This paper presents a novel deep multi-task learning framework for heterogeneous face attribute estimation. While existing approaches typically treat facial attribute prediction as independent binary classification tasks, our work recognizes the inherent correlations between attributes and their varying levels of complexity. We propose a hierarchical architecture that jointly learns multiple facial attributes while accounting for their heterogeneous nature—some being categorical (gender, race), others numerical (age), and others binary (wearing glasses, smiling). Our approach employs a shared feature extraction backbone followed by attribute-specific branches with customized loss functions tailored to each attribute type. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CelebA, LFWA, and MORPH demonstrate that our heterogeneous multi-task learning approach significantly outperforms both single-task models and conventional multi-task approaches that treat all attributes homogeneously. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance while requiring fewer parameters, demonstrating improved generalization across different attribute types and robustness to partial face occlusion and varying image qualities. Furthermore, our analysis reveals interesting correlations between attribute predictions that align with human perception of facial characteristics.

A Combined Approach Based on Fuzzy Classification and Contextual Region Growing to Image Segmentation

This paper presents a novel image segmentation framework that integrates fuzzy classification techniques with contextual region growing algorithms. Image segmentation remains a challenging task in computer vision due to issues such as noise, intensity inhomogeneity, and ambiguous boundaries. Our proposed approach addresses these limitations by first employing fuzzy classification to handle uncertainty in pixel assignments, generating initial probability maps for different image regions. These fuzzy membership functions serve as input to a contextual region growing process that incorporates spatial relationships and neighborhood information to refine region boundaries. The algorithm adaptively adjusts growing criteria based on local image statistics, enabling more accurate segmentation in heterogeneous regions. Experimental results on benchmark datasets including medical images, natural scenes, and remote sensing data demonstrate that our combined approach outperforms traditional segmentation methods in terms of accuracy, robustness to noise, and boundary preservation. Quantitative evaluation using Dice coefficient, Jaccard index, and boundary error metrics shows an average improvement of 12% over state-of-the-art techniques. The proposed framework provides a promising solution for applications requiring precise image segmentation in challenging environments.

Abstract: ControlVAE: Controllable Variational Autoencoder

This paper introduces ControlVAE, a novel framework that enhances traditional variational autoencoders (VAEs) with precise control over the optimization process. While standard VAEs have demonstrated impressive generative capabilities, they often suffer from unstable training dynamics and suboptimal disentanglement due to the inherent difficulty in balancing reconstruction quality and latent space regularization. ControlVAE addresses these limitations by implementing an adaptive control mechanism that dynamically adjusts the weight of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term during training. Using principles from control theory, our approach employs a proportional-integral (PI) controller that maintains the KL divergence at a desired level, facilitating better disentanglement while preserving reconstruction fidelity. Extensive experiments on image generation benchmarks and text modeling tasks demonstrate that ControlVAE achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art VAE variants, with improved disentanglement scores, reconstruction quality, and generation diversity. Furthermore, ControlVAE enables practitioners to explicitly specify their preference for the reconstruction-regularization trade-off, making it particularly valuable for applications requiring precise control over the latent space properties. Our approach not only stabilizes VAE training but also opens new avenues for controllable representation learning in generative models.

Variational Metric Scaling for Metric-Based Meta-Learning

This paper introduces Variational Metric Scaling (VMS), a novel approach to enhance metric-based meta-learning algorithms. While traditional metric-based meta-learning methods rely on fixed distance metrics to compare query and support examples, our proposed VMS framework adaptively scales these metrics through a variational inference process that accounts for task-specific uncertainties. By learning a distribution over metric scaling factors rather than point estimates, VMS enables more robust few-shot learning across diverse task distributions. We formulate this as a hierarchical Bayesian model where metric scaling parameters are inferred conditionally on task contexts. Our method introduces minimal computational overhead while providing significant performance improvements when integrated with popular metric-based meta-learning approaches such as Prototypical Networks and Relation Networks. Extensive experiments on benchmark few-shot classification datasets including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and CUB demonstrate that VMS consistently outperforms baseline methods, with particularly notable improvements in the challenging 1-shot and 5-shot settings. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis connecting our approach to uncertainty estimation in meta-learning, offering insights into why adaptive metric scaling enhances generalization to novel tasks.

Probabilistic Dual Network Architecture Search on Graphs

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning on graph-structured data, but their effectiveness is highly dependent on architectural design choices. In this paper, we propose Probabilistic Dual Network Architecture Search (PDNAS), a novel framework for automatically discovering optimal GNN architectures. Our approach uniquely employs a dual-network strategy that simultaneously optimizes both the macro-level structure (layer connectivity patterns) and micro-level operations (specific graph convolution types) through a probabilistic search space. PDNAS leverages a differentiable architecture search methodology enhanced with a probabilistic sampling mechanism that enables more efficient exploration of the vast design space while maintaining search stability. We introduce a resource-aware regularization term that balances model performance with computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on diverse graph benchmarks, including citation networks, molecular graphs, and social networks, demonstrate that PDNAS consistently outperforms hand-crafted GNN architectures and existing search methods. Our automatically discovered architectures achieve state-of-the-art performance while requiring fewer parameters and less computational overhead, showing particular strength in handling heterogeneous and large-scale graph data. The probabilistic nature of our approach also provides valuable insights into the importance of different architectural components for various graph learning tasks.

Weakly Supervised Relative Spatial Reasoning for Visual Question Answering

This paper addresses the challenge of relative spatial reasoning in Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems, which often struggle with accurately determining spatial relationships between objects in images. We propose a novel weakly supervised learning approach that enables VQA models to better understand and reason about spatial configurations without requiring explicit spatial relationship annotations. Our framework leverages natural language supervision from question-answer pairs to implicitly learn spatial concepts through attention mechanisms that focus on relative object positions. By introducing a spatial relation module that decomposes questions into object references and spatial predicates, our model can effectively capture positional relationships while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on spatial reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms previous methods on spatial questions, improving accuracy by 8.7% on spatial relation queries while maintaining strong performance on non-spatial questions. Qualitative analysis reveals that our model develops meaningful spatial representations despite the absence of explicit spatial supervision. This work highlights the potential of weakly supervised approaches to address specialized reasoning capabilities in multimodal AI systems.

On the Sample Complexity of Learning with Geometric Stability

This paper investigates the fundamental relationship between geometric stability properties of learning algorithms and their sample complexity requirements. We introduce a novel theoretical framework that characterizes learning algorithms through their geometric stability—a measure of how perturbations in the input space affect the geometry of the solution space. Our analysis establishes tight bounds on the sample complexity of geometrically stable learning algorithms across various learning settings, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning paradigms. We prove that algorithms exhibiting stronger geometric stability properties require fewer samples to achieve a target generalization error, establishing a formal trade-off between stability and sample efficiency. Through careful analysis of common learning algorithms, we identify previously unrecognized geometric stability properties that explain their empirical sample efficiency. Our theoretical results are complemented by experimental validation across synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that our bounds accurately predict the sample complexity behavior of various learning methods. These findings provide new insights for designing sample-efficient learning algorithms by explicitly optimizing for geometric stability properties.

Aesthetic Attributes Assessment of Images

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for evaluating and quantifying the aesthetic attributes of images. We propose a multi-dimensional approach that combines traditional computational aesthetics with deep learning techniques to assess various visual elements that contribute to aesthetic quality. Our model analyzes both low-level features (color harmony, composition, contrast) and high-level semantic attributes (emotional evocation, narrative quality, creative intent) to provide a holistic assessment of image aesthetics. Through experiments on diverse image datasets including artistic photography, consumer images, and professional compositions, we demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, with a 17% improvement in aesthetic quality prediction accuracy. Additionally, we introduce a novel attribute-specific feedback mechanism that provides interpretable assessments, enabling practical applications in photography education, content curation, and automated image enhancement. Our work bridges the gap between subjective human perception of aesthetics and computational assessment, offering insights into the complex nature of visual appeal and artistic quality in digital imagery.

Privacy-preserving Q-Learning with Functional Noise in Continuous State Spaces

This paper introduces a novel privacy-preserving approach for Q-learning in continuous state spaces that maintains utility while providing formal privacy guarantees. We develop a functional noise mechanism that directly perturbs the Q-function representation rather than discretizing the state space or adding noise to individual data points. Our method extends differential privacy concepts to functional spaces, allowing for privacy preservation across the entire continuous domain. We prove that our approach satisfies ε-differential privacy while demonstrating how the functional noise adapts to the underlying structure of the state space. Theoretical analysis establishes convergence bounds that characterize the privacy-utility tradeoff in terms of sample complexity and approximation error. Empirical evaluations on benchmark continuous control tasks show that our method significantly outperforms existing privacy-preserving reinforcement learning approaches, achieving near-optimal policies with minimal performance degradation even under strong privacy constraints. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of functional noise mechanisms for balancing privacy and learning performance in continuous reinforcement learning settings.

Near-Optimal Data Source Selection for Bayesian Learning

This paper addresses the challenge of selecting optimal data sources for Bayesian learning in resource-constrained environments. We propose a novel framework that efficiently identifies near-optimal subsets of available data sources while balancing statistical utility and acquisition costs. Our approach leverages information-theoretic measures to quantify the expected information gain from potential data sources and formulates the selection problem as a submodular optimization task with budget constraints. Through theoretical analysis, we establish performance guarantees showing that our greedy selection algorithm achieves a (1-1/e)-approximation of the optimal solution. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, reducing prediction error by up to 35% while maintaining the same data acquisition budget. Furthermore, we provide insights into the trade-offs between model accuracy, computational complexity, and data diversity. This work has significant implications for applications in active learning, experimental design, and distributed sensing networks where judicious selection of information sources is critical for effective Bayesian inference.

The Role of Ego Vision in View-Invariant Action Recognition

Action recognition systems have traditionally struggled with view variance, where the same action appears drastically different when observed from different perspectives. This paper explores how egocentric (first-person) vision can contribute to developing more robust view-invariant action recognition models. We propose that ego vision provides unique advantages for understanding human actions by capturing consistent visual patterns of interactions with objects and the environment, regardless of external viewing angles. Through extensive experiments on multi-view datasets, we demonstrate that incorporating egocentric data during training significantly improves recognition performance across novel viewpoints. Our approach leverages a dual-stream architecture that fuses ego-view representations with traditional third-person observations, enabling the model to extract view-invariant action features. Results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing viewpoint-related errors by 37% compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark dataset containing paired ego and multi-view recordings of complex human activities. This work highlights the potential of egocentric vision as a powerful tool for addressing the persistent challenge of view invariance in action recognition systems.

PointPillars: Fast Encoders for Object Detection from Point Clouds

Object detection in 3D point clouds is a critical component for autonomous driving systems, but existing methods often struggle to balance accuracy and computational efficiency. In this paper, we present PointPillars, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that enables fast and accurate 3D object detection from LiDAR point cloud data. Our approach simplifies the point cloud representation by organizing points into vertical columns (pillars), which eliminates the need for complex 3D convolutions. The PointPillars encoder efficiently transforms a point cloud into a sparse pseudo-image, allowing the detection network to leverage highly optimized 2D convolutional neural networks. Through extensive evaluation on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets, we demonstrate that PointPillars achieves competitive accuracy while operating at 62 Hz on a GPU—significantly faster than previous state-of-the-art methods. Our architecture detects cars, pedestrians, and cyclists with high precision and requires minimal customization across different datasets. The combination of high performance and real-time inference makes PointPillars particularly suitable for autonomous driving applications where both speed and accuracy are crucial requirements.

An End-to-End Attack on Text-based CAPTCHAs Based on Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Network

This paper presents a novel end-to-end approach for breaking text-based CAPTCHAs using Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Networks (CycleGANs). Despite the widespread deployment of text-based CAPTCHAs as a security mechanism to distinguish humans from bots, their vulnerability to automated attacks remains a significant concern. Our method leverages CycleGANs to overcome the traditional limitations of CAPTCHA-breaking systems that rely on segmentation followed by recognition. By formulating CAPTCHA-breaking as an image-to-text translation problem, our approach eliminates the need for character segmentation, which has historically been a challenging bottleneck in attacking modern CAPTCHAs with distorted characters and complex backgrounds. The proposed framework generates synthetic training data and learns mappings between distorted CAPTCHA images and their corresponding text representations through unpaired training samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves remarkable success rates of 87.3%, 92.4%, and 89.6% on three popular CAPTCHA schemes with minimal training data requirements. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates robust generalization capabilities against various defensive distortion techniques. This research highlights critical security implications for current text-based CAPTCHA designs and suggests the need for more sophisticated human verification mechanisms in online systems.

Automatic sampling and training method for wood-leaf classification based on tree terrestrial point cloud

This study presents a novel automatic sampling and training methodology for wood-leaf classification in terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) point clouds of trees. While accurate separation of woody and leafy components in tree point clouds is essential for various forestry applications, traditional methods often require labor-intensive manual sampling and feature engineering. Our approach leverages deep learning to automate both the sampling and classification processes. We developed an unsupervised pre-sampling algorithm that extracts representative points from distinct tree components based on geometric and radiometric properties, significantly reducing human intervention. These automatically labeled samples train a multi-scale feature extraction network that captures both local and contextual information from the point cloud data. Experiments conducted on diverse tree species across multiple forest environments demonstrate that our method achieves classification accuracy of 92.8%, outperforming traditional machine learning approaches by 7-12%. The method shows particular robustness to variations in point density and occlusion effects common in forest environments. This automated workflow substantially reduces processing time while maintaining high classification accuracy, making it suitable for large-scale forest inventory applications and detailed tree structure analysis.

Progressive Network Grafting for Few-Shot Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as an effective technique for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to more compact student networks. However, traditional KD approaches often require extensive training data, limiting their applicability in few-shot scenarios where labeled data is scarce. In this paper, we propose Progressive Network Grafting (PNG), a novel framework that enables effective knowledge distillation under few-shot constraints. Our approach incrementally transfers knowledge from teacher to student by "grafting" structural components across networks in a progressive manner. PNG operates in three phases: (1) identifying critical knowledge pathways in the teacher network, (2) adaptively constructing compatible student network components, and (3) progressively integrating these components while fine-tuning with limited data. Experimental results across multiple vision and language tasks demonstrate that PNG significantly outperforms existing few-shot distillation methods, achieving up to 87% of the teacher's performance using only 1-5% of the original training data. Furthermore, our ablation studies reveal that the progressive nature of our grafting process is crucial for effective knowledge transfer in data-constrained environments. The proposed PNG framework provides a promising direction for deploying high-performance models in resource-limited settings where data scarcity is a primary concern.

GraphMix: Improved Training of GNNs for Semi-Supervised Learning

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful models for semi-supervised node classification on graph-structured data. However, these models often suffer from overfitting and limited generalization capability when labeled data is scarce. In this paper, we introduce GraphMix, a regularization technique that enhances the training of GNNs for semi-supervised learning tasks. GraphMix extends the MixUp framework to graph-structured data by performing convex combinations of both node features and their corresponding labels during training. Our approach creates virtual training samples that encourage linear behavior between training examples, thereby improving model generalization. We further augment GraphMix with a consistency regularization term that ensures predictions remain consistent for the same node under different augmentation strategies. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed demonstrate that GraphMix consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN models, achieving 2-4% higher accuracy while requiring fewer labeled examples. Additionally, GraphMix exhibits improved robustness against adversarial attacks and noisy features. Our method is model-agnostic and can be easily integrated with various GNN architectures, making it a versatile solution for enhancing semi-supervised learning on graphs.

Globally Optimal Registration of Noisy Point Clouds

Point cloud registration is a fundamental problem in computer vision, robotics, and medical imaging. While iterative closest point (ICP) and its variants remain popular, they are susceptible to local minima, particularly when dealing with noisy data. This paper presents a novel approach for globally optimal registration of noisy point clouds that guarantees convergence to the global minimum regardless of initialization. Our method formulates registration as a convex relaxation problem with branch-and-bound optimization, effectively handling noise through a robust error model that adaptively estimates noise characteristics. We introduce a hierarchical search strategy that dramatically reduces computational complexity while maintaining optimality guarantees. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, especially in challenging scenarios with high noise levels, partial overlaps, and outliers. Performance evaluation shows our algorithm achieves global optimality with practical runtime efficiency, making it suitable for applications requiring precise alignment under adverse conditions.
